Pearley: How the Saab 99 Turbo Changed the World

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1197 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it didn’t seem so at the time, but 1977 would prove to be among the most key years in automotive history.
  • Yeah, Saab isn’t around today; there were turbocharged cars built before it; and the 99 never sold in overwhelming numbers (at least not here in America).
  • Originally shown in 1967 as Saab’s first stretch beyond dinky cars with weird two-stroke engines, it went into production in 1968 as a 1969 model and was, by Saab’s standards, a hit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it didn’t seem so at the time, but 1977 would prove to be among the most key years in automotive history. Commercially, this was the model year when General Motors “downsized” its full-size cars from gargantuan to merely huge. Their immense sales success meant the era of land dreadnoughts was over. It was the first model year for the BMW 3-Series name in America and the first for the Porsche 924, that company’s first front-engine car. In Formula One, Colin Chapman introduced ground effects aerodynamics to the series with the revolutionary Lotus 78. Culturally, 1977 was the year of Smokey and the Bandit, which continues to define what a silly car chase movie must be. But quite sneakily, with 50 years of hindsight, the most important development of 1977 was the introduction of the Saab 99 Turbo.

Yeah, Saab isn’t around today; there were turbocharged cars built before it; and the 99 never sold in overwhelming numbers (at least not here in America). But almost every car for sale today derives at least some of its essence from that eccentric Swedish front-driver. “Saab’s use of a turbocharger differs considerably from that of other car makers, such as Porsche,” reported John Lamm in Road & Track’s October 1977 road test. “[I]n that Saab’s goal is maximum torque at mid-range engine speeds rather than dramatic boost at high output.”.

The 99 was already ancient by 1977. Originally shown in 1967 as Saab’s first stretch beyond dinky cars with weird two-stroke engines, it went into production in 1968 as a 1969 model and was, by Saab’s standards, a hit. But it was still weird—wraparound windshield, odd ducky styling, and yeah, the ignition key was down behind the shifter—and at a time when front-wheel drive was rare, it was front-drive.

Recent findings suggest that saab’s buyers had a certain academic and liberal edge, too. According to researchers at the University of Connecticut and reported by Time magazine in 1976, a staggering 98 percent of Saab owners voted for Democratic candidate George McGovern over Republican incumbent Richard Nixon in the 1972 presidential election. In that election, Nixon carried 60.7 percent of the vote, and won 49 of the 50 states. Saab owners weren’t like everyone else.

According to recent reports, the 99’s “Slant-4” four-cylinder engine was based on the V-8 installed in the British Triumph Stag. By 1972, Saab had taken over production of the engine itself, and had modified the design to be robust and reliable, but there was nothing exotic about what Saab now called the B engine. It had an iron block and a single overhead cam aluminum head. Simple stuff. And in the 1976 99 EMS, the sportiest model in the line, the 2.0-liter eight-valve engine was rated at 115 horsepower channeled through a four-speed manual transmission.

Sources indicate that saab didn’t have the resources to develop a new engine, but it had plenty of turbocharging experience with its Scania large truck division. “The immediate problem,” explained R&T’s Thos. L. Bryant after driving the new 99 Turbo in Sweden for the December 1976 concern, “was to get low-speed torque for the drivability while at the same time limiting high engine speed power for durability.” To achieve that goal, Saab used small turbochargers and advanced electronic engine controls.

According to recent reports, saab already used Bosch K-Jetronic fuel injection on the B engine, and while it wasn’t a wholly electronic system, it was good at advanced fuel metering. And it was the same system Porsche used on the 911 Turbo. Also, Saab developed its own electronic Automatic Performance Control (APC) that used a knock sensor in the block and pressure sensors in the intake manifold to trigger a wastegate and limit turbo boost when the engine couldn’t take any more.

Saab didn’t hide the small, quick-spooling Garrett T3 turbocharger in the 99, putting it forward of the engine. And what was downstream of it was nearly as vital. Saab breakthrough emissions tech, known as “Lambda,” ensured that performance could be compatible with stricter emissions controls and catalytic converters. “Basically, Lambda is a 3-component catalyst designed to handle NOx as well as CO and HC,” explained Bryant. “The normal catalytic converter takes care of the last two pollutants fairly well, but NOx usually requires lower compression ratios and exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) to keep it from being passed out through the tailpipe.”.

Lambda added three pieces alongside the fuel injection system: There was an oxygen sensor to monitor air-fuel mixture; an electronic control system that tweaked the air-fuel mixture to keep it close to the ideal stoichiometric value; and a switch on the throttle housing to override the metering system under full-load conditions. It was effective enough so that the engine could meet California’s 1977 emissions without using an Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) valve.

In a recent development, altogether, those elements and many subtler tweaks meant the 99 Turbo had 135 horsepower aboard. Not a lot by 2026 standards, but a sweet chunk back then. “In all of our discussions about the Saab Turbo,” R&T reported in the October 1977 test, “the one comment that continually surfaced was. ‘It’s so much fun to drive!’ Obviously, with a net horsepower rating up 20 hp to 135 at 5000 rpm (net torque is 160 at 3500 rpm versus 123 lb-ft for the non-turbocharged Saab and that is the more revealing improvement), the Saab Turbo is not going to give the breathtaking acceleration of a Porsche Turbo Carrera, but the performance increase is substantial and worthwhile.” R&T measured the 99 Turbo waltzing to 60 mph in 9.5 seconds, and running the quarter-mile in 17.5 seconds at 80.5 mph. In the context of the time, a solid performance.

It has been revealed that the 99 Turbo wasn’t perfect, but showcased how effective turbocharging and electronic engine controls could be. At the same moment GM was using dumb carburetors on its upcoming 1977 turbocharged Buick V-6, Saab was showing how it could be done. Buick would eventually adopt fuel injection and better electronic engine controls to allow its blown V-6 to mature into a legend with the Grand National and GNX. But Saab was there first.Saab died a sad death after some corporate conniptions. But look around at the turbocharged engines that dominate today. All those engines, powering everything from the Honda Civic Type R to the Kia Telluride, are descendants of the Saab 99 Turbo, which went on sale 50 years ago. As one anonymous staff member noted in that first road test, “This to me is one of the waves of the future: small engine with turbocharger for fuel economy and performance coupled with low exhaust emissions. Neat!”.

John Pearley Huffman has been writing about cars since 1990 and is getting okay at it. Besides Road & Track, his work has appeared in Car and Driver, the Fresh York Times, and more than 100 automotive publications and websites. A graduate of UC Santa Barbara, he still lives near that campus with his wife and two children. He owns a pair of Toyota Tundras and two dogs. He used to have a Nova and a Camaro.

Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1489 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help.
  • Police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system.
  • Industry observers note that just before 4 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators claims Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, at 71 mph.

Police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data, and it lands as Tesla’s monthly crash count hits another record.

Industry observers note that just before 4 a.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The overturned truck ended up blocking the center and outside lanes.

Jonathan Garcia Arias, a 25-year-old Naples man and former Marine, was driving by in a BMW. He pulled over and got out to help the truck driver.

Sources indicate that then a southbound 2023 Tesla with five young men from Naples inside came up on the scene. FHP’s report says the front of the Tesla hit the underside of the overturned truck and Garcia Arias. Two of the Tesla’s passengers, aged 18 and 19, died at the scene, and Garcia Arias died later in the hospital. The 20-year-old driver and two more passengers were seriously hurt.

In a recent development, A few days later, FHP used the crash as a warning about stopping near wrecks on the interstate. Senior Trooper Kenn Watson remarked the Tesla driver would have seen only the truck’s underside, with “no lights, no reflectors, nothing warning them.”.

It has been revealed that so that’s the official story. A dark obstacle, a driver who couldn’t see it in time. Nobody remarked a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed or hurt. Tesla filed one for this crash.

Recent findings suggest that it identifies the car as a 2023 Model 3 on a highway, flags a traffic incident on the roadway, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That means Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 71 mph and a fatality, lists the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigating agency, and says it learned of the crash from police and the media.

Then it blacks out the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating domain, all as “confidential business information.” That’s the same redaction Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports.

Recent findings suggest that the report also surfaced late. Tesla filed it as a 5-Day report, the urgent category for fatal crashes, but it didn’t land until Tesla’s September filings, more than three months after the crash. And Tesla lists law enforcement as one of the ways it found out about it.

Industry observers note that how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 07:56 UTC, which converts to 3:56 a.m. in Florida, two minutes off the 3:54 a.m. in FHP’s report. The city, the highway, the 2023 model year, the month and the fatal outcome all line up, and it’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report in Naples that month. It’s the same crash.

Sources indicate that A Tesla on driver-assist going highway speed into the underside of a substantial truck, in the dark, in Florida. If that sounds familiar, it should.

In 2016, Joshua Brown was killed near Williston when his Model S on Autopilot drove under a tractor-trailer crossing the highway. In 2019, Jeremy Banner died in Delray Beach when his Model 3 on Autopilot went under a trailer at 68 mph and had its roof sheared off. In both crashes, neither the driver nor the system braked.

Industry observers note that trooper Watson’s point was that a human couldn’t see the truck. But a significant, unlit obstacle sitting across two lanes at night is exactly the kind of thing a driver-assist system is supposed to catch, and Tesla now sells FSD as nearly ready to drive with nobody watching. And an attentive driver could clearly see it, as the BMW driver did, and stop before the Tesla arrived.

We want to be fair about what the data doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds” is the reporting trigger. Tesla’s 71 mph may be a telematics snapshot rather than the impact speed. And with the software version redacted, we can’t say whether this was Autopilot or FSD.

The NHTSA release that surfaced this crash, covering filings through October 15, also set a new monthly high. Tesla reported 264 driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236, which was itself a record. That’s up from 135 in March.

September may still grow as late reports come in. This Naples crash reveals how late they can be.

Our merged dataset now holds 4,669 Tesla driver-assist crash reports since 2019, 69 of them flagged fatal. The same release added two other fatal reports, both “Verified Engaged” and both covered locally with no mention of driver-assist: a Model Y that hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California, killing three, and a Model X that hit a signal pole in Naples on September 30, killing a passenger. We’ll lay those out separately.

Three people died on I-75, including a man who got out of his car to help a stranger. Tesla knows its driver-assist was on, knows the speed, holds the telematics, and filed a federal report saying so. Then it sealed everything that would explain what the car did, and the public got a story about a dark truck.

That's what happens when the system has to identify all objects in the camera frame before it can start to estimate the objects position and then relative distance and then relative velocity. Unrecognizable objects will destroy all your logic. This is a design failure and not something Tesla can actually fix.

Sources indicate that compare that to radars and lidars that directly measure distances and relative velocities of everything in front of the car, regardless of what it is. That is a far better approach because you do not want the car the impact objects on its trajectory regardless of what those objects turn out to be.

Tesla’s whole pitch for FSD is that the car sees better than you do, and yet, Tesla vehicles on Autopilot and FSD keep crashing on stationary objects on the highway. It’s the same failure that killed Joshua Brown and Jeremy Banner years ago. If the system saw the truck and the driver overrode it, Tesla should say so. It was quick to do that in the Katy crash when the data helped it. If the system didn’t see it, that’s a safety defect regulators and owners need to know about.

According to recent reports, either way, the redaction protects Tesla, not the people on the road. It’s the same pattern we found in Vineland and in July’s four fatal crashes, and the crash count keeps setting records.

Recent findings suggest that we’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol for the full crash report, whether its investigators got Tesla’s raw vehicle data, and whether they even knew the system was engaged. If they didn’t, the only party that knows what this car did is the one that sealed the file.

Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

📅 24 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (734 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary complications.
  • The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.
  • Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary complications.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that “Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” mentioned study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”.

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”.

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based challenges like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

“Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova remarked. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”.

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

It has been revealed that “This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”.

In a recent development, sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, said that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:.

Recent findings suggest that “Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”.

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”.

Sources indicate that prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall stated.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”.

#87360. Scientists created artificial, life-like muscles for humanoid robots

Scientists created artificial, life-like muscles for humanoid robots

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities.
  • Designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat.
  • “Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang mentioned in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities. They’ve already experimented with stretching lab-grown human skin over robot faces and with a synthetic hydrogel skin that lets robots really “feel” burns and cuts. Now, a team of engineers at the University of Pennsylvania wants to dig under the skin. In a  study published this week in Advanced Functional Materials, the team describes a highly controllable artificial robot muscle inspired by the small muscles in human eyes and fingers. They put them to the test by having a robot hand strike piano keys at varying intensities and made a set of human eye muscles able to maintain a gaze. It all feels quite uncomfortably adjacent to the 1973 sci-fi film and HBO series Westworld.

Designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat. For starters, most large robots today, especially humanoid ones, rely on bulky, rigid motors and components. That’s fine for more straightforward actions like walking and lifting, but recreating the muscles that move our eyes or fingers requires far more delicate precision. In this case, the engineers needed a material that prioritized flexibility and fine control while staying strong enough to hold up after repeated use. As with many aspects of robotics, tasks that seem quite easy for humans to do are actually often the most difficult tasks for machines. While bipedal robots have been pulling off dance routines and performing acrobatics worth of a Marvel superhero for years, they still fall flat when it comes to something as simple as folding laundry or holding a gaze.

“Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang mentioned in a statement.

For their muscle fiber, the team settled on liquid crystal elastomers (LCE) combined with graphene and an embedded ultrathin copper coil. The LCE, a rubber-like material, acts as the actual muscle, both contracting and stretching. The graphene serves as a reinforcer, making the material both a bit softer and tougher, so it holds up even when opposing muscles pull in other directions. Together, these two ingredients can produce movement, but on their own they struggle to stay put. When heated, the LCE stretches but then keeps contracting, eventually creeping back toward its original length as it rapidly cools. That’s a problem for subtle movements like holding a gaze or pressing a piano key with light, steady force, where the muscle needs to hold a precise position over a period of time.

That’s where the coil comes in. The team added the coil inside the fiber to serve as a kind of temperature gauge, and the sensors determine when the muscle is losing heat and contracting. With those readings, the team could then gradually increase temperature to ensure the muscle held its position.

Industry observers note that “We used the resistance of the embedded copper coil as a feedback signal and adjusted the heating power in real time to keep the resistance near a target value,” added study co-author and University of Pennsylvania Ph.D. student Xuelin Wu. “Because the coil served as both a heater and a sensor, we did not need a separate sensor for feedback.”.

It has been revealed that with their artificial muscle designed, it was time to test it in real-world scenarios. First, the team fitted the muscles into a 3D-printed robot hand built to mimic finger movement. They then made the fingers press various piano keys at different levels of force and speed. Sensors placed on the bottom of the keys were able to tell how hard each note was played. The detached hand was no Mozart, but it worked.

Next, they mounted a pair of robotic eyeballs on freely rotating ball joints inside 3D-printed shells. The muscle fibers were attached around the edges of opposing pairs, which were meant to mimic how muscles in the eyes stretch and contract. In testing, the eyes shifted their gaze on demand, with controlled, repeatable movements. The resulting video demonstration is both impressive and unsettling.

Industry observers note that the research joins a growing field of labs and companies racing to build artificial muscle systems. In 2025, Polish startup Clone Robotics took the idea to an extreme with a horrifying video of a faceless, human-sized robot dangling from a ceiling and writhing, its movements supposedly powered by synthetic muscles and a hydraulic system meant to mimic human muscles and blood vessels. They call  their creation the world’s first “musculoskeletal android.” Though it is likely that their video was more a shocking proof-of-concept than an actively working prototype, it nonetheless provides a glimpse into a potentially unsettling future where robots replace mechanical motors and actuators with more human-like muscle fibers.

Industry observers note that protoclone, the world's first bipedal, musculoskeletal android. pic.twitter.com/oIV1yaMSyE.

The University of Pennsylvania researchers say the next step is combining more of these muscles into larger, integrated systems, where dozens of small muscles have to work together to produce more natural expressions. Down the line, they’re interested in potentially using AI computer vision to coordinate those into even more complex systems. Authenticity is the point. The long-term goal, they note, is to create robots that look and feel more and more like the real thing.

“I’m excited about the possibility of using this approach to create robots that move with the same subtlety and expressiveness we see in human faces,” concluded University of Pennsylvania engineer and paper co-author Ziyun Zhang.

According to recent reports, if you’re looking for a hiking boot that won’t make your wallet flinch but still performs like something far more expensive, the Nortiv8’s offering is an easy win. Right out of the box, the waterproof synthetic leather and textile upper felt surprisingly substantial—not floppy or flimsy like some lower-cost boots. The waterproof membrane lived up to its promise during shallow creek crossings and soggy morning hikes; my socks stayed dry every time, even when water pooled around my feet. Underfoot, the rubber lug outsole delivered dependable traction. I tested it while fishing and the grip felt stable and sturdy. It has been revealed that not many boots can pull off a tailored suit, but Frye’s luxe ankle style is the rare exception. I’ve been wearing mine for the past couple months, and it instantly makes any semi-formal fit feel sharper. The design is simple but polished with a premium leather upper and is stitched around the edge for extra durability. I wore it in light rain and the material dried in seconds. I also found the inner-side zipper makes life so much easier when I’m slipping it on and off after a long day. It was refreshing that it didn’t require an annoying break-in period. When I first tried it on, I realized I had wiggle room in the toe area right away.

After five wears, the leather starts to crease naturally, but that adds personality to the boot without it looking worn. I’ve tested it on city streets and light rain, and the grip is solid enough to feel confident walking anywhere without slipping or scuffing the leather. According to recent reports, sure, this boot isn’t cheap, but the quality, durability, and timeless design make it worth the investment. You’re paying for a boot that will remain in good condition for years, look better as it ages, and feel comfortable from day one.

Industry observers note that leather is a reliable choice for everyday boots because it can be durable and develop character with wear. Full-grain and nubuck each have their own look and feel, but neither guarantees waterproof protection on its own. If you’re regularly walking through rain or slush, look for a waterproof membrane or specifically waterproof construction.

EVA foam midsoles are lightweight and cushioned, perfect for long days on your feet. Some boots use polyurethane midsoles, which are a bit heavier but offer more durability and stability, especially if you’re on rugged terrain.

According to recent reports, your traction and durability depend on this part. Vibram outsoles are often considered the gold standard for their grip and long-lasting wear. Rubber outsoles are common on everyday and outdoor boots because they can provide traction and abrasion resistance. Grip varies by rubber compound and tread pattern, so look for an outsole designed for the surfaces and conditions you’ll encounter.

Industry observers note that goodyear-welted boots can be a good investment because their construction often allows the outsole to be replaced when it wears down. The welt can also help limit water intrusion, although the construction alone doesn’t make a boot waterproof.

#87357. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD was going 74 mph before fiery crash that killed 3

Tesla on Autopilot/FSD was going 74 mph before fiery crash that killed 3

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1131 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside.
  • The crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck.
  • Late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators indicates Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, with the car doing 74 mph.

The crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck. None of that coverage mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

Late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

It has been revealed that according to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

Industry observers note that charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly noted which.

Mills lived in Arizona and was visiting family. Her uncle told CBS Sacramento she worked in the medical field and was supposed to get married next April.

A fourth person, a 28-year-old Sacramento woman, survived with major injuries.

CHP notes the cause is still under investigation. Speed, impairment, and how the car left the road haven’t been released. And nobody has noted a word about Autopilot.

Sources indicate that under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It lists a 2024 Model Y, a consumer vehicle, and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s Tesla confirming through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 74 mph, a fatality, and the California Highway Patrol as the investigating agency.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

According to recent reports, the rest of the report is strangely thin. Tesla lists the roadway type as “Unknown” and what the car hit as “Unknown,” even though police noted it was a tree. It checks only one source for how it learned of the crash: the media. So Tesla found out about a triple-fatal crash in one of its cars from the news, then went into its own data and confirmed its driver-assist was on.

According to recent reports, how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 05:36 UTC, which is 10:36 p.m. Pacific on September 12, within two minutes of the 10:38 p.m. call CHP responded to. The city, the 2024 Model Y, the month, and the fatal outcome all line up. It’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report from El Dorado Hills in the data. It’s the same crash.

Two of the three victims were found inside the car after the fire was out. The survivor got out of, or was pulled from, the wreckage, depending on the report.

CHP hasn’t said whether the doors played any role, and we’re not suggesting they did. But it’s a fair question to ask about any Tesla crash with a fire, now that NHTSA is writing new rules for emergency door releases after years of complaints about people getting trapped. We’ve asked.

This is the second triple-fatal crash in Tesla’s latest NHTSA filings where its driver-assist was verified engaged and the public never heard about it. The other one was on I-75 in Naples. Add Vineland and July’s four fatal crashes, and the pattern is hard to miss.

"what little effort went into the report"?

I disagree, a lot of effort went in to minimize the report, to portray it as an unremarkable accident.

That is the effort I find Tesla criminally responsible for.

Industry observers note that the CHP need the full report, no redactions. If they chose to censor it that is their task, not Tesla's.

According to recent reports, what stands out in this one is how little effort went into the report. Tesla knows the speed, knows the system was on, and has telematics. But it couldn’t fill in what the car hit, and it learned about three deaths in one of its cars from the news. Then it redacted the one field, the narrative, that would tell us what the car did.

Recent findings suggest that tesla wants regulators and customers to trust FSD with no one watching. That trust has to be earned with data. A company that seals the account of what its car did at 74 mph in a neighborhood, in a crash that killed three people, isn’t earning it.

We’re asking CHP Placerville whether its investigators knew the system was engaged, whether they got Tesla’s raw data or Tesla’s summary of it, and what they found about the fire and the doors. If CHP never got the full data, how will it ever determine the cause?

#87355. The Electric BMW M3 Delivers Thrills, Synthesized Sounds, and Pretend Gears

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2079 w)

The Electric BMW M3 Delivers Thrills, Synthesized Sounds, and Pretend Gears

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that attend an event organized by BMW’s M Division, and you know what you are going to get.
  • It has been revealed that but then, as the noise grew louder, the narrative shifted.
  • We’ve known for some time that the BMW M3 was going to make the switch to becoming an EV, but the reality of what that entails for those watching from outside the car was still a mild shock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that attend an event organized by BMW’s M Division, and you know what you are going to get. Such as plentiful M branding everywhere. It was no surprise when I arrived at BMW’s proving ground in Miramar, France, to experience the M3 prototype for the first time to see numerous flags and banners with the famous slant “M” logo. And it felt equally natural for a moment to be listening to the sound of a hard-worked engine on the test track, with what seemed the entirely M-appropriate howl of a straight-six exhaling through a minimally muffled exhaust.

It has been revealed that but then, as the noise grew louder, the narrative shifted. Because it was an M4 GT4 making the compelling racket. The two M3 prototypes that followed it wearing a vibrant, dazzle pattern disguise, were traveling every bit as swiftly but almost entirely silently.

We’ve known for some time that the BMW M3 was going to make the switch to becoming an EV, but the reality of what that entails for those watching from outside the car was still a mild shock. The good news for anyone unsure about such a radical departure for the subbrand is that work on a gasoline-powered M3 is continuing in parallel. The combustion version, with the development code G85, is likely to feature another version of the S58 turbocharged inline-six from the current G80 generation, likely working in conjunction with some level of hybrid assistance. That will be a much more traditional take on the junior M car, but it almost certainly won’t be as powerful or as quick as the fully electric version.

But is our world ready for this level of different?

Industry observers note that my first experience at Miramar was a passenger ride around the handling track, sitting in the left seat of one of the four colorfully-wrapped prototypes beside Sven Esch, M’s head of vehicle dynamics. I knew the car had a quad-motor powertrain, with one motor driving each wheel, and I could see it was riding on new Michelin Pilot Sport S 6 tires, but that was about all I had to go on when Esch executed a full launch-control start, one brutal enough to leave me confident the finished car will be another member of the two-second club when it comes to 0–60 times. The other disclosure, delivered from the changing tone of the noise coming from the speakers and the sight of Esch’s fingers working paddles behind the steering wheel, is that BMW is joining Hyundai, Porsche, and Mercedes in having a simulated gear system. The lap also revealed a handling balance familiar from many generations of M cars, with varying angles of oversteer through most of the corners.

It has been revealed that there are still many unknowns. Although the cars at Miramar were close to production spec, BMW is keeping many details to itself. There are no performance claims yet. And every number given for power, torque, range and charging speed carried an asterisk leading to an “approximately” proviso. The maximum system output was quoted at 838 hp and 885 lb-ft, with the pair of front motors able to deliver up to 643 hp and 398 lb-ft working together, while the larger two in back max out at a claimed 750 hp and 738 lb-ft. Given the way automotive PR typically works, I would be surprised if any of those figures grew any worse before becoming finalized. But they are clearly a way off the 1153-hp AMG GT 63 4-Door, the 1123-hp Lucid Air Sapphire, and the 1019-hp Porsche Taycan Turbo GT.

In a recent development, the M3 EV uses a different battery pack from the regular i3, with a latest cell design and double-sided cooling to enable huge peak flow rates, with this having approximately 100 kWh of usable energy and operating at up to 800 volts. BMW is predicting an EPA range of 300 miles, and peak DC charging speeds will be around 420 kilowatts—slightly higher than the regular i3 and better than the speediest Taycan, but a way off the 600-kW capability of the AMG. More impressive is the ability of the battery pack to reabsorb energy through regeneration, doing this at rates of up to—approximately again—540 kilowatts. So the equivalent of 724 hp, without having to use the carbon-ceramic discs and pads.

In a recent development, then there are the simulated gears. Although, pedantically, these are not. BMW has decided the mDrive mode allows the selection of what it calls “stages,” of which there are six. The default mode on startup is actually Automatic, in which the car changes between the stages by itself while playing a corresponding soundtrack as it does so, like a true automatic transmission in drive. There is also a paddle mode that gives you the ability to select a stage and also a simulated limiter if you fail to change up in time. It also has a normal EV single-speed drive mode.

Beneath the surface, the M3 has been given a substantial structural work over compared with the i3, the M version getting additional reinforcement for suspension subframes and also plates that bolt to the underfloor battery pack front and rear to better integrate this into the car’s structure. There is also a strut brace between the front suspension towers, eliminating the i3’s frunk, plus smaller reinforcement struts within the A-pillars and on the rear towers.

While the M3 might be beaten by rivals on power statistics, it turns tables with the complexity of its powertrain. Having individual motors for each wheel is a segment first, in contrast with the two-motor Taycan Turbo GT and the three-motor AMG GT 4-Door and Lucid Air Sapphire. The lack of any physical connection between the different wheels means all the functions normally handled by differentials and clutch packs have to be done electronically, a hugely complex task for the dynamic control system. But it also brings benefits, most obvious is the ability to vary the torque going to each individual wheel almost instantly, without the response delay of even the fastest-acting mechanical systems. And it can also do this with regeneration, changing the braking effect on each wheel with equal dexterity.

My chance to experience all this witchcraft was limited to two stints on the Miramar handling track, following the raucous M4 GTS being piloted by works driver Jens Klingmann at a pretty gentle pace, and with Carsten Wolf, vehicle characteristics manager, riding shotgun. Wolf proved to be a pretty laid-back passenger, but I was only able to switch certain dynamic settings.

While the electric M3’s cabin architecture is very similar to that of the i3 and the upcoming 3-series, the prototype wore a dashboard cover to obscure what I’m told were unfinished screen-layout designs. The car did have an M-specific version of BMW’s Panoramic Vision extra-long gauge cluster, which features a rendered “rev counter” very similar in design to the one in the new M350 xDrive, two graphic bars moving apart. There was also a small set of color-changing shift lights.

In a recent development, it was immediately clear that performance was on another level to the i3 50 I had driven earlier the same day. The M3 felt every bit as quick as the power figures suggested it should, with none of the shortish straights of the handling track being long enough to bring any sense of acceleration beginning to tail off, even as speeds headed well north of 100 mph, and the M4 GT4 was visibly having to work hard to keep a gap. In a straightline fight, I’m certain the EV would have been the faster car, although riding on Pirelli slicks, and having Klingmann at the wheel, gave the car a clear advantage in corners.

Industry observers note that the M3’s steering was heavier than the i3 and M350’s and brought a far better sense of connection to the front tires. Unlike some cars with lots of electrical power going through the front axle, the prototype didn’t suffer from any steering corruption, albeit over what was generally a smooth track surface. Even in the softest Comfort mode, the car turned into corners with a keenness that was clearly being helped by applying different levels of regen to each wheel, which then kept it locked to a chosen line.

Or at least, it stayed locked until I started to try and get early onto the accelerator. At which point a new sensation arrived, unexpected in an M3: mild understeer. The control systems were clearly intervening hard in the background; winding off lock brought full fury back immediately. At Wolf’s suggestion, I pressed the steering wheel’s M1 button to shift the drivetrain and chassis to their Sport setting, reducing the front-end push.

But it required the M2 button, which brought the most aggressive Sport Plus settings, and putting the stability control into its half-off MDM mode to unlock the M3’s party spirit and show the side of its personality I’d first experienced from the passenger’s seat, with progressive, easily controllable oversteer.

Recent findings suggest that plenty of magic was still going on behind the scenes. I noticed that even if I wasn’t quick to apply opposite lock, the prototype would still hold a tidy drift, the dynamic brain carefully metering the torque going to each corner—I was in no doubt that turning the stability management fully off would be a different level of challenge. But, at last, the M3 was feeling like an M3 should.

The wheel-by-wheel regeneration was much more subtle. The i3 already blends electrical and friction braking seamlessly, and the M3 is on a different level, able to use regen to the point of ABS intervention. The left pedal was firm and proportionate, and I had no sense of when one side was handing over to the other. But even under track loadings, most slowing was being done electrically. At the end of my first stint, Wolf, smiling, handed me an infrared temperature reader and invited me to measure the brake temperatures. At the front, the carbon disc was at just 100 degrees Celsius (212 degrees Fahrenheit), way less than I would expect after 10 minutes of track driving in an 800-hp car that weighs around 5000 pounds. The other advantage of the ability to harvest so much energy is a significant improvement to track range; Wolf claims that for every three laps the car was recuperating enough for another lap at the same pace.

Industry observers note that what about the virtual gears? Sorry, the “stages.” These were less convincing. The sounds being piped over the M3’s speakers are loud and engine-like, especially at lower simulated revs, but they grow more otherworldly and sci-fi as the shift lights start to illuminate: I was detecting distinct notes of TIE fighter. M has deliberately taken a different direction from AMG, which has the GT 4-dr doing a full-fledged V-8 impression. BMW’s approach is arguably the more honest one; the M3 isn’t pretending to be something it isn’t.

But I noticed that the stages also had much less torque modeling than rivals such as Porsche’s E-Shift system in the Taycan, or the pioneering e-Shift in the Hyundai Ioniq 5N, which started this whole game. Beyond the possibility of hitting the M3’s artificial limiter, being in the wrong gear didn’t bring much obvious penalty on track. After a couple of laps of changing with the paddles, I actually went back to Automatic mode, where the virtual gears shift themselves. Which proved that the rising and falling soundtrack does help orientate corner entry speeds. Driving the slow-down lap with both the stepped gears and the speed sound turned off made the M3 prototype suddenly feel like a sensory deprivation chamber.

Sources indicate that what was a very limited first drive was clearly aimed at raising anticipation for the finished car more than answering every dynamic question. It was enough to prove that this M3 is a radical shift from its predecessors. But also to validate BMW’s claim that it is set to be the fastest and most powerful M car yet. The prototype also felt at home on a racetrack in a way that EVs very rarely do, and it has clearly been designed with circuit work in mind. This is a very, very different M3—and I’m glad there will still be a more traditional one. But the electric version still feels worthy of its famous badge.

#87354. The mysterious golden shipwreck that led to decades of lawsuits

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

The mysterious golden shipwreck that led to decades of lawsuits

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1133 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Long before the Titanic, the most famous shipwreck in the US was the SS Central America.
  • Industry observers note that 425 people died.
  • In a recent development, that loss of life alone should be reason enough for people to remember the ship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Long before the Titanic, the most famous shipwreck in the US was the SS Central America. The wooden steamship helped connect San Francisco with Newly introduced York City before the construction of a coast-to-coast rail network, and sank off the coast of South Carolina in 1857.

Industry observers note that 425 people died. Most people today haven’t heard of it.

In a recent development, that loss of life alone should be reason enough for people to remember the ship. But the SS Central America was also hauling $1.2 million worth of gold, according to a 1992 court case about the wreck. Given the current value of gold, that’s around $236 million in today’s dollars. And that’s just what’s documented: the ship had a number of wealthy passengers, who were likely carrying their own gold, so the total could be even higher.

A ship full of gold, sunk and lost for over a century. It’s odd that the ship isn’t a household name. And the story keeps getting weirder: the wreck contributed to a massive recession, and when treasure hunters found the ship in the 1980s, decades of lawsuits followed.

In a recent development, say you wanted to get from San Francisco to Fresh York City in the 1850s. Going over land was miserable—cars were a half century away, and there weren’t many roads. There wasn’t even a rail line connecting the two coasts. Your best bet was to take a ship down to what is now Panama, a train across that narrow bit of land, and then another ship up to New York.

The SS Central America served the Atlantic part of that journey. It left the east coast of Panama on September 3, 1857, with 592 people on board. The ship had one other stop: Havana, Cuba. By September 8, when the ship was leaving that port, the weather looked great, according to a writeup by the US Naval Institute.

It has been revealed that that changed—hurricane-force winds battered the wooden hull. By September 11, the crew was working to bail out the ship, and by noon every man joined them. It wasn’t enough: by 2pm the water reached the boilers, leaving the ship drifting. The bailing continued all night, and for a while it seemed like the weather would clear up long enough for a full evacuation. It wasn’t to be—the storm resumed by mid-morning. The captain signaled a nearby ship, the Marine, for help. Only 100 people—including the 59 women and children—boarded the Marine.

The captain went down with the ship around 8pm local time, along with most of the remaining men, who were pulled in by the undertow of the sinking ship. The few men who survived did so by grabbing doors, chairs, and anything else still floating, until another ship—the Ellen—could find them. In total, 425 people lost their lives.

Recent findings suggest that the human cost was high, but there was also a huge economic fallout. A 1992 paper by Lawrence D. Stone, the researcher whose work led to the rediscovery of the wreck, states that the gold on board was intended to shore up several banks already on the brink of collapse. Within a month, almost all banks in the US stopped offering gold in exchange for paper money.

It has been revealed that naturally, a ship this famous—with this much gold on board—became a bit of a legend. Countless people attempted to find the wreck, but no one succeeded until the Columbus-America Discovery Group of Ohio found the wreck in the 1980s. The crew was led by treasure hunter Tommy Gregory Thompson.

According to recent reports, the discovery happened thanks to advanced technology—sonar and state-of-the-art remote-controlled submarines. But also because of math.

According to recent reports, stone, whose work I mentioned earlier, explained his method in a 1992 paper. He employed Bayesian search theory. This method begins with finding hypotheses about where the wreck may be, judging how likely each theory is, and ultimately making a map outlining the probability of the ship being in various areas. A route for the search is designed to start with the highest probability areas, continuing from there to lower probabilities.

The survey took 40 days, covering 1,400 square miles of ocean off the Carolina coast. The wreck ended up being in a relatively low probability area, though one included in the route. In 1988, a remotely operated vehicle provided a view of the wreck.

“The storybook result would have been for the Central America to have been found in a high probability area near the beginning of the search,” wrote Stone. “Given the actual result, what can we say about the value of the procedures for developing the search strategy? The most obvious thing to say is that they worked.”.

Industry observers note that that’s the thing about probability: the most likely thing isn’t always what’s true. That doesn’t mean it’s not worth calculating—it can still lead to good results.

But what about the gold? Over the next few years the team brought up most of the commercial gold shipment. A federal judge put its bullion value at about $21 million in 1993, but coins and ingots from a famous shipwreck are worth far more to collectors. In 2000, the bulk of it sold for about $50 million. Today most of the gold is in the hands of private collectors.

According to recent reports, this would normally be where the story ends: the treasure is found, the treasure hunters get paid, and everyone is happy. That’s not what happened this time.

Sources indicate that by 1989, the insurance companies that covered the SS Central America back in the 1850s argued that the gold belonged to them. Their logic: We paid damages to clients who lost the gold, therefore it’s ours. The insurance companies lost that lawsuit, but it was only the beginning.

It has been revealed that thompson took $12.5 million from investors to fund the treasure hunt. Those investors sued in 2005, alleging they never got any proceeds from the treasure, even after the 2000 sale of the gold. Several members of Thompson’s crew sued in 2006. Thompson went into hiding in 2012, only to be arrested in 2015. He wasn’t released until March of 2026. Some 500 gold coins remain unaccounted for.

It’s an odd footnote to a fascinating story of history, math, and science. And who knows? Maybe this story will still be going a hundred years in the future.

And there may be more to the story of the SS Central America. A 2018 expedition recovered more gold from a safe on the ship, in a passenger compartment. There could be more down there.

Latest Update: How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter.
  • “I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.
  • Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a plan centered on the clinic’s foods.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler noted. “You just can’t live like it.”.

According to recent reports, about five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he said.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

In a recent development, bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he noted. “What I was doing was not working.”.

It has been revealed that from his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

During ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

“Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”.

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin stated he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he remarked.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” said Dunkin.

In a recent development, ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin mentioned BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

Sources indicate that “Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” said Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care plan they can sustain over time.”.

In March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he stated.

When Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

In a recent development, while the procedure went smoothly, he said the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he said.

According to recent reports, what surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

Industry observers note that “I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he noted. “I really was.”.

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a new way of eating.

In a recent development, “I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he said. “I still have it for meals.”.

Recent findings suggest that although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler said the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

According to recent reports, “I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler noted. “I’m not kidding you.”.

According to recent reports, he’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he said.

Although he retired from his profession, Bichler mentioned he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he remarked.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

Recent findings suggest that “I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler said. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a new person.”.
