In a recent development, travel is the daily gift of life, but that doesn’t mean travel can’t suck the life out of you, even if you’re not going far. According to a study by the Institute of Environmental Science and Technology at the Autonomous University of Barcelona and McGill University, people travel an average of 78 minutes per day, regardless of mode of transport or distance covered. That means there’s a possibility of adventure in every bike ride, at each bus stop, and even while waiting in the airport security line. (You never know who will break liquid limits or forget to take their pepper spray off their keyring, giving everyone a delay and a story!) But you may also need accessories to keep the adventure comfortable.

No one knows that better than a friend or family member who is always heading to a new destination (typically very far, in this case). The best travel gifts bring more ease and peace of mind whether someone you know is dealing with 78 minutes’ worth of errands, cross-country travel, or long-haul international treks with a lifetime’s worth of layovers.

Other neck pillows don’t support neck movement in all directions; the Cabeau Evolution X Deluxe is a $70 neck pillow filled with customization to make it “just right,” just like Goldilocks. Change the pillow’s circumference, adjust the top or bottom lobes to change its height, and pull the adjustable cord and ball lock for a fine-tuned fit. Cooling vents release excess heat, and it comes with a travel case that compresses it down to half its size. This neck pillow is a 2026 Red Dot Design Awards winner for a reason.

The $45 Ostrichpillow Eye Mask gives you blackout curtain-levels of darkness anywhere, thanks to its adaptive, breathable face contouring that suits all sleeping positions. It’s feather-light at 1 ounce, making it comfortable and lightweight. Contoured eye cups prevent pressure on the eyes and lashes, and the smooth-edged nose bridge prevents irritation. Plus, it’s designed to not pull or tangle your hair. It comes in seven color options, including lively options like butter yellow, lavender, and cornflower blue.

I’ve been a major proponent of the “fanny pack worn across chest” since way before “crossbody” entered the vernacular. It’s hands-free, and they’re easier to shove into a backpack to meet the “carry-on and personal item” rule than a purse. My $25 JanSport Fifth Avenue Fanny Pack still holds up after years of heavy use. I’ll attach my keys to the strap, throw my favorite chapstick, headphones, and earplugs in the smaller front compartment, and stow my phone, wallet, and passport into the main compartment, which doesn’t eat my belongings like other purses in my possession. It’s served me well on daily commutes, errand runs, and neighborhood walks.

This carry-on is a splurge at $945, but its lifetime warranty and anodized aluminum shell mean it will last for many journeys, even after some rough-and-tumble handling from baggage people (that just adds personalized patina). It has TSA-compliant locks to stop snooping eyes and prevents the bag from bursting mid-flight. The 360-degree silent wheels let you drag or roll this luggage however you please. We also love this carry-on for its plentiful storage, including a zippered garment compartment and two internal pockets. A built-in compression pad with straps helps compact overpacking.

Industry observers note that this $200 backpack from Thule is my go-to travel backpack and is my most-used personal item. It fits easily under seats and comes with a chest strap, water bottle holder, and a stowable divider with TPU lining that’s excellent for keeping dirty clothes separate from the clean ones. The back panel fully unzips, letting me open the backpack fully like a suitcase. And I can rest easy knowing my electronics are protected in the plush 17-inch laptop and tablet sleeves. Its water-resistant finish keeps my wares dry in the rain, and the expandable middle section gives me more wiggle room when I’ve overpacked and lets me compress the goods when the bag is full.

Gear and Commerce Editor Tony Ware, meanwhile, is a huge fan of the 27L TuffSkin YETI Ranchero, which sports a Y-shaped easy-pull RipZip Opening in the front that provides full access to the pack’s main compartment and internal pockets, plus the GroundControl Base that ensures it stands upright when put down. He’s taken it from DC to Hawaii, Europe, and Asia packed with two laptops, a stuffed Peak Design Tech Pouch, sometimes multiple headphones, and more, and it’s the most reliable carry-on he’s tried.

Recent findings suggest that this $395 piece of checked luggage from Monos is made from a durable, aerospace-grade polycarbonate shell, making it practically unbreakable and resistant to water and dents after hard impacts with walls, poles, and floors. The wraparound zipper adds almost two inches of depth, so you can pack an extra outfit or two (or bring back souvenirs). Handy features like a telescopic handle, whisper-quiet wheels, and a TSA-accepted lock allow for easy movin’ throughout the airport. Even the included freebies are practical: The roller luggage comes with an anti-microbial, silver ion-coated laundry bag, two shoe bags, and a vegan leather luggage tag.

According to recent reports, the $219 40-Liter Baboon to the Moon Go-Bag is my duffel bag of choice for weekend trips or pet-sitting stints. I’ve gotten my money’s worth out of my baby pink bag, which has been by my side at conferences in Chicago, trade indicates in Nevada, jaunts to Washington, D.C., and Philadelphia for concerts, and train rides to my hometown. Wherever she goes, I follow, thanks to a water-repellent coating, stash pockets, and—best of all—her agreeableness with TSA or gate agents as a carry-on. B2TM (the abbreviated name for the firm) added a laptop sleeve and compression straps to its most recent version of the Go-Bag, meaning I can ditch my laptop backpack and pack smarter than ever, AKA: I can shove more crap in there. It will be a while before my Go-Bag goes to suitcase heaven; when it does, I will be ready to throw down my credit card to get a replacement.

The $118 Halfday Garment Duffel makes the most of every bit of space. It unfurls to resemble a traditional zippered garment bag, with included hanger loops and a strap to prevent clothing from falling out. Zip up the sides to shape it into a duffel bag, and add shoes, jeans, and accessories. It’s carry-on compliant for most airlines, and comes with a trolley sleeve to slide over a suitcase handle. Consider it a go-to for business travel, weddings, and weekend trips. Mary Poppins would be jealous.

The $54 Thule Compression Cube Set turns days of outfits into a compact, stowable rectangle. I use the medium cube for T-shirts, jeans, and leggings, and keep smaller items, like socks, bras, and underwear, in the smaller cube. I don’t travel without these cubes, and they’ve held up.

Don’t be blindsided by overweight luggage with this $10 portable bag scale from travel inspira. It’s easy to use: Switch between tare weight, kilograms, and pounds with the press of a button. The LCD display is easy to read, and the rubberized handle keeps hands comfortable while weighing bags. An auto-off feature preserves battery power, and a low battery indicator indicates when it’s time for a replacement. A 110-lb. weight capacity accommodates even the heaviest luggage.

Unlike other luggage tags, the $8 Ovener Silicone Luggage Tag has a built-in metal rivet and steel loop, meaning it won’t stretch out, snap, or tear. Its flexible silicone adds to its durability, and a name window helps quickly identify luggage without revealing too much to prying eyes. Nine total colors add personality and help a suitcase stand out. It comes in a pack of two—no bag left untagged!

Recent findings suggest that if you’re shopping for someone who loves something super personalized, beyond just color, the $19 Grommet Bag Tag from Visitag is for them. You can customize the front and back, or just the front: choose from 12 tag colors, six emoji locations (for an extra $2.50 per emoji), 12 characters of embroidered front-and-back text, and 17 thread colors for the embroidery on either side of the tag. The ID card is located inside the bag tag, giving just enough privacy. Durable and fun, and a way to make your suitcase stand out from every other spinner on the carousel … what more could someone want in a travel gift!?!

Recent findings suggest that the $29 Apple AirTag is a savior to anyone who has ever lost a device or bag. Its precise tracking makes it even easier than before to find bags; a louder speaker and redesigned chime help with the hunt. Consider upgrading to a four-pack to cover all your bags. The Chipolo Loop Rechargeable Bluetooth Tracker is a great Bluetooth tracker for Android phones, or any phone really, thanks to its universal compatibility with Apple Find My or Google’s Find Hub.

I’ve used this $38 BAGGU 3D Zip Set to store extra cords, emergency must-haves like Band-Aids and hand sanitizer, and to keep shoes separate from clothes. My favorite use for these utilitarian pouches is stowing all my goops and other toiletries. The large pouch expands to 10 inches by 7 inches; the medium one expands to 8.5 inches by 5 inches; and the smallest expands to 7 inches by 3 inches. Recycled ripstop nylon means I don’t have to be so gentle with these durable pouches, and they’re machine washable, a must for cleaning up rogue spills.

Industry observers note that these $40 Matador FlatPak Toiletry Bottles hold 90 milliliters of volume at half the bulk, so you’ll have enough shampoo, body wash, conditioner, and lotion for the entire trip. Flip the cap to dispense, and unscrew it to access the large fill opening. These space-saving travel bottles are five times lighter and almost four times more compact compared to their silicone counterparts. We also love the organization’s Waterproof Canister to protect vitamins, pills, 1ml/2ml travel scents, and other small bits.

Sources indicate that this $40, 16-ounce bottle from Zojirushi is just as high-quality and reliable as the firm’s rice cookers (another gift we love to give). It features an electropolished SlickSteel interior that resists stains and prevents corrosion, plus a safety lock that prevents spills from accidental lid openings. An air vent on the mouthpiece lets water flow down the sip spout without gushing or overflowing, lessening the risk of spills. And one has kept our hot and cold beverages at a pleasant temperature for entire transcontinental flights. Looking for a bit more capacity? This bottle is also available in a 20-ounce size.

Sources indicate that the $129 LARQ PureVis 2 significantly improves on its original PureVis bottle, which we reviewed in 2023. It now comes with USB-C charging, water intake tracking, and a filter straw that reduces chlorine, VOCs, and PFAS (PFOA/PFOS). It still includes powerful UV-C LED purification that runs every two hours and eliminates 99% of biocontaminants like E. Coli from your water and bottle. The Advanced filter tackles everything from the essential filter, along with haloacetic acids (HAAs, a disinfection byproduct), lead, and flame retardants, with an increased filter life of 40 gallons. Double-wall insulation keeps drinks cold for 24 hours, making it excellent for long travels. Choose from 23 or 34 ounces.

The $38 VIM & VIGR 15-20 mmHg Merino Wool Graduated Compression Socks help improve blood flow and reduce leg achiness after hours in a pressurized cabin. Plus, the merino wool naturally regulates temperature, wicks moisture, and resists odor, making these a double-whammy for comfort. These compression socks are also ideal for hiking and make a great gift for anyone who spends a lot of time on their feet. VIM & VIGR creates compression socks with fun designs, because life is too short for boring socks.

It has been revealed that the Trtl Men’s Travel Hoodie is a $140 sweatshirt designed for long flights in chilly cabins or cross-country car trips in the cooler months. It may look like a regular hoodie with a kangaroo pocket, but a closer look reveals travel-focused features. It comes with a large zippered pocket and two smaller pockets that secure keys, headphones, phones, and a passport while keeping them within reach. Other travel-friendly features include a triple-layer hood that softens sounds in loud environments (e.g., Baby on Plane, Man with Undiagnosed Sleep Apnea Snoring, Bachelorette Fallout, etc.), lower armholes for easy removal in tight spaces, and no neck tags for comfort. And yes, it has thumbholes! Pair this travel hoodie with our favorite neck pillow and/or some noise-canceling headphones (keep scrolling for suggestions) for a perfect nap in transit.

Between cabin pressure and whatever passes for a meal in economy, a man’s guts may be going through things before you reach the gate (as a vegetarian often fed chickpeas and/or lentils, I’m speaking from experience). Well, these $109 pants were made for that, and other things. The four-way stretch fabric, with 11% elastane, plus a laser-perforated panel across the back let out the heat while you’re stuck in your seat. And a hidden elastic waist and drawstring keep the pants up without having to worry about a belt that might slow things down going through security (though Roark did add belt loops in case you have to rush to a more upscale dinner when you land). But wait, there’s more! Zip pockets can secure a passport, and a stash pocket in the back is deep enough for a phone when you’re fumbling with luggage. We’ve worn a pair from DC to Kona, as well as Atlanta to Tokyo, and would highly recommend them over sweatpants if you’re looking for long-haul comfort (particularly to warmer destinations) that lets you look more put together. And, while Roark doesn’t make these specific pants in a women’s style, they do have other options.

It has been revealed that TSA may have loosened its shoes-off security rules, so you may not have to loosen your laces. But like everything when flying, that’s subject to change (especially if you get pulled aside for an extra screening). Plus, even if you can keep them on in the airport, you might want to take them off somewhere over the ocean. And if you’ve ever tried to tie your shoes again in a cramped economy row, you know it requires some contortionist skills. Not with Kizik shoes. The laces are just for looks. The shoes are designed so the heel compresses as you slip your foot in, then springs back into place (up to 30,000 times a pair). Some have a disguised mechanism, while others (like the $129 Athens 2 above, available in many colorways) show the compression cage. And they’re comfortable from Day One, thanks to the breathable stretch-knit upper (or soft leather on the Vegas 2), insole, and rocker sole/high-rebound midsole, which helps as you rush through a connection or explore a city. So go ahead, kick those shoes off when the seatbelt sign goes off.

It has been revealed that the $149 Purple Harmony Anywhere Pillow is for those who are picky about where they rest their head while counting Z’s, whether it’s in a hotel, on a friend’s couch, or while roughing it outdoors. The pillow packs luxury in a compact size: the Honeycomb GelFlex Grid and Talalay latex core keep the pillow firm and cool, while giving plenty of neck support. A moisture-wicking mesh cover keeps things airy, because a hot pillow makes for unhappy travels. Need something more targeted for those long hours in 32C? The Purple Back Pillow is great for portable lumbar support, and has made multiple overnight flights more bearable for us.

Plane cabins and train cars can get chilly; the $90 Rumpl Travel Puffy Blanket balances warmth and comfort with packability. In fact, it’s almost as large as a throw blanket and packs down to the size of a 32-ounce water bottle (shown above for perspective, but not included). Even better, it easily clips onto a backpack. Choose from sunset-inspired shades or your favorite solid color to show off your style while keeping cozy.

These $359 Bose QuietComfort Headphones make an excellent, practical gift and are essential for travel: Planes and trains can be noisy, and playing your media sans headphones is a party foul on every mode of transportation. Bose makes some of the best noise-canceling headphones for airplane travel, from over-ear models to true wireless earbuds. This updated model comes with pill-shaped earcups, a 24-hour battery life, Immersive Audio, QuietControl noise cancellation that mutes practically all outside sound, and updated ActiveSense Tech to smooth sound spikes in Aware Mode.

Industry observers note that not everyone likes significant over-ear headphones (like the Bose above), or the feeling and more limited battery life of true wireless earbuds. Well, Marshall has a solution: The $229 on-ear Milton A.N.C. Bluetooth 6.0 headphones, which bring active noise cancellation to a less typical form factor. Six microphones feed the adaptive noise canceling, which is surprisingly effective despite not having the benefit of a complete seal around the ear. Plus, a charge lasts 50 hours with ANC on, and 15 minutes plugged in can get you 9.5 hours more, so Upcoming York to Singapore and back ain’t a thang. And adaptive loudness/EQ/spatial audio settings help give those days in the air even more vibes. There’s a USB-C-to-3.5mm cable for wired listening (just remember your seatback entertainment system adapter, and to have the headphones charged because they don’t run passively). They fold up and only weigh 200 grams, so they’re perfect in an already-stuffed personal item, maybe even a jacket pocket. And they’ve got that classic Marshall cool, all textured, leather-like vinyl with brass logo/control knobs. You’ll be rockin’ even when you’re not walkin’ ….

It has been revealed that we haven’t met wireless earbuds that haven’t announced “battery low” at some point before a flight ended, which isn’t optimal, especially if an attempt at getting some sleep is involved. But these $99 Bose wired earbuds will never give you up, never let you down, never get run down and desert you. Run off the USB-C port of any smartphone, tablet, or laptop, these bring back a newtro style Bose hasn’t made in a decade. And they are unlikely to discontinue it again anytime soon, considering the overwhelming positive response. Using the proprietary QuietControl algorithms that make other Sound By Bose products so good, they cut most perceived noise while providing a convenient three-button in-line remote that switches between Quiet, Aware, and off modes, plus offers playback controls. Plus, multiple eartip-and-stability band size combinations ensure a secure fit. And even if one comes loose on the way in/out of the included case, the 4.2-foot cable means you won’t have that moment of terror that an earbud rolled three rows back.

This $80 Anker Universal Charger combines compatibility with outlets from more than 200 countries into one power block charger. It detects local voltage in one second and is Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory (NRTL)-certified for safe, stable charging. Unlike other international outlet adapters, this one is 25% smaller and designed to stay securely plugged in. And its USB-C/USB-A ports can charge four devices at once, including tech that requires higher voltage, like laptops and tablets.

In a recent development, no outlet is guaranteed in this world, but Anker’s $135 Laptop Power Bank keeps your devices charged when a place to plug in is nowhere to be found. Although it’s branded as a laptop power bank, it can also charge headphones, phones, handheld gaming devices, and more. It can charge an iPhone to full battery at least three times before running empty. The power hub can charge four devices at once. Two built-in USB-C cables mean you won’t have to root around for a charging cable when you need to recharge your tech. It also has a USB-A and USB-C port if you have a proprietary charger for a specific device.

Industry observers note that physical books can be clunky while traveling, especially as a voracious reader. The $160 Rakuten Kobo Clara is a black-and-white eReader that comes ad-free from the jump. I personally prefer it to the Amazon Kindle (which will cost you $170 to go ad-free) for this reason. The Rakuten Kobo Clara BW has 16 GB of storage and can carry up to 12,000 eBooks or 75 audiobooks. An optional Dark Mode makes for better nighttime or dark cabin reading, while ComfortLight PRO adjusts brightness, color temperature, and blue light to help you sleep easier while traveling.

This $80 JBL Clip 5 portable speaker packs pro sound into a pint-sized package. I always bring a small speaker like this one when I’m traveling so I can bump my getting-ready playlist from something that’s more powerful than my phone speakers. Pack it into a personal item or carry-on, or attach it to your person with an improved carabiner clip that sports a wider opening. The JBL Clip 5 has 12 hours of playtime on a single charge, is waterproof and dustproof, and can connect to other JBL Auracast-enabled speakers to get the party started when the plane lands.

According to recent reports, capture travels, adventures, and precious moments in high fidelity with the $700 Insta360 X6 8K Camera. Dual custom-built Sony 1/1.1″ square sensors, a 4-nanometer AI chip that can make edits of your day’s adventures while you sleep, and two imaging chips create quality images and video that feel just like the IRL moment, and 140 minutes of battery runtime keeps the camera rolling for every moment on the itinerary. Built-in stabilization, windproof microphones, and waterproofing up to 65 feet help you capture all the action, wherever it is. This travel gift is excellent for the travel vlogger and adventure enthusiast who records trips for friends, family, and followers to enjoy.

Driving the Scion Kei Truck: Fun, But Not a Real Solution for Most Americans

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, what started as a government-subsidized program to provide cheap, industrious transportation for a Japanese economy that had been ravaged by World War II has become a genuine American fixation.
  • Sources indicate that as with all vehicles not originally built to U.S.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, what started as a government-subsidized program to provide cheap, industrious transportation for a Japanese economy that had been ravaged by World War II has become a genuine American fixation. In mountainous resort towns in Colorado, Faulkner farmland in the Delta, and Northeast metropolises, the pint-size Kei truck has become a popular target for importers bringing examples from Japan. Now Toyota is set to dump fuel on that fire, as a brand-new kei truck from the resurrected Scion brand will be offered in the U.S. market in 2027.

Sources indicate that as with all vehicles not originally built to U.S. standards, federal Department of Transportation rules have limited American kei enthusiasts to importing 25-year-old examples of the miniature trucks. To be frank, most of these tired examples drive as one would expect of a work truck with a quarter century under its belt. Toyota’s incoming example is the exact opposite, as I got the chance to find out during a half-dozen laps of a half-mile cone course at Eagles Canyon Raceway outside Dallas.

Industry observers note that officially known as the Scion by Toyota Kei-01, the rebadged Daihatsu Hijet is powered by a 660-cc three-cylinder gasoline engine making around 53 hp, which is fed through a continuously variable automatic transmission. The Kei-01 is limited to 25 mph, far short of the 70 mph or so a Japanese-market Hijet can accomplish. That threshold was deliberately chosen to comply with federal safety requirements for low-speed vehicles, which mandate that the vehicle go faster than 20 mph but not faster than 25.

Sources indicate that yet that modest limit didn’t mean acceleration was lacking. When I moved the hilariously toylike shifter into drive and matted the gas, the Kei-01 jumped off the line like a puppy smelling sausages, growling and uncoordinated. The lack of gear ratios kept the tiny engine at high rpm, although the missing tach meant I couldn’t verify how fast it was spinning. Regardless, maximum speed was easily reached, according to the speedometer displaying kilometers per hour.

The ergonomics of a kei truck meant I sat on top of the front wheels and had the Toyota-badged steering wheel tilted into my lap. Also, this being a product designed for the Japanese market, the steering wheel was positioned on the right; Toyota has no prepares to reverse the layout for us. With 14-inch wheels and what are barely soccer-ball-diameter tires, the Kei-01 was agile to a fault; I suspect you could pretty much turn it inside a single Costco parking space. Directional changes happened rapidly, although the steering is high geared, and even slow-speed maneuvers elicited a special charm. That stated, I wouldn’t want to haul it around a tight corner at any rate of speed. And the ride quality could be described generously as rudimentary. I bounced up and down in my adjustable seat over Toyota’s provided gravel course, the interior loudly rattling the whole time. However, as a dedicated work truck, this was hardly disqualifying.

According to recent reports, A button in the center console promised locking four-wheel-drive, though I didn’t get to use it. Slowing the Kei-01, with its curb weight of just over 2000 pounds, was as easy as letting off the accelerator. But front disc and rear drum brakes seemed powerful enough. Considering the modest limiter, you could just yank the analog, wire-operated parking brake.

Toyota hasn’t skimped on features. A central touchscreen tucked into the dashboard will supposedly have Apple CarPlay functionality when the Kei-01 arrives in the U.S. next year. Push-button start and slider-style climate controls will also be fitted as standard. For those who have bemoaned the rise of haptic-touch features, the Kei-01 will be the freshest breath of interior design air you’ve had in some time. Icons on the Kei-01’s dashboard even promised ADAS features like lane-departure control and collision warnings. Some of the touch surfaces were hard, and the doors felt featherlight, but who really cares?

According to recent reports, the Kei-01’s payload capacity, scaled to its diminutive dimensions, is just 600 pounds. But the three sides of the load bed can be folded down separately, boosting utility, meaning that trips to Home Depot are more likely to be limited by speed than cargo weight. A storage deck behind the seats is well suited for backpacks and toolboxes, and there are flat storage spaces on the dashboard and built into the roofline.

Before you check your credit score, there is a brutal catch to the possibility of buying the Kei-01. Toyota has stated it won’t sell the vehicle to individuals initially, with access limited to fleet operators.

Sources indicate that the proposal is to target luxury resorts, university administrations, and other institutions with the need for such compact utility. This makes sense given both the likely lack of profit in individual trucks and the logic of putting the trucks into the hands of what are likely to be safe, responsible customers with their own private road networks. Toyota hasn’t revealed pricing yet, but the Kei-01 will almost certainly carry a sizable upcharge over the equivalent Hijet, which costs about $9000 in Japan, with U.S. versions being built in Indiana.

The brutal truth is that a maximum speed of 25 mph means the Scion Kei-01 simply isn’t suited to road use in much of the U.S. Even in the center of cities like Upcoming York, where speed limits are largely set at that number, traffic normally flows considerably faster when free to do so. The prospect of trying to drive a Kei-01 on a faster-flowing highway surrounded by inattentive traffic is slightly terrifying. Toyota’s decision to keep the bulk of Kei-01s away from public roads is prudent, if a little disappointing. I’ve never had more fun going 25 mph.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that BACK PAIN DOESN'T care about your substantial prepares to sail through life in comfort, making it hard to do everything from getting in a workout to sitting at your computer. Relief can come in many forms, including regularly stretching and strengthening the surrounding muscles, but sometimes, it can also involve using one of the best inversion tables to ease pressure on your back.

It has been revealed that “An inversion table is a device that allows you to hang at an angle, or even upside down, with your feet secured,” explains Max Shlykov, MD, an orthopedic spine surgeon at the Maryland Spine Center. “This position stretches and decompresses the spine and surrounding muscles.”.

It’s important to get this out of the way now: An inversion table won’t magically cure your back pain or fix the underlying cause of it. But it can temporarily ease your pain and the tension that’s contributing to it. Inversion tables tend to be especially helpful for people with chronic back problems like herniated discs, sciatica, degenerative disc disease, muscle spasms, or general stiffness, according to Shayan Ghadamabadi, DPT, a physical therapist at Michigan State University Health Care Physical & Occupational Therapy.

Sources indicate that the best inversion tables are sturdy enough to support your height and weight, with adjustable hanging angles, Dr. Shlykov says. “Models that are more lightweight may be easier on your back to use and set up,” he adds.

According to recent reports, you’re not born knowing how to pick an inversion table, making it vital to choose wisely. Here’s what to consider when looking for one of these pain-relieving tools, plus sturdy options to try. Because you need to know how to actually use one of these tables, we included advice for beginners to help put you on the right path to greater comfort.

Sources indicate that teeter’s FitSpine X3 Inversion Table hits all our best marks thanks to its durability, extended ankle lock handles, and secure, comfortable fit. The device is made with heat-treated steel for unmatched strength and support, and the foam backrest prevents your body from slipping or sliding while inverted, according to Dr. Wallace.

The comfortable table is lined with acupressure nodes to target and release trigger points, and Dr. Wallace says the FlexTech bed moves with your body to enhance decompression and improve range of motion. You can also rest assured about safety features, as the patented wrap-around ankle cups are secure and supportive. Dr. Mesiwala says this is crucial for proper relaxation and effectiveness. What’s more, the lumbar bridge can help release lower back tension and alleviate glute pain triggered by sciatica.

You’ll also get access to a free personal training app with a library of video and audio guides for on and off the inversion table, Dr. Verma claims. The only qualm? It may be difficult or time-consuming to assemble.

Read More: The Best Compression Boots, Tested By Us.

Sources indicate that the Innova ITX9900 Heavy Duty Inversion Therapy Table is a budget-friendly option that doesn’t compromise on quality, according to Dr. Wallace. It offers a six-position adjustable pin system for safety locking and consistent inversion, a large, padded backrest, and soft-touch foam handlebars for easy access to getting in and out of position, he says. This table is great for anyone, but it’s particularly good for beginners thanks to its ease of use and adjustable headrest, height, and footrest.

This inversion table also features a True Balance System, which helps users find their center of gravity for smooth, seamless inversion. Not only will this maximize tension release, but it can also improve spinal decompression. Another pro: The headrest is adjustable, too.

It has been revealed that when it comes to getting a full, comfortable stretch, the EP-560 is a safe bet. It features patented wrap-around ankle supports, an ergonomic T-grip ankle lock, and an easy-dial foot platform for a more comfortable, secure fit. The backrest is also a game-changer. Most inversion tables use a simple foam material; the EP-560 ComforTrak backrest is designed to reduce friction and enhance spinal stretch and decompression. We also love that it’s pretty customizable. It comes with built-in tools for easy adjustability, including a Lumbar Bridge for deeper traction on the lower back and Acupressure Nodes that target muscle tension.

The device is made out of an ultra-durable, heat-treated steel, adding an extra layer of strength and support. If you’re a little closer to the 300-lb range, this is a solid option.

Industry observers note that it’s on the pricier side, but the Harison Electric Inversion Table is a top pick for both Dr. Mesiwala and Dr. Verma thanks to its adjustable footbed, memory-foam backrest, and heavy-duty build. The device is made with seamless welding and a steel frame to support up to 350 pounds, and the ergonomic ankle lock design is supportive without feeling too tight or restrictive. Security is also a top priority, and the table includes a high-quality safety belt that allows you to strap in while inverted (on top of the secure ankle holders).

In a recent development, the table is heavier than other options on this list, but it’s foldable for easy storage. It also includes a 30-day trial and replacement of spare parts within one year for no extra cost.

If you’re looking for an inversion table that doubles as a massager, here’s your pick. The vertical massage pad covers the entire spine with a contoured lumbar pad for a close-up massage and vibrating sensation, and the in-unit heating pad provides warmth to the lower back. There are also multiple mode settings to suit your massage and heat preferences, and the included user manual provides all necessary instructions and details.

This model has a new, improved ankle-holding system to reduce pressure on the ankles when inverted, while still ensuring a secure, protective fit. There’s also a six-position pin system on the side of the machine that lets you adjust the angle without dismounting the device.

Each inversion table accommodates different heights, so it's key to read the fine print. The Teclor Inversion Table adjusts to fit people up to 6'8", making it a good option for taller users. It also can support up to 350 pounds, one of the largest weight capacities you’ll find.

In a recent development, this is a relatively simple inversion table, and the low price supports that. But you’ll still get a comfortably padded back, cushioned handles, and an easy-to-reach handle for adjustability. The ankle-holding system is thickly padded, too. A double-locking system helps to ensure your device is firmly in place when it’s in use. When you’re done inverting, it folds up small enough to stash in a closet.

Read More: The 6 Best Compression Boots to Support Muscle Recovery.

Consider the Teeter FitSpine LX9 the slightly more luxurious version of our top pick, the X3. This has all the elements users love about the X3, including that durable heat-treated steel frame and padded back, but in a slightly sleeker, user-friendly design. The LX9 has an eight-point floating suspension system for a large range of motion, along with reinforced padded handles for a comfortable grip.

Enjoy eight acupressure nodes to help relieve muscle tension while you hang. The included lumbar bridge is adjustable and works to tweak your hip alignment. The LX9 has a step-through design with a specialized boarding platform to make it easy to get on and off. There’s even a built-in storage caddy to hold your gear while you invert.

Using an inversion table isn’t as simple as diving into a fresh set of dumbbells. These devices require you to move your body upside-down, making it important to know what you’re doing and how to ease into the process.

It’s crucial to start with a “modest” angle vs. going into a full-out inversion when you’re starting out, according to Raymond Agostino, DPT, owner of Agostino Athletics in Fort Myers, Florida. “The goal is to introduce your body to the position and create a gentle traction effect without overwhelming your system,” he claims.

Agostino suggests starting with a gentle recline, like 20 to 25 degrees for 30 to 45 seconds and see how you feel. “If you feel comfortable and don't experience dizziness, increased pain, or other symptoms, you can gradually increase the time or angle over future sessions,” he notes. Agostino recommends only changing one variable at a time—angle and inversion time—to ease yourself in. “You don't need to go farther upside down and stay there longer all at once,” he says.

When you’re inverted, you may feel a pressure sensation in your head or a mild “head rush,” Agostino says. “When your head is positioned below your heart, blood pressure and pressure within the eyes can increase, which is one reason inversion feels very different from simply lying flat,” he explains. You might also feel a feeling of fullness in your head or facial pressure. “Those sensations should remain mild and should resolve when you return upright,” according to Agostino.

Agostino points out that you don’t get a trophy for going completely upside down. “If a smaller angle provides the stretch or relief you're looking for, there may be no reason to progress to a full inversion,” he says.

Industry observers note that safety is paramount when shopping for an inversion table. "It’s ideal to find a product with comfortable ankle straps and safety locks to keep you secure and in place," indicates Kushagra Verma, MD, a board-certified orthopedic spine surgeon at DISC Sports and Spine Center. You also want to make sure the table can be controlled and manipulated by the user if you plan to use the device alone. Inversion tables should be used with caution, especially if you’re a beginner, says Rahul Shah, MD, a board-certified orthopedic spine and neck surgeon at Premier Orthopaedic Associates. Additionally, older adults and those who have chronic dizziness, high blood pressure, glaucoma, inner ear problems, heart disease, and/or severe injuries should avoid inversion tables without talking to their doctor first, he says. Keep this in mind, too, per Agostino: “A little pressure may be expected. Feeling like something is wrong is not something you need to train yourself to tolerate.” If it feels like your back pain is worsening, or if you develop newly introduced numbness, tingling, weakness, or radiating pain, Agostino recommends that you stop using the inversion tale.

Sturdiness and durability are crucial for preventing accidents or instability while you’re upside down, Dr. Verma says. He recommends always looking for a product made with high-quality materials, such as stainless steel, to provide better support and longevity. Be sure to read customer reviews and seek expert opinions on the machine's sturdiness when shopping. Of course, all the selections on our list have been vetted in this way.

In addition to safety features, all experts agree that it’s crucial to consider how much weight an inversion table can safely hold. (The machine should clearly state this in the product description.) Because the machine puts you in a rather compromising position, maximum weight capacity is key for keeping you safe and at ease, Dr. Shah claims. Going over the weight capacity raises the odds that the table will break or flip while you’re on it, potentially injuring you in the process, Agostino says.

It’s vital to consider the table's length to ensure it accommodates your size and height, notes Ali Mesiwala, MD, a neurosurgeon and complex spine expert at DISC Sports and Spine Center. Most inversion tables are adjustable for a customized fit, but it’s best to ensure the maximum height is within your range for effective use. The width of the table is another key factor, as a wider table can offer more stability during inversion, particularly if you’re on the taller or heavier side, says Brian Wallace, DC, a chiropractor at Pinewood Family Care. As a general rule of thumb, the width of the table should be wide enough for your core to conformably fit and not fall to either side, Dr. Shah adds.

Depending on your needs, different inversion tables include add-on features like lumbar spine support, heat, memory foam, or massage elements, Dr. Wallace notes. These extra features are not a necessity, but they can be beneficial if you’re looking for added comfort and therapeutic benefits, he says. Just remember: extra add-ons should be considered second to the table's fundamental stability, comfort, and safety.

An inversion table isn’t the cheapest tool you’ll use to reduce your back pain, but there is a range to consider. Most tables will run you anywhere from $150 to $450, with higher-priced models having additional features like heat, memory foam, and massage.

Recent findings suggest that to track down the best inversion tables, Men’s Health editors, including contributor Korin Miller, consulted three orthopedic surgeons, a neurosurgeon, a chiropractor, and two physical therapists to learn more about the important features to look for in an inversion table. From there, we looked at the most popular inversion tables on the market and narrowed the field based on our experts’ requirements. Each inversion table was ranked based on factors such as size, weight capacity, and safety features. This story was first published in August, and was updated in November to reflect the most recent products on the market, along with advice on how to use these machines.

Extended inversion can cause excessive blood flow to the head and lead to nausea, vomiting, and dizziness, so Dr. Mesiwala recommends using an inversion table for a maximum of five minutes at a time, up to twice a day. If you’re a beginner, he suggests only inverting for 30 seconds once a day as you get your bearings.

Sources indicate that the best time to use an inversion table is typically when your muscles are relaxed, such as after a workout at the end of the day, states Dr. Wallace. Remember: You should not be inverted for long periods, and it’s best to start slowly and work your way up to time and frequency.

This is ultimately up to you. Some people feel comfortable with their arms by their sides or crossed over their chest, while others prefer to stretch them overhead. You can also put your arms on the support bars. Essentially, you should do whatever feels comfortable to you.

#87345. Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

📅 26 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (922 w)

Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.
  • Recent findings suggest that weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women.
  • GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Recent findings suggest that weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

Industry observers note that to investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

The average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

In a recent development, these differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

It has been revealed that in the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

It has been revealed that these findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she noted.

It is important to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

According to recent reports, sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is important for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she noted.

In a recent development, “I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”.

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

Industry observers note that “Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Recent findings suggest that hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve key aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

Industry observers note that “For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence currently available,” she said.

According to recent reports, “It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”.

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

Industry News: How much trash is on the moon? About 412,000 pounds.

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that but these leftovers aren’t all space junk.
  • A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since the Soviet Union’s Luna 2 probe crashed into the moon’s surface in 1959, the first-ever human-made object to reach the moon, humanity has racked up over 140 missions to our only natural satellite. These missions have delivered 12 humans, seven lunar rovers, and 412,000 pounds (187,000 kilograms) of discarded materials to the moon’s surface. That’s the weight of a Boeing 747 passenger plane.

Recent findings suggest that but these leftovers aren’t all space junk. In fact, some of this debris may prove useful for future lunar exploration.

A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.

Recent findings suggest that early moon exploration missions, like NASA’s Apollo missions, would land on the moon using a non-reusable lunar module, indicates Cowley. “It would land, and then the top part of that module would return back to lunar orbit to rendezvous with the command module and return back to Earth. So, the base part of this vehicle would remain.”.

Industry observers note that leftover lunar rovers—manned or unmanned land vehicles used to explore the moon’s surface—also contribute to the growing mass of junk. These include China’s robotic Yutu rover, which sent information back to Earth for 31 months, as well as those that crash-landed, like the United Arab Emirates’s Rashid rover.

Other trash on the moon includes scientific equipment, toolboxes, and lunar impactor probes. These are devices that smash into the moon’s surface, not by accident, but to fulfill specific objectives, like close-up imaging or to fire rocks and dust into the air for analysis.

Images of the moon’s barren landscape might make you think that these lunar leftovers simply sit around undisturbed until the visit of the next crewed mission. But that’s not the case.

The moon is an incredibly harsh environment. It’s “constantly bombarded with micrometeorites,” explains Cowley. These tiny rock chunks, along with intense radiation, sunlight exposure, and dramatic temperature swings, will steadily wear down and damage objects.

The iconic American flag planted on the moon by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin in 1969, for example, has likely been bleached almost white by the sun.

But some of this damaged, degraded material could still have value for future moon exploration. Cowley notes samples of human equipment on the moon could be assessed to understand how the environment alters them.

Studying the impact of micrometeorites on equipment, for example, “might allow us to produce better solar cell or solar panel protection, so they don’t get degraded for humans when humans may eventually live on the moon,” notes Cowley.

In 1960, scientists predicted the world would end on November 13, 2026.

Why can’t we just launch all of Earth’s garbage into the sun?

Ahead of looks by NASA and the China National Space Agency to send crewed missions to the moon in the next five years, more equipment will likely amass on the lunar surface. But there are reasons to think these future missions may leave less of a mess behind.

In a recent development, “You might see more emphasis these days on vehicles that have a reusable aspect,” states Cowley. “Maybe the lander can land as one unit and take off as one unit again,” he says. Spaceships in development like SpaceX’s Starship Human Landing System (HLS) strategy to adopt this reusable design.

In a recent development, even if more equipment doesn’t accumulate on the moon, Cowley states the ESA has made plans to reuse some of this moon trash. One project has explored the potential of 3D printing methods to incorporate lunar scrap into fresh materials. Such efforts will have to account for the likelihood that such materials will be contaminated by lunar dust—sharp, shard-like particles of the rocky lunar surface that can prove a further hazard to machinery.

Cowley says that the lightweight aluminum that makes up the shell of many lunar vehicles could be melted down using concentrated sunlight.

“Rather than bringing things here with you or mining them on the moon,” claims Cowley, “you could actually just reuse the old equipment in the same way we recycle stuff down here on Earth.”.

It has been revealed that that lunar “junk” may prove invaluable to the first humans to one day call the moon home. Or, as the old saying goes, one person’s trash is another person’s treasure.

Recent findings suggest that tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany. The manufacturer confirmed today a first €3 billion investment in a upcoming production building at Giga Berlin designed for up to 1 million Cybercabs a year, with production planned for 2029.

Recent findings suggest that that’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one. Under current EU rules, a driverless vehicle model is capped at 1,500 registrations a year.

Plant manager André Thierig announced the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.

Sources indicate that if you ever wondered, what we would be doing at Giga Berlin with all the land that we have… We are expanding! Cybercab production is coming to Giga Berlin! Today we declared a first investment of around € 3b in a new manufacturing building with an anticpated start of… pic.twitter.com/vpcDdxoqlW.

It has been revealed that per Tesla’s statement, the €3 billion pays for the latest production hall north of the existing plant, plus ancillary buildings and a second wastewater treatment plant. Tesla aims to file the building application before the end of the year, break ground in the first half of 2027, and start production in 2029. The company states it will be “the technologically most advanced Tesla factory in the world.”.

Recent findings suggest that it leaked a few hours earlier. Steven Scholtysek, an automation engineer at the plant, posted that Elon Musk personally signed off on the project last week and that the new hall will be bigger than the original factory.

Recent findings suggest that the building isn’t new. Tesla laid out a plan to take Giga Berlin to 1 million vehicles a year in its 2023 permit filings and has been clearing land for it since. What’s new is the product. Until today, Tesla had only remarked the second hall wouldn’t be another Model Y factory.

Giga Berlin still builds only the Model Y. Tesla has been hiring again at Giga Berlin this year as European demand came back, with a goal of 7,500 cars a week. Even at that pace, the plant would fall short of the 500,000 units a year Tesla promised when it opened in 2022.

Tesla is also adding 4680 battery cell production at the site, with 18 GWh of annual capacity planned.

So the new hall alone is rated for twice what the entire existing plant was supposed to build. And it comes after Musk tied the Berlin expansion to the plant’s works council election in March, warning workers against IG Metall’s influence.

Recent findings suggest that the EU has a type-approval path for fully driverless vehicles, but it’s a “small series” scheme limited to 1,500 registrations per vehicle type per year across the whole EU. In March, the Commission lifted that cap for automated valet parking. Robotaxis are still stuck in the small-series track.

Industry observers note that tesla also has no approval anywhere in Europe for its software to drive without supervision. The Dutch RDW approved the supervised version, now called Tesla Assisted Driving, and nine other countries recognize that approval. It still requires a driver paying attention. The Cybercab has no steering wheel.

Rules can move in three years. The Commission has said it wants large-series approval for other driverless uses, and a UN regulation for automated driving systems is in the works. But as of today, Tesla is committing €3 billion to a vehicle it can’t sell in volume in Europe.

Tesla could export from Berlin, of course. But 1 million Cybercabs a year on top of Giga Texas implies a robotaxi business many times bigger than anything on the road today. Texas, where Cybercab production started in April, had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October. And Tesla just opened personal Cybercab orders at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 monthly subscription, usable only inside its Robotaxi geofences.

Sources indicate that tesla can’t even launch its driver-assist system in Europe under its own name. What it’s rolling out there isn’t “Full Self-Driving.” It’s “Tesla Assisted Driving,” a level 2 system that needs a driver watching the road at all times, and it took a long fight with regulators to get it approved in 10 countries.

According to recent reports, the Cybercab is a much harder sell. No steering wheel, no pedals, so it has to be certified as a level 4 vehicle with nobody inside to take over. That’s a completely different approval from anything Tesla has gotten in Europe. As of this spring, the EU mentioned no automaker had even used its existing driverless approval path.

Recent findings suggest that and the US program doesn’t inspire confidence. Robotaxi is still confined to geofences, still off highways, and it keeps crashing: Tesla had reported 22 incidents to NHTSA by July, and our analysis of the data earlier this year put it at one crash every 57,000 miles, roughly 9 times worse than the average human driver, with a safety monitor on board. The only reason those crashes don’t get more attention is that they happen at low speed. Of course they do. Tesla keeps the cars on slow city streets. Put the same system on the autobahn and we’d expect more crashes, and worse ones.

Sources indicate that that’s the kind of news you have to want to believe. Tesla’s driver-assistance efforts are actually running into serious trouble in Europe. They still haven’t received approval for Level 2++ in Germany, while Mercedes, for example, already has it. They’ve also been told they can no longer use the term FSD because it’s considered misleading advertising. More importantly, Tesla isn’t conducting any Level 4 testing here, and that’s going to be a prerequisite for getting approvals in Europe. You can’t just self-certify your system in this field over here. So this is pretty typical Tesla news. A lot of hype, but absolutely nothing behind it.

This is Musk’s modus operandi for the last few years: bet on autonomy before it’s ready. Tesla removed the Cybercab’s steering wheel assuming the software would be solved by the time it mattered. It wasn’t, and now Tesla is putting €3 billion into a German factory on the same assumption.

Good for the workers in Grünheide, and maybe the hall can build something else if this doesn’t work out. But spending €3 billion to build up to 1 million steering-wheel-less cars a year for a market where Tesla can’t legally run a single one, based on a program that hasn’t left the geofence in Texas, is extremely risky.

Recent findings suggest that will there be one unsupervised Cybercab carrying paying passengers in Europe when the Grünheide line starts in 2029? We wouldn’t bet on it.

Being stranded at the airport is no fun. You can only eat so many Auntie Anne's pretzels and play Candy Crush for so long; eventually, you need to get to your destination. But what if that destination is 1600 miles away, every flight in the country is grounded, and there are no rental cars or trains available?

Industry observers note that well, you could take an Uber to a local Ford dealership and drop $48,000 on a new Ford Bronco. And according to a report from NBC News, that is exactly what Tara Harding did.

According to NBC, Harding and two of her employees were in Charlotte, North Carolina for training, and were set to fly back home to Bismarck, North Dakota last Friday. That is, until the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded all flights across the country. Thousands of flights were cancelled or delayed as a result.

According to recent reports, the three women began to look at alternate transportation options, but none of them had any luck. There were no rental cars, buses, trains, or ride shares that could get them home. They were stuck in Charlotte. Harding called her husband to let him know, which is when her mother-in-law made a suggestion: “Why don’t you guys go buy a car?”.

Harding decided to investigate that possibility. Being what she described to NBC as a self-proclaimed “Ford girl,” Harding texted a local Ford dealer. The salesman stated he would wait until the women arrived, which they did around 7:45 pm. Two hours and $48,000 later, Harding was the proud owner of a new Ford Bronco. The road trip was on.

Sources indicate that harding is a nurse practitioner, and she owns her own clinic; she had patients scheduled for Monday, and she said she wanted to get her employees back home to their family. So, they covered the 1600 miles by driving 27 hours straight. The women took turns behind the wheel, sleeping while the others drove, while gas stations and drive-thrus provided the necessary fuel for both the Bronco and its occupants.

Industry observers note that originally, Harding said she planned to sell the Bronco once she got home. However, she added that while she was catching up on sleep, her husband took it for three drives and decided he wanted to keep it. So, the nationwide flight may have cost Harding $48,000—but at least she now has a cool new Bronco, and one heck of a story to tell.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest research highlights that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.
  • The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.
  • Both measures were linked to mortality risk and demonstrated similar ability to predict it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest research highlights that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and demonstrated similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

It has been revealed that for free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

From this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:.

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

It has been revealed that the average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

Sources indicate that the study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own indicated modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

According to recent reports, several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Recent findings suggest that overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, stated that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

According to recent reports, “Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”.

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, noted that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

Recent findings suggest that “It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” stated Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she remarked.

Sources indicate that theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he said.

In a recent development, “And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” remarked Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he remarked. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Recent findings suggest that strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

“I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD’s upcoming, larger entry-level EV will go on sale in Europe, but it won’t be called the Dolphin Surf as expected.

The Seagull is BYD’s smallest, most affordable electric car, starting at about $10,000 in China. In Europe and the UK, it’s sold as the Dolphin Surf, and in other overseas markets, it’s called the Dolphin Mini.

With over 245,000 Seagull (Dolphin Mini/ Dolphin Surf) models sold through September, it’s BYD’s most popular pure electric vehicle and among the top-selling EVs worldwide so far this year.

After launching the second-generation “Great” Seagull in China, a larger, more advanced version, BYD was expected to introduce it overseas as the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.

Industry observers note that apparently, that will not be the case. BYD will introduce the updated version overseas, but according to the Spanish media outlet TestCoches, it will replace the larger Dolphin hatch rather than the Dolphin Surf.

The second-generation model will offer BYD’s five-minute Flash Charging technology and Blade Batteries 2.0.

Recent findings suggest that in China, the newly introduced Seagull is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000). For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super Trade-In” promotion, bringing the starting price down to just 62,900 yuan ($9,500).

Recent findings suggest that the second-gen Seagull measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and 150 mm longer in wheelbase than its predecessor.

Thanks to the added space, BYD’s newly introduced Seagull now offers room for five passengers, up from four in the outgoing version.

Instead of a front-wheel-drive powertrain, the newly introduced version switches to rear-wheel-drive. The setup uses a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from 55 kW (75 hp).

It has been revealed that with BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. To go from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

According to recent reports, even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes just 3 minutes longer (12 minutes) to charge from 20% to 97%. However, Flash Charging is not included as standard on the two cheapest entry-level variants.

While the bigger dimensions and Flash Charging were the biggest updates, BYD also added a few premium extras.

To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system.

Inside, BYD revamped the interior with its latest in-car software and technology. The upcoming setup includes a larger 15.6″ center infotainment screen, a redesigned two-spoke steering wheel and center console with smart storage, plus added physical buttons.

All versions are equipped with BYD’s DiLink 150 smart cockpit system and a 140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system.

In a recent development, the optional DiPilot 300 system with God’s Eye B intelligent driving assistance is available. It includes a roof-mounted LiDAR to provide ADAS features such as City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking.

According to recent reports, in China, BYD offers the latest Seagull EV with two Blade 2.0 LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh. The former provides a CLTC range of up to 320 km (199 miles), while the latter provides up to 420 km (261 miles).

In a recent development, the current Dolphin Surf measures 3,990 mm in length, and the Dolphin is 4,290 mm long. Selling the updated version as the Dolphin makes more sense, given how much closer in size it is.

BYD will continue selling the Dolphin Surf in Spain and throughout Europe, with the updated model now featuring five seats and a few other key improvements.

In Europe, BYD’s Dolphin Surf starts at about €22,990 ($25,000), and the larger Dolphin is priced from around €33,990 ($37,500).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, is no stranger to wildfires.
  • Earlier this year, four mother-baby orangutan pairs and one adult female orangutan (genus Pongo) were rescued from areas in Ketapang (a regency in the West Kalimantan province) impacted by the fires.
  • Recent findings suggest that they were taken to an orangutan rescue and rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, West Kalimantan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, is no stranger to wildfires. Horrific wildfires burned in 2015 and 2019, the latter of which set ablaze around 1.6 million hectares of Indonesian forest and land. However, the scale of destruction from this year’s El Niño-intensified fires throughout the island is unprecedented, according to the nonprofit International Animal Rescue.

Earlier this year, four mother-baby orangutan pairs and one adult female orangutan (genus Pongo) were rescued from areas in Ketapang (a regency in the West Kalimantan province) impacted by the fires. They were dehydrated and malnourished, and some had burned their feet, likely because they stepped on embers as they crossed burning peatland.

Recent findings suggest that they were taken to an orangutan rescue and rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, West Kalimantan. The center is run by Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI), a nonprofit dedicated to primate and habitat conservation in Indonesia. YIARI’s medical team kept an eye on their recovery, and then conducted health examinations to make sure they were all ready for release. The last of these examinations revealed that three of the females were pregnant.

“Their return to the wild is therefore especially key, giving these mothers the opportunity to raise their future young in a safer forest habitat,” International Animal Rescue, YIARI’s founding partner, wrote in a statement.

Industry observers note that experts ultimately chose to release them at Batu Nyambu Protected Forest. While also in West Kalimantan, its roughly 23,000 hectares of land and nearby forests haven’t been affected by the recent fires. Batu Nyambu has plenty of natural food, fresh water, nesting trees, and space. But getting the females and their babies there wasn’t simple—they had to travel by road, boat, and on foot for a total of 12 hours. Luckily, they had support from local communities and traditional leaders.

It has been revealed that “We are grateful for the support of the community, village governments and traditional leaders,” said Argitoe Ranting, YIARI’s Director of Operations. “The long-term success of conservation efforts depends not only on protecting the area, but also on the role of the people living around the forest in safeguarding habitat and preventing various threats to wildlife.”.

Most fires in Indonesia are associated with human activity such as using fire to clear land for plantations and agriculture.
