📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, automotive manufacturing is a laborious, resource-intensive process. While the complex metropolises that are modern car factories work well for high-volume products, it is often prohibitively expensive for automakers to retool these plants to create distinct body panels for limited-production models. Now a California-based organization called Machina Labs aims to plug that gap with an innovative metal manufacturing process that promises speed, flexibility, and cost-savings.

See all results for used cars for sale near 94043.

In a recent development, machina’s business is based around its RoboCraftsman platform, which it basically pitches as a factory in a box. The system uses a pair of large robotic arms to perform a variety of tasks on metal panels, from striking designs into pre-stamped panels to fully forming new pieces. The robotic arms are controlled by software that can switch between different projects as quickly as Machina can upload new designs, and the system also scans the completed panel to see if any additional work needs to be done, and to trim, finish, and heat treat the pieces. The entire setup can be folded into two shipping containers that can then be easily transported.

In a recent development, machina Labs was founded in 2019 and so far has mostly served clients in the aerospace and defense industries. But now Machina wants to enter the automotive space, launching a newly introduced division called Machina Rebellis. With its RoboCraftsman platform, Machina aims to give automakers a way to skip the costly retooling process, with its technology providing a more efficient method to quickly craft customizable body panels, allowing OEMs to efficiently build more distinctive limited-edition cars.

It has been revealed that machina’s interest in the automotive world started a few years back when it built a truck called the Anvil, based on the Ford F-150 Lightning, to demonstrate the unique body panels its metalworking machines could produce. While still fairly crude, this early prototype got Toyota’s attention, and the Japanese automotive giant is now an investor in Machina Labs via Woven Capital, Toyota’s venture capital division.

Recent findings suggest that the process has improved vastly since the Anvil was built, and to demonstrate this, Machina Labs created a new show vehicle, the Lassen, which is being shown at the Los Angeles auto show. Based on a Toyota Tacoma, the Lassen wears a unique hood, tailgate, and fenders, showing off the sort of customization that Machina’s process is capable of. Machina worked with Callum, the design house formed by Ian Callum, to pen the look of these panels before manufacturing them using the RoboCraftsman platform.

See all results for used cars for sale near 94043.

Sources indicate that while the Lassen isn’t a drastic departure from a standard Tacoma, the changes that Machina made would typically take around four to six months to produce via traditional methods, the manufacturer said at a media event at its second factory in Chatsworth, California. Using its RoboCraftsman platform, Machina was able to take the Lassen from sketches to a finished product in just two and a half weeks.

Industry observers note that the Lassen highlights off Machina’s two main capabilities. The hood and tailgate demonstrate the RoboCraftsman’s ability to re-strike pre-stamped panels with custom designs. The Lassen’s tailgate has a bold embossed Machina script, while the hood also says Machina and has a topographical map of its namesake, Mount Lassen in California. The RoboCraftsman platform can put just about any design on a metal panel, and Machina also had tailgates on display featuring a retro Toyota design and a Los Angeles Rams logo.

The fenders, meanwhile, are entirely latest panels formed by the RoboCraftsman, and they have a bulging, powerful look. These fenders started as a sheet of metal—Machina works in both aluminum and steel—before being shaped by the robotic arms. This process is a bit slower than the re-striking process, which can take minutes to complete, but a fully formed panel can be finished within hours.

Sources indicate that machina believes its RoboCraftsman platform is best suited to production runs in the hundreds and thousands. This could include special-edition models for large OEMs, or working with aftermarket companies to create body kits and other visual customizations. OEMs can also use Machina’s process to quickly create body panels for early pre-production vehicles, typically an expensive and time-consuming part of the development cycle. In the future, Machina also envisions sending its RoboCraftsman units directly to OEM manufacturing sites to speed up the process even further.

Over the past decade, high-end carmakers realized there is a lot of money in personalization, leading to a surge of one-off and limited-production supercars, designed to the exacting specification desired by their wealthy buyers. These cars, often hand-built, are incredibly expensive. Machina Labs claims that its RoboCraftsman platform could democratize customization, with the speed and flexibility at which it can work allowing automakers to save money and offer personalized details on more ordinary, everyday vehicles.

The RoboCraftsman platform provides a way to promptly manufacture custom body panels, and the flexibility to switch among a large number of different projects in a short amount of time. The Lassen serves as a proof of concept as Machina courts automotive companies, and seeing the RoboCraftsman operate in person, we certainly see a space in the automotive world for Machina’s quick and flexible manufacturing innovation.

Nihilism Is Not What You Think

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Recent findings suggest that since Friedrich Nietzsche, philosophers have grappled with the question of how to respond to nihilism.
  • I define nihilism narrowly as the negative and eliminativist thesis of denying objective values.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Recent findings suggest that since Friedrich Nietzsche, philosophers have grappled with the question of how to respond to nihilism. Nihilism, often used as a derogatory term for a "life-denying," destructive, and perhaps most of all depressive philosophy, is what drove existentialists to write about the right response to a meaningless universe devoid of purpose. This is why I've published an academic article on the topic. As nihilism is commonly used as a derogatory term, even in the works of Friedrich Nietzsche, it will prove helpful for the purpose of this post to take a "value-neutral" view on nihilism and achieve conceptual clarity of the term nihilism, beyond some sort of "life-denying" philosophy.

I define nihilism narrowly as the negative and eliminativist thesis of denying objective values. Moral nihilism, therefore, refers to the meta-ethical thesis that there is no objective morality, no inherent goodness or wrongness, a view that many existentialists agree with. The concern here, however, is existential nihilism, which can be defined as the denial of life being meaningful and the universe having a purpose. Whether moral and existential nihilism entail each other is beyond the scope of this post, but they at least stand in a close relation.

Industry observers note that existentialists are by definition, therefore, all existential nihilists, though not necessarily moral nihilists or atheists. As is commonly joked about existentialist thinkers, with the exception of Sartre, they do not appreciate being labelled as existentialists. Just like moral nihilism is often negatively associated and equated with immoralism, existential nihilism is often associated with destructive behaviour and suicide. These positions, however, should not be confused or seen as standing in a necessary causal relationship.

Existential nihilism, despite its negative connotations, should therefore not be seen as a label, but rather as something that is taken as a fact or at least a widespread view in the modern world, from which existential philosophy takes off. The popularity and critical acclaim of contemporary works such as BoJack Horseman, True Detective, and Rick and Morty exploring existential nihilism make it one of the most popular philosophical views in folk philosophy.

It has been revealed that in his defence of scientism, Alex Rosenberg makes the case that many of “life’s persistent questions” can be answered by science, among them: “Is there a God? No. […] What is the purpose of the universe? There is none. What is the meaning of life? Ditto. Why am I here? Just dumb luck.” It is no coincidence that these answers closely mimic the diagnosis provided by (the atheists among) existentialist thinkers. This line of argument is common in at least the atheistic tradition of existentialism.

In a recent development, but in the face of evil and chaos, it is questionable whether, even with the existence of a supposed deity, our lives are bestowed with any meaning. Theistic existentialists like Kierkegaard, Shestov, and Jaspers would deny such.

Sources indicate that the absurd stems from the fact that though life is without meaning and the universe devoid of purpose, man still longs for meaning, significance, and purpose. For existential thinkers like Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Sartre, and Camus, this conflict was central to their philosophy.

The Woodland version is bigger and more powerful than the standard Toyota bZ, and it may be a better deal right now.

Toyota now sells three electric SUVs in the US (see which one is the best fit for you): the bZ (previously called the bZ4Z), C-HR, and bZ Woodland.

The C-HR is a smaller, sportier crossover SUV, while the bZ Woodland adds a larger, more rugged option.

Toyota is at the moment offering a deal on the 2026 bZ Woodland for Black Friday that might be worth a look.

In a recent development, the deal includes 0% APR financing for 72 months, plus an extra $1,000 Holiday Bonus Cash. Toyota said that if you finance a latest 2026 bZ Woodland for 72 payments, it will cost $13.89 for every $1,000 financed.

In comparison, the standard 2026 bZ is available with 1.99% interest for 72 months at $14.75 for every $1,000 financed.

For leasing, the standard 2026 Toyota bZ is cheaper, starting at $369 per month. The deal is for a 36-month lease with $4,369 due at signing for an effective cost of $490 per month.

However, that’s for the single-motor FWD version. Upgrading to AWD will cost around $606 a month for the same 36-month lease with $4,369 due at signing.

Toyota is promoting 2026 bZ Woodland leases as low as $449 a month. That’s also for a 36-month lease with $4,448 due at signing.

The Toyota bZ Woodland comes standard with a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain, delivering a combined 375 horsepower, which is 37 hp more than the standard bZ SUV with AWD.

Toyota’s standard bZ is offered with FWD and AWD powertrains. FWD models deliver either 165 hp (XLE FWD) or 221 hp (XLE FWD Plus and Limited FWD), while AWD models produce a combined 338 hp.

The Woodland model is also 6″ longer than the standard bZ, opening up an additional 30 cubic feet of cargo space on the inside.

Toyota’s bigger SUV also adds a rugged look and off-road capabilities with 8.3″ of ground clearance and up to 3,500 lbs of towing capacity.

Other rugged upgrades are standard, including All-Terrain tires, black side molding, roof rails, and black wheel arch cladding.

Inside, both come with a 7″ digital cluster and a large 14″ touchscreen running the latest Toyota Audio Multimedia system with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

Although it uses the same 74.7-kWh battery as the standard bZ, the Woodland version offers slightly less driving range because of the added power and off-road equipment. The 2027 bZ Woodland has an estimated range of up to 281 miles with all-season tires, or 260 miles with the optional all-terrain tires.

Industry observers note that in comparison, the bZ is available with two battery packs: 57.7 kWh and 74.7 kWh. The base XLE FWD uses the 57.7 kWh battery, while the XLE AWD and FWD Plus, Limited AWD, and FWD models use the 74.7 kWh battery.

The standard 57.7 kWh battery provides an EPA range of up to 236 miles, while the 74.7 kWh battery provides up to 314 miles for FWD and 288 miles for AWD.

Both the bZ and bZ Woodland have a native NACS port, so drivers can use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. It takes around 30 minutes to charge the battery from 10% to 80%.

The 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland is available in Base and Premium trims, starting at $45,380, or over $10,000 more than the standard bZ.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THE HOLIDAYS AND GLP-1 can feel like a cruel joke. Mashed potatoes and gravy? Come on. Pumpkin pie? Dude. Your grandma’s urge to Eat! Eat! What’s wrong with you? It can be a lot.Luckily, we’re far enough along in this whole GLP-1 experience that researchers and experts now know how people who take the weight-loss medications can not only survive the holidays—but actually enjoy them, gravy and all. We talked to some of these smart people to come up with your GLP-1 game plan—both at the table, and for around the table when those relatives you only see once a year get sassy.

A POPULAR STRATEGY is to skip a dose for the holiday week. But doctors tend to recommend against this strategy.

Recent findings suggest that vijay Kasi, MD, PhD, cardiologist at Orlando Health states that you might even experience short-term changes in blood pressure and blood sugar spikes, which is really only a concern if you are diabetic. Now would missing one GLP-1 dose severely impact the heart? Not really.

Sources indicate that dr. Kasi states increased risk for cardiac events is more likely to happen when people quit the medication for good and slide back to unhealthy eating habits. A 2026 study found that any heart benefit from taking a GLP-1 disappears after two years. Those same people were linked to a 22 percent increased risk of stroke, heart attacks, and early death.

Sources indicate that but again, we’re talking about a week—not two years. So what’s wrong with resuming a day or two after the holiday? If you are still adamant about skipping a dose, resuming it immediately after is recommended. “If they ate a really large meal and then immediately took the medication, they may feel very uncomfortable,” says Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center. “But if they wait 24 hours and the meal has moved through their system, then it probably won't be as problematic.”.

According to recent reports, the real concern doctors have is if people continue to delay their GLP-1 schedule for multiple weeks. Dr. Ali states people stop feeling the effects a week after they stop the medication because that’s how long it stays in your system. Appetite returns and so does food noise—the persistent and intrusive thoughts related to cravings or obsessing over how much food you ate. Ashley Koff, RD, author of Your Best Shot, says other concerns that may promote overeating are that you no longer have a delay in gastric emptying and an alteration or sheer lack of fullness signaling. “When you stop this medication abruptly you go from [constant] sustained hormone back to your own which works at best for 2 to 5 minutes when triggered by food,” she says.

While one day of eating more than usual won’t make a significant change to your health, Dr. Kasi says that some people do struggle to get back on track after the holidays end. “For a few people, it may be easy, but a vast majority trying to break away from their established regimen might have problems.”.

DOCTORS ARE GENERALLY against taking a smaller dose than usual because it is not included in FDA guidelines for how to safely and effectively use a GLP-1. “If a lower dose wasn't effective for you beforehand, it's not going to be effective for you right before a holiday either,” claims Dr. Ali. “It’s similar to skipping a dose.”.

Recent findings suggest that there is one exception. Dr. Ali states people who have attained a healthy weight or reached their goal weight may be able to lower their dose or take it less frequently as a maintenance strategy.

“For some people who have been on it for a long time, they titrate down to the most effective dose,” states Heidi Skolnik, MS, CDN, nutritionist and author of Your GLP-1 Game Strategy. “You're trying to find what's the lowest amount that still is effective for you.”.

According to recent reports, lowering your GLP-1 dose is a conversation you’ll want to have with your doctor ahead of the holiday season. Experts say to avoid self-prescribing.

Recent findings suggest that IF YOU’RE ON a GLP-1, your plate will likely look different from your relatives who are scooping up massive portions of carb-heavy sides. With a lower tolerance for small portions and a change in appetite, your choices will involve a delicate balance of trying to meet your nutritional needs while also not making your stomach hurt from overindulging. You can, of course, still enjoy as many courses as you like.

If you are going to someone’s house, Skolnik advises calling ahead and asking what’s on the menu so you can proposal in advance. For appetizers, you’ll want to avoid any high-fat items. “It's okay if you don't hit your protein and fiber goals. But what you don't want to do is eat a lot of high fat,” she says. “This is because your gastric system is slowing down. With high-fat foods, you may not digest all of that.”.

Industry observers note that not sure what’s high-fat or not? Play it safe and bring your own appetizer. Not only are you being a hospitable guest, but you’ll have something you can eat. Skolnik recommends:.

According to recent reports, don’t think that you’re banned from eating any certain foods, but with small portions, you have to know if it’s worth indulging. Koff says to use the "Delicious to Me" rule. Stop after the first bite to assess how much you enjoy the food. “I give them what that means on a scale they devise from 1 to 10, where a 7 or greater means it’s delicious and a go.”.

In a recent development, so include those carb-heavy sides like mac and cheese and creamy mashed potatoes—just keep it to around a quarter of your plate. The majority of your plate should include a mix of vegetables and protein, which Skolnik states is usually manageable with turkey.

Common side effects of GLP-1 use include nausea from drinking and a reduced craving for alcohol. If you can tolerate one or two, both dietitians say to go for it. A drinking variation of the “Delicious to Me” strategy is the “9 Sips” rule. “You still need to factor in what sugar, caffeine, and alcohol will do but a smaller amount is the win while still enjoying,” states Koff. You’ll also want to drink water at regular intervals while you’re drinking.

Industry observers note that if you want to avoid being pressured into drinking, Skolnik says to also have a drink on hand with a lime slice to give the appearance of an alcoholic drink. “Nobody has to know what's in your glass.”.

Industry observers note that no need to ruin a favorite dessert by trying to choose only high-protein items. If you want to save your appetite for an extra slice of pie, Koff notes to go for it. Just make sure to meet your nutritional needs in different ways as with a protein drink before dinner or supplements.

It has been revealed that IT’S NOT JUST the food you need to navigate; the interactions matter too. Depending on your family situation, you may need to set some firm boundaries on or redirect comments related to your weight or appetite. That doesn’t mean the holidays are the time to announce to everyone you’re on a GLP-1 (unless you want to). Some phrases you can use include:.

Industry observers note that skolnik indicates having an ally is extremely notable if you’re expecting other people to comment on your eating habits or your looks. They can help to redirect any uncomfortable conversation, provide support for your choices so you don’t feel isolated, or just provide emotional support. “Have someone else in the room with a code word or a look that signals them to intervene and change the conversation or divert attention away,” she says.

Even if you don’t have an ally physically next to you, have someone available on the phone that you can text or call. Skolnik states to escape to the bathroom if you need and use it as a place to recenter.

To avoid offending people who probably spent hours cooking, it can also be helpful to practice polite ways to turn down second helpings or pass on specific dishes.

“When the giving of food is looked at as love, the receiving of it is love,” notes Skolnik. “But you can still receive the love without the food.”.

#87231. Before public bathrooms, women were kept on a ‘urinary leash.’ Then department stores changed everything.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1712 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Before public bathrooms, women were kept on a ‘urinary leash.’ Then department stores changed everything.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What’s the weirdest thing you learned this week?
  • Today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty.
  • For most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What’s the weirdest thing you learned this week? Well, whatever it is, we promise you’ll have an even weirder answer if you listen to PopSci’s hit podcast. The Weirdest Thing I Learned This Week hits Spotify, YouTube, Apple, and everywhere else you listen to podcasts every-other Wednesday morning. It’s your new favorite source for the strangest science-adjacent facts, figures, and Wikipedia spirals the editors of Popular Science can muster. If you like the stories in this post, we guarantee you’ll love the show.

Today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty. VV’s co-host Kristina dove into the history of public toilets—and the longstanding lack thereof, at least for women.

For most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee. Historians call this the “urinary leash.”.

You might be wondering how this could possibly be a gendered issue, given the universality of the need to urinate. There was almost certainly a time when humans of all types could duck behind trees (or not) and relieve themselves with pretty similar levels of comfort and ease. But by the time Ancient Romans were using public latrines in the 2nd century BC, women of good standing weren’t supposed to go anywhere near them.

So when “monkey closets”—the first public flush toilets—debuted at London’s Great Exhibition in 1851, women didn’t benefit much. Some men thought women would be (or maybe should be) too embarrassed to enter a public restroom, so they were often excluded. And sometimes, if bathrooms were installed for women, they were sabotaged by men who took offense. By the time municipal toilets started popping up, they were often isolated and unsupervised, which meant even women willing to break the taboo had to worry about safety concerns. A woman on the go might come across a genteel lounge reserved for ladies, but they were designed for swooning in and kept decidedly toilet-free.

Ergo the “urinary leash”: you could only travel as far as your bladder allowed. That’s about two to five hours, if you don’t want to put your health at risk. Keep in mind that this was before cars, so a trip across the city would easily take up a good chunk of that time.

According to recent reports, the options when you were away from home were pretty grim. You could take a wide-stance squat over a grate, if you were desperate. On the one hand, bloomer crotches were split down the middle to allow for easy evacuation. On the other hand, a woman would have four to eight layers of skirts to try to protect from backsplash. Wealthy ladies might use a fancy porcelain urinal called a “bourdaloue.” (Fun fact: Many antique dealers now sell these as gravy boats.).

Industry observers note that the solution? Department stores. Obviously the actual solution was just providing women with decent public bathrooms, but no one bothered to do so until the owner of Marshall Field’s in Chicago realized that safe, clean toilets would draw women to the store—and allow them to shop for longer. Their luxurious facilities opened in 1907, and not a moment too soon. They featured extra-wide stalls (for bustles, naturally) and a staffed nursery.

Harry Selfridge, who rose up in the ranks at Marshall Field’s before striking out on his own, later took the idea to London when he opened his eponymous department store there. But he actually upped the ante and added hot running water, telephones, writing desks, and more. (Editor’s note: Please bring back department store coworking spaces.) Marshall Field’s and Selfridge’s weren’t doing this for the sake of women’s lib; a safe place to pee meant women could spend more time out of the house, which meant spending more money. But these spaces did set a precedent that helped activists push for women’s restrooms in more places, and they also made it easier for suffragists to hang out and strategize. In 2023, Selfridge’s celebrated its place in the history of peeing in public with Exhibition, an artwork by Gray Wielebinski reflecting on the rich cultural significance of communal bathrooms—and the threats they still face today.

In a recent development, these days, access to public bathrooms is nowhere near as widespread as it should be. That’s especially true for trans people, who have been subjected to a wave of state laws attempting to restrict which restrooms they can use. As the history of public toilets—and the dreaded urinary leash—should remind us, a bathroom isn’t “just a bathroom,” and restrictions on their use have a chilling effect on autonomy.

For more on the massive cultural impact of department stores, check out Vanity Veritas.

Recent findings suggest that because this week’s episode featured three special guests, I decided to keep my fact short. Cockney rhyming slang—a code that came out of East London in the 19th century—is not a subject I have a lot to say about, but it is something I want to make sure you know exists. Contrary to popular belief, there’s no strong evidence that this cheeky and cryptic lexicon arose to facilitate criminal acts. But whatever fueled its creation, it’s persisted in various subcultures to this day. The system works like this: pick a phrase that rhymes with the word you’re actually referring to, then drop the part that actually rhymes. Tricky? Yes. Whimsical? Very.

If you’ve ever wondered why that fart sound you make with your lips is called a “raspberry,” you have Cockney Rhyming Slang to thank. Fart rhymes with raspberry tart, which then gets shortened to raspberry. Things get stranger when you move into double and triple rhyme territory. “Bottle and glass” meant arse, so “bottle” did too. Then “bottle” got rhymed with Aristotle, which got shortened to “Aris,” which got rhymed with plaster of Paris. Congratulations, “plaster” now means butt.

You can check out a full dictionary of Cockney rhyming slang—with folks weighing in to confirm words or mark them as made-up “Mockney”.

Sources indicate that opera diva Maria Callas famously shed her weight with the help of a tapeworm, just like loads of Victorian women did. Right? Well, not quite. In fact, the truth is probably even more disgusting.

Actual opera singer (and Rachel’s sister!) Chelsea Feltman did a deep dive on Callas for Vanity Veritas a while back, so she dove into the nitty gritty of the tapeworm myth for this week’s Weirdest Thing.

It has been revealed that maria Callas really did drop a troubling amount of weight over the course of 18 months in the 1950s, and she really did have a beef tapeworm. But according to a 2022 review in Parasitologia, the idea that the tapeworm was her go-to weightloss hack is actually backwards. She most likely caught the tapeworm as the result of the high-protein, rare-meat diet she favored for weight loss. Sources disagree on whether Callas ever infected herself on purpose, but the fact remains that this parasite was not a diet hack: Even a five-meter beef tapeworm wouldn’t cause much weight loss, though it could definitely leave you vitamin-deficient. Some tapeworms can even form cysts in your brain.

Industry observers note that the idea of popping worm pills popped up in December 1912, when the Washington Post reported that a society woman in Peoria had paid for two suspicious capsules that her husband then analyzed. Inside, he said, he found tapeworm parts. The woman, the vendor, and the government agent were never named, which strongly suggests this story was probably at least kinda made up. The next day, the surgeon general said he’d never seen such a pill, and the Hygienic Laboratory’s director called it the wildest story he’d heard in a while. The legend kept growing anyway, with a bigger price tag in an Ohio paper in 1914 and a comic-strip “diet doctor” with wriggling capsules in 1927. It may even trace back to an 1899 Indiana medicine-show man arrested for giving patients artificial tapeworms to “pass” as proof his cure worked. Mostly, this seems to be a cultural meme that served to mock vain, silly women.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, this hasn’t stopped real people from trying to take advantage of this fake historical trend. In 2013, Iowa’s state medical director warned about a patient who’d swallowed a tapeworm they bought online.

(If you’re looking for the picture of the cheese-baited tapeworm-catching device, here you go.).

In the early 20th century, about 100 American women died of cervical cancer every day. The only diagnostic test was a biopsy, and by the time women experienced symptoms it was usually too late for anyone to help them. The test that changed it all came from a Greek immigrant who never set out to find it.

George Papanicolaou moved to Newly introduced York in 1913 and drifted through odd jobs, including playing violin in a restaurant and a stint as a famously bad carpet salesman. He finally landed a lab gig under Charles Stockard, a prominent eugenicist who wanted to understand human reproduction as a means of better controlling it (ugh). There, Papanicolaou found he could swab live guinea pigs for cervical cells instead of doing invasive biopsies. He wondered whether the method would work on humans.

His wife Mary became (human) guinea pig number one. For 21 years, she gave a sample almost every day—roughly 7,600 pap smears—while also staining slides, recruiting friends, and later training the technicians who read results. George introduced her to people as “my wife and victim.”.

In 1925 George spotted cancer cells in a hospital sample. He took that historic discovery to a 1928 conference sponsored by eugenicists, where he presented blurry slides to doctors who preferred the biopsy method over his smear concept. Things… didn’t go well.

According to recent reports, it took Stockard’s death, a upcoming boss for George, a collaboration testing more than 3,000 women, and artist Hashime Murayama’s vivid cell illustrations to turn the test into a medical landmark. By the late 1950s, women were lining up around the block for pap smears, and US cervical cancer deaths fell by about 70 percent.

Latest Update: Why Cancer Biomarker Testing Is Personal for Mark-Paul Gosselaar

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Known for his iconic roles on “Saved by the Bell,” “NYPD Blue,” “Franklin & Bash,” and “Found,” Mark-Paul Gosselaar knows how to grab an audience.
  • Now, he’s using that star power to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing while sharing how he prioritizes his own health and well-being.
  • “Health is a huge thing for my wife and I, and our family,” Gosselaar told Healthline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Known for his iconic roles on “Saved by the Bell,” “NYPD Blue,” “Franklin & Bash,” and “Found,” Mark-Paul Gosselaar knows how to grab an audience.

Now, he’s using that star power to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing while sharing how he prioritizes his own health and well-being.

“Health is a huge thing for my wife and I, and our family,” Gosselaar told Healthline. “We are constantly aware of new technologies.”.

Having seen people in his life navigate cancer diagnoses, Gosselaar is now raising awareness about the role of biomarker testing in cancer treatment through his partnership with AstraZeneca and its Meet Your Mark campaign.

According to recent reports, the campaign aims to educate people facing cancer diagnoses and their loved ones about how biomarker testing may help doctors make more informed, personalized treatment decisions. It also encourages patients to discuss testing with their healthcare teams.

“Biomarkers may tell doctors the specific type of cancer present and if targeted therapies or immunotherapy might help,” Mark Socinski, MD, oncologist and Executive Medical Director of the AdventHealth Cancer Institute, told Healthline.

He explained that biomarkers are typically genes or proteins that doctors measure through blood or tissue tests. They are used to help guide treatment in numerous diseases but are especially powerful tools in many types of cancer.

In a recent development, “They help decode why cancers behave differently, even when two people have the same cancer type,” said Socinski. “However, while biomarker testing provides useful information, it does not guarantee a specific outcome.”.

Despite those limitations, Socinski sees promise in the shift from one-size-fits-all cancer treatment to care tailored to each patient’s specific cancer characteristics.

Industry observers note that “Biomarker testing does play a critical role here, and it is important for people to be aware of the potential benefits,” Socinski said. “It may help change the course of a person’s treatment journey.”.

Gosselaar hopes that greater awareness of biomarker testing can help people facing a cancer diagnosis feel more informed about their treatment options.

It has been revealed that “A lot of the time, when a loved one or someone who has been diagnosed with cancer [it can] feel like your world is in a tailspin,” he said. “I wanted to get the word out for anyone who’s going through a cancer diagnosis, or a caretaker, to know that biomarker testing is an option, because even though two cancers are similar, their tumors can act very differently and biomarker testing may help the medical expert with more personalized treatment.”.

As part of the campaign, Gosselaar took part in a commercial, something he hadn’t done since before his days on “Saved by the Bell.”.

“This was the first time that I actually had to be on set and not be a character; I had to be me talking about this very serious glitch,” he said.

While it was a challenging experience, he mentioned it was also fulfilling.

In a recent development, “I enjoyed the process, and to be able to use my platform to be able to spread the word; it means a lot to me,” he said. “I’m very selective of the things that I want to attach myself to, and this seemed like the right fit.”.

He particularly enjoyed recreating Zack Morris’s signature “timeout” gesture from “Saved by the Bell,” which allowed his character to freeze time and speak directly to the camera.

“Using something from the past that was such a symbolic gesture to so many people of my generation that are now my age and possibly going through [cancer] or knowing someone who’s going through [cancer to] direct them to [this campaign], means a lot,” he remarked.

Beyond his efforts to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing, Gosselaar is equally focused on taking care of his own health.

In a recent development, getting quality sleep is one of his top priorities. He sleeps on a high-tech mattress that monitors sleep stages, heart rate, heart rate variability, and respiratory rate. He also uses a biometric health and fitness tracker, prioritizes healthy eating, and uses saunas and red light therapy.

“We do everything that we possibly can, but I’m less about longevity and more about just living a healthy lifestyle,” Gosselaar said. “I want to continue doing the things that I’ve done since I was a child…without feeling held back by my health.”.

Industry observers note that as he embraces his 50s, he said he’d like to live a long life for his children and future grandchildren. He started taking his health seriously in his 40s after undergoing shoulder surgery.

“[It] really made me realize [that] all the damage I had done in my 20s and 30s sort of adds up later in life, and that’s probably something that I would tell the younger me… to preserve a little bit more and take [an] approach that recovery is just as important as the workout because I did not use my recovery very well; it was not a priority for me,” stated Gosselaar.

He also makes time for himself every day. He said doing so makes him a better person and more able to care for his wife and four children.

According to recent reports, “[It’s] something that I believe in; that I need to do something for myself before I can do something for someone else. Or if I do something for someone else, then I have to equalize that by doing something for me,” he noted.

Daily physical activity also helps support his mental well-being.

Recent findings suggest that “I need to do something where I challenge myself, and it could be as simple as a walk. It could be as simple as just getting outside and lifting something heavy [or] taking bags of groceries and taking the long way into your house,” Gosselaar remarked.

“Like challenging yourself with picking up things, you know, taking backpacks from the car from your kids and seeing if you can carry three in one hand…or going into the gym and spending an hour in the gym, or 30 minutes, or just moving.”.

When he’s in the sauna, he works on breathing and clearing his thoughts.

Recent findings suggest that “Some people need to meditate, some people need to talk to somebody. I encourage all of that because I think all of that helps,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve done them all. I’ve done the cold plunging, I’ve done all that stuff…some of it works, and some of it doesn’t; it’s whatever you believe in. So I just encourage people to stay healthy and move, get outside, and help other people.”.

#87229. Rejecting Oppression, Embracing Joy

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (882 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Rejecting Oppression, Embracing Joy

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • What makes a literary character—or a living person you’ve just met—seem intensely human?
  • In a recent study of over 400 readers, 19 percent reported “experiential crossing” in which the language and characters of a book they were reading entered their daily lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

What makes a literary character—or a living person you’ve just met—seem intensely human? Besides the movements people make and the sensations they describe, their attitudes can show their humanity. In literature, characters who resist social oppression make more compelling protagonists than those who quietly occupy a society's bottom rungs. Most inspiring of all may be characters shocked by abuse because, despite poverty, sexism, and racism, they believe they deserve joyful lives.

In a recent study of over 400 readers, 19 percent reported “experiential crossing” in which the language and characters of a book they were reading entered their daily lives. “It’s as if the character has started to narrate my world,” wrote one participant (Alderson-Day et al. 2017). Getting to know literary characters can broaden readers’ understandings of human life if those characters’ experiences differ from readers' own.

Sources indicate that when characters’ experiences match those of readers, their crossover into readers’ worlds can feel life-affirming, especially if their experiences rarely appear in published fiction. At a book signing in Cambridge, a woman thanked author Junot Díaz for creating Beli, a central character in his novel The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao. “I had a life a lot like Beli’s,” the reader told him. Tears kept her from saying more (Díaz 2018).

Born in the Dominican Republic, Belicia (Beli) Cabral is sold as a child after her mother dies and her father is imprisoned for offending the dictator, Rafael Trujillo. During her nine years as a slave, her “father” burns her back with hot oil when she tries to attend school. After a distant relative rescues Beli, she grows into a tall, strikingly beautiful young woman. A relationship with Trujillo’s brother-in-law wrecks her life, however, when his henchmen force her to have an abortion and beat her nearly to death. She escapes to Newly introduced Jersey, where she marries, but her husband abandons her and their two children. To support her son and daughter, she works several minimum-wage jobs, persisting even after she develops breast cancer. Beli is abusive and violent not just to her children but to neighbors, shoppers, and police officers. Throughout her life, she retains her sense of self-worth, refusing to believe she should be exploited because she is female, Dominican, and Black.

Sources indicate that recent studies affirm that the suppressed emotions caused by social inequality harm people’s physical and mental health (Kiehl 2024). The effects of racism have received more attention than those of social class, whose influence many people still deny (Kiehl 2024). Beli and readers who see their lives in hers experience disrespect caused by sexism as well. Her ability to inspire readers stems not from her suffering, however, but from her sense that she is inferior to no one and deserves a good life.

Junot Díaz’s character-narrator, Yunior, hints that Beli can’t see disaster coming because even after being enslaved and burned, she can’t imagine how badly people will treat her. “Like everybody in this damn story,” he writes, “she underestimated the depth of the shit she was in” (Díaz 2007). Beli’s refusal to accept that she is in danger highlights not just her sense of self-worth but her belief (at least in her youth) in other people’s goodness. Yunior illustrates her capacity for joy, which blazes forth in her dancing. A complex character, Beli terrorizes her neighborhood and hurts her children, but her humanity is never in doubt. Her will to survive and her rejection of abuse ensure that whether or not readers see themselves in her, she will enter and inhabit their lives.

Like lay readers, psychologists can learn from imagining Beli because in creating characters, authors build models of minds (Alderson-Day et al. 2017; Bernini 2021). Participants in psychological experiments still come disproportionately from “WEIRD” (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) populations, especially North American and European universities (Henrich et al. 2010). Novels like Díaz’s Oscar Wao guide readers to imagine the mental world of a woman who experiences horrors but retains her self-worth and desire for joy. Until scientific studies can include more of the world’s population, literature can complement information revealed through experiments by making a wider range of human experiences imaginable. Most human of all may be the belief that no matter how other people see you, you deserve to thrive.

Sources indicate that alderson-Day, B., Bernini, M., & Fernyhough, C. (2017). Uncharted features and dynamics of reading: Voices, characters, and crossing of experiences. Consciousness and Cognition 49, 98-109.

It has been revealed that bernini, M. (2021). Becket and the Cognitive Method: Mind, Models, and Exploratory Narratives. New York: Oxford University Press.

Díaz, J. (2007). The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao. Newly introduced York: Penguin.

Díaz, J. (9 April 2018). The silence. The Latest Yorker, 24-28.

Henrich, J., Heine, S. J., & Norenzayan, A. (2010). The weirdest people in the world? Behavioral and Brain Sciences 33 (2-3), 61-83.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Volkswagen’s revived Scout brand finally has vehicles coming off the line in South Carolina, but they’re validation units, not customer cars.
  • That’s two years later than the 2026 production start the manufacturer was talking about before it even broke ground on its $2 billion factory.
  • Sources indicate that according to Scout’s announcement dated November 12, construction at the Production Center north of Columbia is in its final phase and most of the manufacturing equipment is installed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Volkswagen’s revived Scout brand finally has vehicles coming off the line in South Carolina, but they’re validation units, not customer cars. Scout confirms the first deliveries of the Traveler SUV and Terra pickup won’t happen until 2028.

That’s two years later than the 2026 production start the manufacturer was talking about before it even broke ground on its $2 billion factory.

Sources indicate that according to Scout’s announcement dated November 12, construction at the Production Center north of Columbia is in its final phase and most of the manufacturing equipment is installed. The Body Shop, Paint Shop, and Assembly Shop are all being used for the first validation builds.

The Body Shop is the most automated part of the plant. Scout says more than 750 robots join roughly 160 parts into each body, laying down about 5,000 weld points per vehicle, with AI-supported weld monitoring and a metrology system checking the results. At full capacity, the shop is designed to handle about 40 vehicles per hour.

Bodies then go through an electrified paint shop before landing in final assembly, where they’re married to the chassis and get their wiring, glass, seats, and wheels.

CEO Scott Keogh is clearly happy to have something physical to point to, saying that “what we are building in Blythewood is no longer a promise on paper.”.

Sources indicate that scout also shared photos of a Terra pickup and a Traveler parked inside the plant. Its own fine print notes that they show “concept and validation vehicles” with optional features, so don’t read too much into what’s on display:.

It has been revealed that fair enough. But Scout is also careful about what this stage is. Teams are confirming the equipment is installed and works, and checking engineering, buildability, and parts maturity. Process validation and scaling up to production speed come later. Validation builds will continue “into 2027,” followed by pre-production builds, and then customer deliveries in 2028.

The tech giant says the plant will create more than 4,000 jobs, and it’s spending another $300 million on an onsite supplier park expected to support about 1,000 supplier jobs.

When Keogh laid out the plan in late 2023, Scout mentioned it would start production in 2026 with deliveries shortly after. That was still the target when Scout broke ground in Blythewood in February 2024.

In a recent development, by the Traveler and Terra unveiling in October 2024, production had moved to 2027. Keogh then said in March that he expects the first customer to get a vehicle “sometime in 2028,” and that’s now the official line in Scout’s own press materials.

Sources indicate that it might not even be the end of it. Industry forecaster AutoForecast Solutions has the Traveler starting production in September 2028 and the Terra in March 2030. Scout hasn’t confirmed those dates, but it hasn’t given more precise ones either.

The product itself has also changed under the hood. Scout launched as a pure EV brand, then added the “Harvester” range-extender option at the reveal. According to Keogh, Scout has more than 160,000 reservations, and 87% of them are for the gas-generator version. Those are $100 refundable reservations, not orders.

Der Spiegel reported earlier this year that integrating the range extender, which wasn’t part of the original plan, was among the technical problems pushing the timeline back.

In a recent development, for comparison, Tesla unveiled the Cybertruck in November 2019 and delivered the first ones four years later, a delay that was widely mocked. Scout is now on a similar four-year path from reveal to customer, and that’s for the SUV it’s launching first.

A working body shop with 750 robots isn’t vaporware. Scout has a real factory, a real workforce, and two vehicles that people clearly want. 160,000 reservations is a substantial number for a brand that hasn’t sold a single vehicle in 46 years.

But validation builds are an early step, not a finish line. Scout still has to go through pre-production, prove its processes, and ramp to rate, and every one of those stages is where fresh automakers usually lose time. Rivian and Lucid both learned that the hard way.

September 28? So we're 23 months away? I'm surprised the validation build yadda yadda stuff is supposed to take so long. It's not like VW doesn't know how to do this stuff, and that's a lot of money and equipment to sit mostly idle while 180,000 reservations holders are waiting for their cars. Maybe they're waiting for the market to change or are considering a whole other brand or product line?

According to recent reports, and the market Scout was designed for in 2022 no longer exists. The EV tax credit is gone, and most of Scout’s own reservation holders picked the gas generator. In the US, the range-extender market is still early, unlike in China, where they are already popular.

Industry observers note that but by 2028, Ford, Ram, and Jeep all plan to have range-extended trucks and SUVs on sale. Scout’s main advantage was being early with a cool, rugged, American-built electric truck. That advantage shrinks every quarter.

Recent findings suggest that we’re still rooting for these vehicles. The Traveler and Terra are among the best-looking designs in the segment. But a $100 reservation is easy to walk away from, and the question is how many of those 160,000 people are still waiting in 2028.

Latest Update: Boost and Booster Seats: Comparing the Turbocharged 2026 VW Tiguan and Mazda CX-50

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The horsepower wars are not relegated to machines purpose-built for performance.
  • In a recent development, of course, building a holistically satisfying family car involves more than just adding power.
  • Both models here—the Tiguan SEL R-Line and the CX-50 Premium Plus—represent the pinnacle of their lineups and are thus quite expensive as far as small family SUVs go.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The horsepower wars are not relegated to machines purpose-built for performance. Nowadays, it feels like nearly every automaker has some sort of higher-output solution available across a surprisingly wide swath of its fleet, including seemingly pedestrian family vehicles. Some might come via electrification, but in the case of the two vehicles before us today—the 2026 Volkswagen Tiguan and 2026 Mazda CX-50—these hi-po conveyances twist the asphalt with good old-fashioned gasoline and turbochargers.

In a recent development, of course, building a holistically satisfying family car involves more than just adding power. Extra oomph might satisfy the driver, but automakers must pay attention to a whole host of other factors to make things just as peachy for the passengers. Let’s see which of these two compact SUVs does just that.

Both models here—the Tiguan SEL R-Line and the CX-50 Premium Plus—represent the pinnacle of their lineups and are thus quite expensive as far as small family SUVs go. The Tiguan’s lineup starts at $32,280 for the S, and our tester bookends the other side of the offerings at $46,170 as tested. The CX-50 is less expensive, starting at $31,395 for the Select model; our range-topper’s window sticker came in slightly more affordable than the VW’s at $45,210.

See all results for new 2026 Mazda CX-50 for sale near 07047.

It has been revealed that neither of these vehicles is a screaming deal, but you can save a bit of scratch on the VW. Skip our car’s $850 Avocado Green paint, $405 auto-dimming rearview mirror, and $365 in floor mats and bumper protectors, and the price delta evens out. Our Mazda’s Cypress Green paint was only $200 by comparison; all-weather floor mats and a cargo liner added another $390 to its bottom line.

Since both models are the top of their pops, you get a stout list of features. The CX-50’s Premium Plus niceties include a surround-view camera, auto-dimming inside and side-view mirrors, rear automatic braking, and blind-spot monitoring. The Tiguan SEL R-Line takes things a step further with massaging front seats (something Mazda doesn’t offer on any vehicle it sells), plus a more aggressive R-Line appearance package that deletes most of the brightwork around the windows and front fascia.

According to recent reports, looks can be deceiving. The Tiguan’s boxy form may appear larger in all dimensions, but it exceeds the Mazda only in overall width (by nearly four inches, including mirrors) and height (by two to three inches). The CX-50 has about an inch more overall length, wheelbase, and ride height.

In a recent development, slip inside, and the CX-50 puts more stock in front legroom, where it beats the Tiguan, but the Mazda’s rear passengers must make do with fractionally less gam space. Owing in part to its more upright body shape, the Tiguan takes the cargo-capacity crown, offering better volume whether the rear seats are up or down.

See all results for latest 2026 Mazda CX-50 for sale near 07047.

When it comes to cabin aesthetics, both are swinging for the fences. The CX-50’s white-on-black interior carries plush touch points and premium materials, and we love how many physical buttons, dials, and switches exist across nearly every surface. The tucked-away infotainment screen feels like a vestige of an earlier age, and it sort of is—the CX-50 is due for an update that brings it in line with the latest CX-5, for better or worse (read our latest long-term CX-5 update for more on that).

HIGHS: More guts than the average canopic jar, superb bump suppression, feels fancy.LOWS: Creature-comfort corner cutting, tighter rear-seat accommodations, not a highway-fuel-economy hero.VERDICT: A rocket that could use more pockets.

The Tiguan’s cabin is also top-notch. Our tester’s two-tone brown and black interior looks and feels no less luxurious than an Audi’s, and we enjoyed the door-to-door strip of wood, which adds some extra variety. Of course, the latest-gen Tiguan is all about the screens, which in this case comprise a normal digital gauge display and a 15-inch repurposed highway billboard. In addition to having more cargo capacity, the Tiguan also has more places to stash your stuff.

According to recent reports, we have one weird thing to point out, but it’s bound to be vital to somebody. Both cars have heated steering wheels, but the Mazda’s heating element seems confined to between 9 and 10 o’clock on the left and between 2 and 3 o’clock on the right, while the rest of the tiller remains icy to the touch. Volkswagen’s engineers, on the other hand, smartly realized that if you pay for a heated steering wheel, you probably want one that’s warm the whole way around.

Even among high-strung turbo fours, the No Replacement for Displacement adage still holds true. The Mazda CX-50’s 256-hp turbocharged 2.5-liter makes less horsepower than the Tiguan, but the larger mill churns out an absurd 320 pound-feet of torque. All-wheel drive is standard, as is an archaic six-speed automatic transmission. The CX-50 is the lightweight here, tipping the scales at 3864 pounds.

In a recent development, by comparison, the Tiguan’s 2.0-liter turbo four makes just 258 pound-feet of torque, but at 268 horses, it bests the Mazda on raw horsepower. All-wheel drive is standard here as well, and the transmission is a more modern-feeling eight-speed auto. The whole Teutonic shebang carries about one more human’s worth of mass in its structure, weighing 4023 pounds on our scales.

In a recent development, if you’re assuming that the lighter, more torquey SUV will outperform its competition, you’re right, but the gap is small. The last CX-50 we tested hustles to 60 mph in 6.4 seconds—two-tenths ahead of the Tiguan—and the Mazda’s 167-foot stop from 70 mph bests the VW by nine feet. From there, things really tighten up: The CX-50’s 14.9-second, 92-mph quarter-mile sprint is just a hair ahead of the Tiguan’s 15.0 seconds at 96 mph. With a 5-mph rolling start, the two reach 60 within a tenth of each other. From 50 to 70, the Vee-Dub takes the lead, requiring just 4.5 seconds to the Mazda’s 4.8. The Mazda notches a victory around the skidpad, maintaining 0.84 g of lateral grip against the Volkswagen’s 0.78 g.

HIGHS: Posh cabin trimmings, slightly more spacious inside, the most fun we’ve had in a VW SUV in a while.LOWS: Not our favorite infotainment interface, not our favorite brake pedal, traditional German road compliance.VERDICT: Fun for the whole family, driver included.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, the CX-50’s lighter curb weight and slicker-looking silhouette don’t translate to stonkin’ fuel-economy benefits. The two vehicles are nearly evenly matched by EPA estimates—both earned 29-mpg highway and 25-mpg combined ratings, but the Mazda’s 23-mpg city value tops the VW’s by one. The script flipped on our real-world 75-mph highway fuel-economy test, however, where the Tiguan overachieved with a 31-mpg result, out-skinflinting the 28-mpg Mazda, which fell short of its EPA highway estimate.

According to recent reports, both SUVs are fun to drive and reward time spent behind the wheel, with each vehicle carrying its own little idiosyncrasies. There are a few parts of the driving experience where we think the CX-50 shines, and others where the Tiguan feels better.

According to recent reports, the Mazda’s cabin may be louder at wide-open throttle (and tied at a 70-mph cruise), but overall, it seems quieter in day-to-day operation, especially over the zydeco washboards that Ann Arbor calls roads. The CX-50’s bump damping is superior, making for a slightly more luxurious ride quality than the Tiguan, which carries some of that stereotypical German stiffness in its suspension tuning—but one person’s “flinty” is another person’s “composed,” so it really boils down to whether you want that additional poise in your daily driving. (The Tiguan SE and base S offer smaller wheels with cushier tire sidewalls.).

Industry observers note that when it comes to pedal feel, the Mazda takes the crown; the Tiguan’s brake pedal is a little mushy, and the throttle is a little too eager to open ’er up with a gentle tip-in. On the other hand, we preferred the Volkswagen’s heftier steering feel. The Mazda’s six-speed automatic handles gear changes deftly, but it’s clear from our on-ramp-style acceleration testing that the VW’s two extra gears are, in fact, providing a benefit. (Highway fuel-economy results reflect that as well.) It’s not like you’ll notice either gearbox doing its job, though.

By the skin of its teeth, the Volkswagen Tiguan claims the championship belt that it lost to the Mazda CX-50 in a 2024 two-car comparo. Back then, we said the CX-50 was worth the upcharge over the more efficient, more spacious Volkswagen because we preferred the Mazda’s cabin and driving dynamics.

According to recent reports, now, the Tiguan is the one that costs more, and while it remains more efficient and more spacious than the CX-50, it picked up some major slack in the interior-design department, and it drives just about as well. The 2026 Tiguan is an excellent all-rounder. It’s a wonder what a newly introduced generation can do.

Mathematicians make a breakthrough in 174-year-old problem

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, while mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers.
  • Recent findings suggest that the underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward.
  • Industry observers note that it took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, while mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers. For some in the field, their fascination with the perniciously complex concept runs so deep, that they liken their obsession to a lingering disease. But after a decade of analysis, an international team of mathematicians has made the first major breakthrough in the ongoing Four-Color Problem saga in 30 years. At this year’s Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS) conference, investigators laid out the optimal, most efficient algorithm that solves the Four-Color Problem.

Recent findings suggest that the underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward. In 1852, 19th century English mathematician Francis Guthrie posited that you only need a quartet of hues to fill every border-enclosed region on a map. Think all territories, regions, states, and nations filled in with only four colors. The first proof was introduced in 1879, and seemed solid for 11 years. That is, until Guthrie’s colleagues found an error in the calculations.

Industry observers note that it took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program. However, many in the mathematical community took issue with the digital discovery after having difficulty verifying it themselves.

According to recent reports, A more accessible proof arrived in 1997, but even then, the algorithmic system became painfully slow as sample maps grew larger. A handful of mathematicians around the world have pondered upcoming approaches to the problem ever since—including University of Copenhagen computer scientist Mikkel Thorup, who likens his interest to a “four-color disease.”.

Industry observers note that “I would guess that at least 1,000 mathematicians have caught the four-color disease, spending months trying to make it work but never quite succeeding,” Thorup mentioned in a university profile. “It is the disease people have suffered from since 1852.”.

In a recent development, it took years, but Thorup and his colleagues made progress after uncovering a novel detail regarding map-like surfaces known as planar graphs. The researchers realized these graphs feature many more reducible arrangements than experts previously assumed. This provided them a much more discreet set of starting points.

“Think of reducible configurations as handles you can grab hold on to start four-coloring,” added study co-author and Technical University of Denmark (DTU) mathematician Carsten Thomassen. “We show that graphs do not contain just one handle, but an astonishing number of them. Nobody knew that before.”.

Instead of one or two handles in a graph, the team could now identify many more handles throughout any given map. This allowed them to simultaneously begin filling regions with four colors, which exponentially quickened the overall process. Thomassen stated this boosted their algorithm from quadratic time (where calculation speed increases proportionally to the square of an input size) to linear time.

Sources indicate that “This means that if a map contains ten times as many regions, the computation only becomes about ten times slower. With the previous algorithm, it would have become about 100 times slower,” he added.

According to recent reports, but does this really change anything beyond theoretical mathematics? According to researchers, the answer is a resounding “yes.”.

“The remarkable thing is that because there are so many handles, the idea can also be applied to other kinds of surfaces besides a flat map,” noted Thorup. “For example, surfaces with holes, such as a swim ring or a piece of…cheese.”.

Okay, so the implications may be somewhat subtle for most people’s day-to-day lives. That doesn’t change the fact that mathematicians finally worked through symptoms of their disease for the first time in 30 years. As to why Thorup and his colleagues spent a decade on a theorem whose major immediate implications are “cheese,” he had a relatively succinct explanation.

“Because mathematicians are slightly crazy. Most of what mathematicians work on consists of very nerdy questions,” he said. “We become obsessed with this type of problem because it challenges the human intellect. And if we find the answer, we’ll probably also find answers to other mathematical puzzles.”.

  • After a particularly strong 2025—movies like One Battle After Another and Sinners proved to be true standouts—how does 2026 pick up?
  • Recent findings suggest that but we always like to look at not only what’s been good to date, but also what we can still be excited for—and that includes everything.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that AS A HUGE fan and follower of both movies and sports, the former has one major advantage: There's always something to look forward to. As a fan of the Latest York Jets, I don't always have that luxury. As a fan of watching films, though, not only is there always something worth my time on the major screen or streaming, but there's always several flicks down the line that will sound great or intriguing for one reason or another. Will they all turn out great? Of course not. But with sports and movies alike, excitement tends to be all about hope.

After a particularly strong 2025—movies like One Battle After Another and Sinners proved to be true standouts—how does 2026 pick up? With strength and energy, that's how. The year has been filled with all sorts of great movies, from horror (like 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and Obsession) to epics (like The Odyssey), to some pretty great comedies (like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie and The Invite). It’s been a good year.

Recent findings suggest that but we always like to look at not only what’s been good to date, but also what we can still be excited for—and that includes everything. We’re talking stuff on the calendar already, stuff we suspect could come out this year, and even stuff making noise in places like the Sundance Film Festival. Throughout the year, this list evolves from our most anticpated movies into our favorite movies, and always looks quite different in December than it did in January.

For now, we've got a lot we’ve loved, but still a lot to look forward to as well. Below, we've listed nearly 100 movies on our radar that we think you'll be really interested in seeing.

If you're interested in a killer chimpanzee B-movie slasher, then Primate is for you. The movie delivers what it promises. Ben the chimpanzee does some very terrible things on screen but it makes for quite an enjoyable experience.

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple.

Industry observers note that 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple is a direct sequel to last year's 28 Years Later. And while the great Danny Boyle doesn't return to direct, the movie is helmed by the more-than-capable Nia DaCosta and once again counts Alex Garland as its screenwriter. The real assets, though, are the movie's leads: Ralph Fiennes and Jack O'Connell are sensational, magnetic every minute they're on screen amidst all sorts of post-apocalyptic chaos. Bring on part three.

Here's a quick pitch for The Rip: Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. The longtime friends team up once again for The Rip, a cop thriller in the vein of movies you've probably seen several times before... but done particularly well. This twisty crime story involves a police team finding a ton of money in a stash house (the titular rip), and figuring out who may or may not be corrupt. In addition to our beloved duo, the cast is shockingly stacked: Steven Yeun, Kyle Chandler, Scott Adkins, and One Battle After AnotherAcademy Award nominee Teyana Taylor are all on board.

Industry observers note that SAM RAIMI FANS, ASSEMBLE! For the first time since 2009, the master of gross effects and frenetic cameras is back with an original horror story in Send Help. Rachel McAdams plays a Survivor superfan who gets stuck on an island with her dickhead boss (Dylan O'Brien), and then the antics begin. Think Cast Away meets Misery meets Drag Me to Hell. It's great stuff.

Sources indicate that jason Momoa and Dave Bautista are a pair of cool dudes who, with The Wrecking Crew, set out and did exactly what they intended to do: Make a badass buddy action comedy. The movie finds the pair playing estranged brothers who reunite in Hawaii to investigate their father's mysterious death; From there, we get lots of jokes, and a lot of (very violent!!!) action. It's a good time! Honestly, if they want to make a couple sequels to this, I'd be her for it.

Part This Is Spinal Tap, part Josie and the Pussycats, and part Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Moment is Charli XCX's movie for anyone who enjoys her music, persona, or both. A really fun movie about music, stardom, and celebrity in 2026.

Pillion was technically released initially in 2025 (and was also included on our list of favorite movies of that year), but we didn't want to miss an opportunity to recommend it to people once again. This unique film follows a man (Harry Melling) who engages in an unexpected BDSM relationship with a biker he meets at random (Alexander Skarsgård). The movie is quite the tonal balancing act, at times funny, intense, raunchy, and heartbreaking, but it all comes together by the end. A delightful movie, and a great showcase for both leads.

Industry observers note that the classic novel comes to life on the major screen once again, this time from Promising Young Woman and Saltburn director Emerald Fennell, and with Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi in the lead roles. Fennell, an Academy Award winner for her work on Promising Young Woman, has both big fans and big detractors at this point—but her take her, while book purists haven't been thrilled, is a big, visually stunning epic romance. Robbie and Elordi are both up to the task as well, bringing a charged energy to roles that really need it. Alison Oliver, who recently shined on HBO's Task, is another major highlight in a supporting role. An original soundtrack from Charli XCX helps to set the anachronistic mood and feels like a real cherry on top.

Recent findings suggest that this action-thriller, based on a book by Don Winslow, looks like a very solid entry in the genre that we're going to call "Somewhat Resembles a Michael Mann Film." And reviews have confirmed as much—the movie has often been compared to Heat, and while its tough to compare to Mann's 1995 masterpiece, we'll take just about anything in that vein. Look: If someone tells you there's gonna be a crime thriller in the vein of Heat with Chris Hemsworth, Mark Ruffalo, Halle Berry, and Barry Keoghan leading the cast, how could you not be on board?

One of our coolest directors, Gore Verbinski, makes his grand return with Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die—his first movie since 2016's A Cure For Wellness. If you don't know Verbinski by name, you should know several of his movies: the original Pirates of the Caribbean trilogy, The Ring, and Rango are among the standouts. Good Luck follows Sam Rockwell as a man who claims to be from the future and fighting off a rogue artificial intelligence. While the movie takes some pretty tough and labored tangents into on-the-nose satire, Rockwell's performance and the practical effects keep the movie afloat as a fun sci-fi romp.

Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie.

Despite the title, you don't need to know anything else about Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie before going to see it. Sure, this story of two inept dudes in a band who just want to play music at a bar—and go through all sorts of ordeals, including time-travel, to do it—has existed before in both web series and television series form. But you can just go in and laugh and the absolute madness of the movie. Trust us—you'll have a good time with this one if you're into "madness that makes you laugh." This is a long-term passion project of Matt Johnson, who became well known recently for directing the underrated BlackBerry. His brash talent is again on display here.

We're always in on Glen Powell, and How to Make a Killing marks his first foray into A24's world as a leading man. This black comedy neo-noir comes from Emily the Criminal director John Patton Ford and follows Powell as a man who decides to take out a few members of his family in order to increase his chance at making a whole bunch of money via inheritance. The supporting cast joining Powell isn't too shabby: Margaret Qualley, Jessica Henwick, Ed Harris, and Topher Grace are all along for the fun.

Recent findings suggest that the Napa Boys is a very specific cut for comedy fans. Remember when all those nondescript American Pie direct-to-video sequels were coming out? "American Pie Presents:.."? The Napa Boys imagines itself as one of those: self-impressed raunchy comedy with little tact—crossed, naturally with the wine bro nature of 2004's Sideways. As a result, we get a movie that presents as a sequel to a franchise that both has long been running out of juice, and, in our world, never was. If you get the truly absurd brand of parody being presented here, you're going to get a real kick out of it.

Industry observers note that hoppers feels like a throwback to the golden age of Pixar. Not only is it an original story (at a time when the legendary animation studio has often been leaning into sequels, prequels, and more), but it's a sweet and funny one at that. Following an animal-lover who uses Avatar-style technology to transfer her consciousness into a robotic beaver body that can discover what animals are thinking and saying, Hoppers actually turns into something of a conspiracy mystery story. With a voice cast that includes Jon Hamm, Dave Franco, and Meryl Streep among others, it's a fun one for the whole family.

Look. This is one of those movies that you really don't have to overthink. It's Alan Ritchson—Reacher himself—taking on a giant alien robot monster thing. This is as much of a throwback to '80s-style action filmmaking as we're ever going to get, and it delivers as promised. The fact that the rest of the cast includes staples like Jai Courtney, Esai Morales, and Dennis Quaid is just a bonus.

According to recent reports, undertone has been positioning itself as A24's next huge horror hit—and we'll see how it lands. The filmfollows a supernatural podcaster who gets sent some particularly spooky recordings; Its soundscape has brought tons of hype, with many calling it the scariest experience of the year. A simple premise like that sometimes makes for a very solid horror movie.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir(who also wrote The Martian), Project Hail Mary is a story of space exploration and a regular guy (played by Ryan Gosling) who gets involved. Phil Lord and Chris Miller (who are responsible for the Spider-Verse movies and directed 21 Jump Street) are behind the camera for this one, which has already proven to be a big, big hit. Gosling is basically on his own out in space for most of this, but it also includes a fun little alien guy named Rocky and a nice supporting performance by Anatomy of a Fall star Sandra Hüller. The visuals here are worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

Sources indicate that 2018's Ready or Not was one of the most fun horror films of the last decade, and now eight years later we get to see Samara Weaving's lead sucked back into the same twisted, bloody, violent games. The supporting cast—including David Cronenberg (!!!), March MH Flex star Elijah Wood, Sarah Michelle Gellar, and The Pitt's Shawn Hatosy—is fantastic. The movie kind of keeps with the form of the first Ready or Not, so if you liked that one, you'll certainly have a fun time with this one.

According to recent reports, forbidden Fruits follows a secret coven of witches operating in a shopping mall. Like, guys, some premises you just have to accept for how good they are and see them out. The movie is a campy, fun, twisty turny ride. Understand what you're getting into—a little bit of horror, a little bit of satire, and some fun twists—and it's going to be a good time.

Zazie Beetz (Atlanta, Deadpool 2) gets to lead her own horror/thriller movie with They Will Kill You, where she plays a woman who answers a help-wanted ad for a housekeeper in a luxury apartment building, only to find herself fighting for her life. The movie is pretty similar in tone to fellow horror/comedy Ready or Not 2, which we just talked about. But They Will Kill You leans more into its John Wick-style action and Kill Bill style plot, which sets it apart. The supporting cast, which includes Patricia Arquette, Heather Graham, and Industry star Myha'la, make it extra worth it.
