The Naked Truth About Taking Your Inner Ape for a Walk

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Walking is a key milestone for human development, an activity done for recreation, and can be an Olympic sport.
  • Sources indicate that A key characteristic of human gait is that we land on our heels at the end of swing—something found also in African apes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Walking is a key milestone for human development, an activity done for recreation, and can be an Olympic sport. Walking is a critical and integral behavior across the animal kingdom. It's also something that can be leveraged with deliberate practice. And it's been going on for millions of years since our proto-human ancestors were learning to stand upright, walk bipedally, and land on their heels.

Sources indicate that A key characteristic of human gait is that we land on our heels at the end of swing—something found also in African apes. My research career included diving deep into the neuromechanics of human walking and especially the way sensory feedback and spinal cord motor control vary functionally while we move. I was fascinated by the fact that the most critically controlled part of the step cycle is heel strike—just when your foot lands and weight begins to shift onto the new stance leg.

Sources indicate that so my eye was drawn to the recent work, "Heel-strike Mechanics Reveal Evolutionary Trade-offs in Hominin Bipedalism" by Nicholas B. Holowka et al.

These researchers studied bipedal and quadrupedal locomotion of chimpanzees and humans and examined forces and angles of the foot at the beginning of stance. They found that chimpanzees had much larger ranges of foot-strike angles than humans and often did not land heel-first.

Industry observers note that impact forces and loading rates are much higher with heel-striking, but metabolic cost is lower. This work suggests that the primitive leg anatomy of early hominins meant either high impact forces or poor walking economy. A convergent solution for less mechanically stressful, more economical, and larger travel ranges arrived via "evolution of larger heels and lower limb joints.".

According to recent reports, but can we turn heel-strike walking into striking with our heels? The timing of when you put your foot down at heel strike is the most dangerous part of the entire step cycle. If we make a mistake, or we slip on something, or the ground gives when we put our heel down and our body begins to shift weight onto that leg, we can have a catastrophic failure and a fall. Which is the ultimate failure for the locomotive system.

Sources indicate that so it's critical to avoid a catastrophe, and evolution of bipedal locomotion has incorporated neurological connections that assist in controlling this. But the opposite side of that is that it's also an opportunity. And that's where self-protection and martial arts training factor in.

Recent findings suggest that that critical part of the step cycle is an excellent time to take that heel and stomp it onto an attacker's instep or the top of their foot. You can jam all your weight that's already moving forward to normally be accepted by your stance leg. But now it's to destabilize your opponent.

Sources indicate that this is something I teach when guiding martial arts practice: harnessing the natural movement of the body as the base layer for tactical reaction. Martial arts like Bagua Zhang center core practice on circle walking, where locomotion is central to the performance of discrete actions. We can connect our evolutionary advantage in walking to become a powerful application of self-protective action. This allows us to fully express the functional connectivity within the nervous system, mostly subliminal and automatic, in deliberate mindful action.

That correlates to a little over 17 million orders for the game so far, according to the report, with 75 percent of pre-sales going for the PlayStation 5 version and the other 25 percent for Xbox Series X|S consoles. The chart highlights a fairly typical exponential curve growth over the last five months since pre-sales kicked off: a long period of incremental gains, followed by rapid acceleration in the last few weeks.

And GTA VI-based revenue seems likely to keep coming in to creator Rockstar Games’s coffers at quite a clip, considering initial reviews for the game have been stellar so far. While it may not be your typical automotive-themed driving game, the latest release seems all but sure to guarantee Grand Theft Auto remains a serious part of car culture for some time to come.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Presumably as a way of marching ever forward towards its (alleged) 100 million player goal for Battlefield 6, EA has announced that the multiplayer shooter will be getting its first free trial later this month.

This is, of course, specifically for players to sample the core, paid component of the game, as the recently launched Redsec remains free-to-play. Redsec, however, offers modes like battle royale and Gauntlet, which aren’t quite the traditional Battlefield experience.

The Battlefield 6 trial arrives next Tuesday, November 25. It will run for one week, ending the following Tuesday, December 2. The trial will be available on all platforms, but won’t include all content from the full game.

According to recent reports, instead, players will have access to three of the game’s maps and five of its modes. Siege of Cairo will be there alongside Season 1’s two upcoming maps: Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields. It’s not the strongest line-up of maps, considering Eastwood is already cut from the larger Fort Lyndon battle royale map that Redsec players should be quite familiar with, but it’s something.

According to recent reports, as for modes, you can pick from Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch. Battlefield Studios didn’t say what the fifth mode is going to be, but a dedicated blog post with more information is set to arrive next week.

Beyond the trial's content itself, the timing is certainly great. Battlefield 6 just received one of its biggest patches, kicking off the second phase of its first season. So far this season, we’ve seen two new maps, several new weapons - but more importantly, solutions to problems the game’s had since launch, as well as fixes to longstanding bugs.

Industry observers note that the miserable XP progression Battlefield 6 launched with is far more tolerable. Challenges and Assignments are much easier to understand and actually finish. The often maligned weapon dispersion has been toned down. Some of the wildest vehicle bugs have been fixed. And Portal has a host of experiences that go beyond just bot farms.

In essence, Battlefield 6 feels like its reached its 1.0 status, which makes this a great entry point for latest players, even if the trial could've used more of the game's better maps.

Waymo halts highway operation nationwide after CA DMV pause

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Waymo has pulled its vehicles from highways nationwide after the California Department of Motor Vehicles ordered the manufacturer to pause highway operation in the state, following a viral video showing a Waymo trying to pass a police blockade.
  • Waymo is Google’s robotaxi subsidiary, which has been operating autonomously on public roads in some form since 2017.
  • The vehicles can be hailed through Waymo’s app, and operate with no driver in the driver’s seat, 24/7 in the covered areas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Waymo has pulled its vehicles from highways nationwide after the California Department of Motor Vehicles ordered the manufacturer to pause highway operation in the state, following a viral video showing a Waymo trying to pass a police blockade.

Waymo is Google’s robotaxi subsidiary, which has been operating autonomously on public roads in some form since 2017. It has now expanded to 15 areas, recently adding another 250 square miles just last month.

The vehicles can be hailed through Waymo’s app, and operate with no driver in the driver’s seat, 24/7 in the covered areas. Since it can operate at any time but only within geofenced areas, this counts as “level 4” autonomy, as compared to the level 2 autonomy available on most consumer vehicles.

Sources indicate that until recently, Waymo only operated on city streets. These are more complex than highways, but lower speed. Accidents are more common on city streets than on highways, but can be more spectacular on highways given the higher speeds involved.

In a recent development, most driver assist systems have been rolled out gradually, starting with highways, due to this lower complexity. But Waymo started with city streets first, bucking that trend.

The manufacturer started offering rides on highways late last year, but only in limited markets. It had been testing highway operation for several years prior, typically with a driver and with no public ridership.

According to recent reports, everything was going pretty well, with Waymo declaring its autonomous vehicles have stopped 841 injuries over the course of their 271 million miles of operation. And in terms of competition, Waymo is far ahead of Tesla’s Robotaxi effort.

Sources indicate that but then, the viral internet stepped in. Last week, a video surfaced showing a Waymo trying to pass two police cars who were trying to slow down traffic on I-280 in Northern California. This is one of the main routes through Silicon Valley, and the opening of highway operations drastically reduced ride times in the area.

The video shows two police cars behind a construction vehicle, lights on and spread out across the freeway. Then it pans to show a Waymo vehicle moving quickly in the far left lane. One of the officers accelerates and swerves in front of the Waymo vehicle, at which point the Waymo swerves and slows down. (One media citation says that the video seems to have been sped up by the original poster, but we’ve embedded the short local news report on it above).

In response to this, the California DMV contacted Waymo and ordered the firm to pause highway operations while it examines the incident. The order was made on November 11, but wasn’t reported until today.

The DMV cited multiple instances of Waymo vehicles incurring into construction zones, not simply the one viral clip above. It noted that previous incidents had occurred and been noted, and corrective actions were implemented, but that the incidents keep happening.

Recent findings suggest that this is a very rare situation which Waymo handled poorly. Waymo will add this case to their their test suite. They'll probably ask the CHP for their in car videos of other cases and convert those to be additional test cases. Waymo has been very willing to admit when their vehicles make mistakes in rare situations and fix it so that it doesn't happen again.

Sources indicate that waymo's vehicles are compared against perfect driving and Waymo accepts that as an aspirational goal. I note Tesla lacks the confidence in their system to even apply for the California permit to begin autonomous testing.

DMV’s pause will remain until Waymo can demonstrate “effective corrective actions” have been taken.

While the DMV’s order only applies to California highways, Waymo also paused highway operations in other states. It remains operating on city streets in all coverage areas.

Update: Waymo emailed us this statement after it saw this article.

In a recent development, “Safety is at the foundation of everything we do. Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that nesting season has officially begun for the seabirds visiting Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii. The first egg of the season was laid by a black-footed albatross (Phoebastria nigripes) or kaʻupu in Hawaiian. Field biologist and photographer Dan Rapp captured video of this exciting first, which Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge shared on social media.

It has been revealed that black-footed albatrosses are typically the first to lay eggs beginning in November. The Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis) or mōlī in Hawaiian, will lay their eggs in late November through December. Every fall, this remote group of islands about 1,250 miles from Honolulu temporarily becomes the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species, and includes the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species.

Industry observers note that one special albatross couple has already been spotted—George and Geraldine. The duo is together for the 10th straight year. George was first spotted exactly one month ago on October 18, and the couple was reunited by October 22. The pair are short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian. Short-tailed albatrosses can live up to 50 years and are monogamous—clearly.

Wisdom, a particularly famous bird in these parts, has not been spotted just yet. The over 70-year-old Laysan albatross is the oldest known banded wild bird in the world. She was first identified and banded in 1956 by wildlife biologist Chandler Robbins after she laid a single egg. Biologists estimate that she has produced 50 to 60 eggs and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime. In 2024, Wisdom became the world’s oldest known wild bird to successfully lay an egg at the estimated age of 74. In March, she became a grandmother again.

Viewers can take in the sights and sounds of the albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates.

Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform various courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch albatross chicks in all their fluffy glory.

GLP-1s May Help Lower Diabetes, Heart Risks Better Than Standard Prevention

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GLP-1 drugs are more effective in helping prevent type 2 diabetes than the commonly prescribed medication metformin, according to a upcoming study.
  • Researchers mentioned GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro were more likely to reduce blood sugar to healthy levels in people with prediabetes and obesity.
  • They added that people prescribed GLP-1 medications had a lower risk of progressing from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GLP-1 drugs are more effective in helping prevent type 2 diabetes than the commonly prescribed medication metformin, according to a upcoming study.

Researchers mentioned GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro were more likely to reduce blood sugar to healthy levels in people with prediabetes and obesity.

They added that people prescribed GLP-1 medications had a lower risk of progressing from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

The researchers noted that GLP-1 consumers also had a lower risk of death from any cause as well as fewer heart attacks, strokes, and heart failure events compared with metformin users.

Recent findings suggest that “The great news with prediabetes is that it’s still possible to reverse the progression of the disease,” mentioned Vinicius de Sousa Barzon Serra, MD, a study author and research fellow in cardiovascular medicine at the Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, in a press release. “This research may add to the case for considering GLP-1 medications earlier for certain patients, rather than waiting until they develop type 2 diabetes.”.

Serra noted that metformin still remains an effective treatment for people with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.

“This is less about replacing one medication with another and more about discussing additional options with specific patients,” he mentioned.

Industry observers note that the researchers presented their findings at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago. The research has not been published yet in a peer-reviewed journal.

David Cutler, MD, a family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, wasn’t involved in the study, but noted the findings were “quite impressive.”.

“It elevates the comfort of prescribing GLP-1 drugs as a front-line treatment,” he told Healthline.

Robert Eckel, MD, a former president of the American Heart Association who was likewise not involved in the study, agrees the research provides more options for patients and prescribers.

“GLP-1s provide another option for prevention, perhaps as an add-on therapy. However, costs and access to these medications are important factors,” stated Eckel, an endocrinologist at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, in the press release.

In a recent development, for their study, the researchers analyzed the medical records of 256,000 adults in the United States with prediabetes and obesity. About 76% of the subjects were women, and the average age of the participants was 52.

About half of those studied were taking GLP-1 drugs with the active ingredient semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, or dulaglutide.

The other half had been prescribed metformin, a medication used to help manage blood sugar levels in adults and some children with type 2 diabetes by decreasing glucose production in the liver, reducing glucose absorption from food, and improving the body’s insulin sensitivity.

The researchers reported that the people in the study who were taking GLP-1 drugs had a 1.5 times higher chance of reversing high blood sugar to healthy levels compared to people who were using metformin.

The researchers also noted that GLP-1 medication consumers had a 31% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes and a 41% lower risk of death from any cause.

They added that GLP-1 medications were associated with 15% fewer heart attacks, 20% fewer strokes, 25% fewer cases of heart failure, and 8% fewer cases of atrial fibrillation (AFib), a common type of irregular heartbeat.

The researchers cautioned that their study is observational and, therefore, cannot prove a cause-and-effect relationship. They also noted they relied on prescription records, so the frequency and dosage at which patients took their medication was not reflected.

In addition, the GLP-1 drugs were grouped together, so individual differences between medications were not considered.

Recent findings suggest that eckel noted in the news release that the benefits for people taking GLP-1 drugs were probably mainly due to weight loss. Eckel noted that the research results open up a wide range of possibilities.

“This is an vital finding because the GLP-1 receptor agonists are commonly used today and this is a population that in the transition from prediabetes to diabetes are at increasing risk for cardiovascular disease,” Eckel noted in a taped interview alongside the study findings.

Cutler pointed out that several GLP-1 drugs also target blood sugar levels and insulin production. They could be effective in people with prediabetes who don’t have weight management challenges.

Cutler noted that these people, however, might be reluctant to take GLP-1 drugs because they may not be experiencing symptoms of their prediabetes but could develop side effects with the medications.

“They would not be getting any immediate benefits,” Cutler said. He added that metformin, which was first used clinically in 1958, remains an effective alternative. “It’s been proven safe, effective, and it’s very cheap,” Cutler said.

It’s estimated that 40 million people in the United States have diabetes, with more than 90% of those cases being type 2 diabetes, a chronic condition characterized by high blood glucose levels that results from the body’s ineffective response to insulin or insufficient insulin production.

It’s also estimated that 115 million adults in the United States have prediabetes, a condition in which a person has higher-than-normal blood sugar levels but not high enough to be diagnosed as type 2 diabetes.

Around 5–10% of people with prediabetes develop diabetes every year. More broadly, up to 70% of people with prediabetes eventually develop diabetes.

It has been revealed that medication is sometimes prescribed for people with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes. Lifestyle changes can help reverse type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, as well as prevent the progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

Among those lifestyle modifications are:.

Cutler noted the lifestyle changes needed to prevent type 2 diabetes are pretty clear.

“The most vital thing for people with prediabetes to know is they should lose weight, reduce their carbs, exercise daily and, if that doesn’t work, then consider medication,” he noted.

#87218. Industry News: In Defense of Clever Hans

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1387 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: In Defense of Clever Hans

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1387 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Proponents of facilitated communication (FC)—a discredited intervention in which a nondisabled facilitator helps a profoundly autistic person spell out sophisticated messages on a letter board or keyboard—really do not like it when critics point to the famous case of Clever Hans, calling this analogy “indefensibly dehumanizing” and, as Marina Weiler recently argued on this site, “cruel.”.
  • But the Clever Hans argument is not, as critics charge, about “comparing autistic people to animals.” It is about illustrating how subtly and unintentionally behavior can be cued.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Proponents of facilitated communication (FC)—a discredited intervention in which a nondisabled facilitator helps a profoundly autistic person spell out sophisticated messages on a letter board or keyboard—really do not like it when critics point to the famous case of Clever Hans, calling this analogy “indefensibly dehumanizing” and, as Marina Weiler recently argued on this site, “cruel.”.

But the Clever Hans argument is not, as critics charge, about “comparing autistic people to animals.” It is about illustrating how subtly and unintentionally behavior can be cued.

According to recent reports, no one explicitly taught this horse to stop tapping his hoof at some predetermined signal. He learned from observing tiny, unconscious movements of his trainer’s head that a commission of experts sent to observe Hans’ seemingly extraordinary abilities couldn’t spot, even under close scrutiny (a graduate student in psychology finally figured it out). If a horse can learn to respond to signs barely observable to the human eye, FC skeptics (such as myself) point out, humans can certainly do the same, and likely to even more imperceptible—or not so imperceptible—cues, such as changes in breathing, pitch, or posture; verbal prompts; or shifting the letter board in the air.

Importantly, facilitators are also subject to influence in the form of common psychological biases. An amazing example of how strong the desire to believe can affect facilitators aired earlier this year on "The Today Show." After publishing his first novel, speller Woody Brown and his mother, who facilitates for him, were interviewed by Jenna Bush Hager. As a camera positioned behind the pair documented, there was absolutely no correlation between Woody’s random jabs at the letter board and the articulate responses his mother “read.”.

Sources indicate that in short, the Clever Hans story is raised as part of the case that authorship in spelling cannot be judged based solely on how it looks to the observer. Especially because it is so easy to expose facilitator control: Just ask the speller to produce information that is definitively unknown to their facilitator, i.e., by showing them an object that the facilitator hasn’t seen and asking them to identify it. This has been done in dozens of studies dating back to the 1990s, and FC has failed every time. A recent review confirms that independent authorship in any form of FC—including more recent variants, Rapid Prompting Method (RPM) and Spelling to Communicate (S2C)—has never been demonstrated under controlled conditions.

In response, the spelling community has simply refused to participate in any more of these tests. I will never understand why the debate didn’t end there. That is just not how the scientific method operates. Good research starts with the null hypothesis—the assumption that the intervention under investigation doesn’t work. Once evidence is obtained of a positive effect, conscientious researchers try to account for any other possible factor that could explain their findings, such as the placebo effect—or, in the case of FC, facilitator control. It is only once these other explanations have been ruled out that efficacy can be established. Instead, FC researchers offer “qualitative research” (i.e., interviews with spellers who use FC products to prove FC) and indirect, technology-intensive studies involving eye-tracking apparatuses, computer algorithms, FMRI, and accelerometers that claim to prove FC works even though the facilitators in these tests are never blinded.

In a recent development, by far, the most baffling question I’m asked by spelling proponents is, “Why do you care?” In other words: If I object to spelling, I should just not use it with my profoundly autistic son, Jonah. Why do I have to oppose it so publicly?

I’ve thought about this a lot recently, because spelling has become the wedge issue that is fracturing the profound autism community. And I am heartsick, because I know this diminishes our power to effect the changes our kids desperately need to flourish.

But spelling is not like vitamins, diet, brushing, or any of the countless alternative therapies that parents of profoundly autistic children, myself included, have experimented with since our kids were small. We can’t just agree to disagree, because the demands of spelling proponents put my son at risk even if he is never introduced to a letter board. Their increasingly successful fights to force school districts and state disability agencies to pay for spelling instruction and facilitator access drain resources from desperately underfunded systems.

And, if spelling is normalized with no validation requirements whatsoever, what’s to stop an unscrupulous provider—at some point in the future when my husband and I are gone—from telling our four other kids, "Jonah spelled that he doesn’t want to see you, so you’re no longer allowed to check on him" or "Jonah spelled that he actually gave his iPad to the aide who had stashed it in the trunk of his car" or "Jonah spelled that he wants to transfer his guardianship/SSI rep payee to his group home manager" or "Jonah spelled that he consented to sex with another resident of his group home." The opportunities for exploitation are so obvious and so tremendous that I’m shocked that spelling proponents refuse to even consider them.

But even if this problem did not affect Jonah at all, I would still care about the spellers—how could I not? Profound autism has stripped so much agency from my son. But Jonah’s basic communication does allow him to exert some control over his life, and we try to maximize those opportunities as much as possible. He tells us what he wants: ketchup and hamburger and French fries, “fun list” with Mommy, Costco with Daddy, water park with… anyone who will take him. Many spellers have similar levels of verbal communication, but practitioners teach parents that this speech is “unreliable” or “scripting” and should be ignored in favor of what is spelled. I just can’t imagine how frustrating it must be to be completely stripped of any ability to communicate your needs and preferences.

Finally, as someone who has spent more than a quarter of a century loving someone with profound autism, and spending a lot of time with other profoundly autistic people and their families, I resent what I can only describe as the character assassination perpetuated by spelling proponents, who locate the refusal to participate in controlled studies with the spellers themselves—who allegedly, to a person, find these tests so dehumanizing and offensive they could not possibly enroll on principle.

Spelling skepticism in the face of both the overwhelming evidence of facilitator control and documented harm is rational, not “hate speech.” Spellers, if they were really as brilliant as their prose suggests, would understand that. They would eagerly partner with researchers because they would know that controlled tests represent the fastest path to insurance coverage, public funding, curricular inclusion, and legal standing.

According to recent reports, so no, I just do not believe that every single one of the estimated 10,000 spellers in this country is so petty, so selfish, that they would let the estimated 30 million nonspeakers around the world languish, "locked in silent cage[s],” simply because they’re insulted that mainstream experts and policy makers would dare ask for evidence. I am certain, in fact, they would be demanding to provide it.

Spelling proponents have thrown around a lot of accusations, claiming that critics are uninformed or ableist or just protecting their professional turf. But this debate is actually the same one that has unfolded countless times in a community in which 90 percent of families have experimented with alternative treatments: Does it work—and not just according to anecdotal evidence, but under controlled conditions? Secretin failed that test. So have the gluten- and casein-free diet, chelation, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and auditory integration training, among others. FC failed that test also.

If proponents believe those studies were faulty, they should absolutely test again. Until then, it is incumbent on our institutions—government agencies, school districts, the media, healthcare systems—to protect the fundamental right of profoundly autistic people to authentic communication.

It has been revealed that lutz, Amy S.F. (2023). Chasing the Intact Mind: How the Severely Autistic and Intellectually Disabled Were Excluded from the Debates That Affect Them Most. Oxford University Press.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • After introducing the Neira Concept at the 2026 Gaikindo Indonesia International Auto Show (GIIAS) in July, Hyundai is gearing up to open pre-orders on November 20.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai revealed the production-ready Neira EV for the first time, a three-row, seven-seat electric SUV set to launch in Indonesia on November 20.

After introducing the Neira Concept at the 2026 Gaikindo Indonesia International Auto Show (GIIAS) in July, Hyundai is gearing up to open pre-orders on November 20.

The Neira is a pretty “big” deal as Hyundai’s first locally produced seven-seat electric SUV in Indonesia.

Ahead of its official debut on Friday at GAIKINDO Auto Week (GAW) 2026, Hyundai offered a closer look at the upcoming Neira.

It has been revealed that the electric SUV is essentially a Hyundai-badged version of the Kia Carens Clavis EV that rolled out last year. Aside from the Hyundai logos, a few minor tweaks to the front and rear ends, and latest wheels and headlights, it’s a near replica.

Inside, both are equipped with dual 12.3″ instrument display and center navigation screens, plus an added climate control panel.

Hyundai didn’t reveal battery or powertrain specs, but the Neira is expected to use the same 42 kWh and 51.4 kWh battery packs as the Carens Clavis EV. The former offers an MIDC range of up to 251 mi (404 km), while the latter has up to 304 mi (490 km) on a single charge.

Both batteries can be charged from 10% to 80% in around 39 minutes using a 100 kW DC fast charger.

The Kia Carens Clavis is 4,550 mm long, 1,800 mm wide, and 1,708 mm tall, with a 2,780 mm wheelbase, so Hyundai’s Neira will likely be about the same size, if not slightly bigger.

Hyundai stated the Neira has four key advantages: A higher ground clearance, Hyundai Bluelink connectivity tech, a Blind-spot View Monitor (BVM), and easy third-row access.

A post shared by Hyundai Motors Indonesia (@hyundaimotorindonesia).

Ahead of its upcoming launch, Hyundai is taking the electric 7-seater on a trip to prove its capabilities, going from Kilometer Nol in Banda Aceh to Banda Neira, which is about 4,000 kilometers (about 2,500 miles).

While Hyundai may export the Neira EV to overseas markets like India, don’t expect it to reach the US.

Hyundai already sells a three-row, seven-seat electric SUV, the IONIQ 9, which is built at Hyundai’s Metaplant in Georgia.

Industry News: Tested: 2027 Subaru Forester Wilderness Hybrid Is a Fuel-Economy-Hero Of a Soft-Roader

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Decades before the advent of the soft-roader, Subaru was building everyday cars with a limited amount of extra off-road capability.
  • Recent findings suggest that naturally, Subaru has now combined the two by offering a Forester Hybrid in Wilderness trim.
  • Industry observers note that our expert editors test every vehicle we review.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Decades before the advent of the soft-roader, Subaru was building everyday cars with a limited amount of extra off-road capability. So it should be no surprise that its Wilderness line of slightly more capable crossovers has been a hit. So, too, has Subaru’s integration of hybrid systems, in an era when buyers of volume cars such as the Forester are happy to get their hands on anything that means greater efficiency.

Recent findings suggest that naturally, Subaru has now combined the two by offering a Forester Hybrid in Wilderness trim. The recipe seems like a sales hit waiting to happen, but is it worth the extra complexity?

Industry observers note that our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

Subaru finally brought a hybrid powertrain to the Forester for the 2025 model year. A new Wilderness was introduced a few months later, but it lacked the gas-electric system available on the basic car. The Forester Wilderness Hybrid combines the two, allowing Subaru to offer a system peak of 194 horsepower from a 2.5-liter flat-four and a 1-kWh battery pack.

According to recent reports, EPA-estimated fuel economy is down slightly from the basic Forester Hybrid, but the 33 mpg city and 29 mpg highway are still both solid numbers for a crossover with 9.3 inches of ground clearance and Yokohama Geolander all-terrain tires. For most buyers, that improvement alone should justify the price, which is $1000 more than the basic Forester Wilderness.

Powertrain: 2.5-liter Atkinson-cycle flat-four, lithium-ion hydride battery pack.

Power: 194 hp @ 5600 rpm (peak system output).

Transmission: continuously variable automatic, all-wheel drive.

EPA mpg: 33 city, 29 highway, 31 combined.

Sources indicate that befitting the Wilderness Hybrid’s soft-roader credentials, the media drive took place on the dirt, grass, and gravel roads of a private ranch. While this made for beautiful scenery, it did little to showcase what the car could do as a daily driver or challenge its off-road capabilities.

Industry observers note that those capabilities did impress on a more technical off-roading course that Subaru built for the event, although that comes with the caveat that the company presumably built the course with the car’s limits in mind. Even though this is ultimately still a relatively conventional crossover with nothing like the articulation of a more extreme off-roader, the all-terrain tires were capable of handling substantial ruts and steep hill descents.

Sources indicate that approach, break-over, and departure angles of 23.5, 20.6, and 25.5 degrees, respectively, are identical to the nonhybrid Forester Wilderness. This hybrid crossover has the clearance to get over obstacles a car camper or kayaker might find on the trail to their favorite outdoor-recreation spot. The biggest frustration here was the low resolution of the X-Drive off-road menus built into the infotainment screens, a feature that felt behind the respectable capabilities of the crossover itself.

It has been revealed that while the off-road performance is what sets the Wilderness apart from its more pedestrian Forester Hybrid brethren, limited on-road testing suggests that the car feels similar in everyday situations. Given the all-terrain tires, that’s a solid achievement, even if the end result is still relative mediocrity. This Forester is no performance car, and anyone who might have been expecting a canyon carver will instead have to make do with relaxed acceleration and a frustrating continuously variable automatic transmission.

In a recent development, the Forester is a tentpole for Subaru because it combines the basic compact-crossover shape today’s buyers want with some degree of utility in all forms. The Wilderness goes one step further in providing even more capability, but its day-to-day strength will be how little it sacrifices to do that.

According to recent reports, the Forester Wilderness Hybrid drops 5 mpg of efficiency in the city in comparison to the standard Forester Hybrid, for 33 mpg. The basic Forester Wilderness, by contrast, gets just 24 mpg in the city. The hybrid remains relatively comfortable and quiet on the road too, which is great news for buyers who do not want to hear harsh noises from all-terrain tires and the unique drone of a Subaru boxer engine all day.

Industry observers note that still, the Wilderness line is differentiated by its capabilities. Buyers looking for a soft-roader do expect to use the car on a trail every so often, which makes the Wilderness Hybrid’s lack of a spare tire a major problem. Since components of the hybrid system are packed where a spare would go on a normal Wilderness, buyers of this car will either have to find another way to carry a fifth tire or contend with the reality that a flat could derail their outdoor adventures in a worse way than the same problem would in the nonhybrid model.

It has been revealed that that missing spare tire is one of two major drawbacks for the Wilderness Hybrid. The other is the towing capacity, down from 3500 pounds to just 1500. Both of these are serious limitations for buyers who have certain use cases in mind for their soft-roader, but neither is necessarily a problem for the average buyer. The price difference is not negligible, but fuel savings should cover the difference in cost within a few years. For most buyers, that makes the Hybrid the obvious choice.

In a recent development, buyers looking at other hybrid soft-roaders could also consider the new Toyota RAV4 Woodland and the Honda CR-V Trailsport. The Subaru is the only one of the three hybrids with conventional full-time all-wheel drive, although that specific differentiator is not necessarily a game changer for buyers who will be spending most of their time on the street. For those who do need to venture a little further a little more often, though, the Forester Hybrid Wilderness seems like the strongest choice.

Industry observers note that subaru’s Wilderness models are sold with synthetic StarTex interiors meant to be easily cleaned, and this particular vehicle even includes a synthetic steering-wheel cover in lieu of the usual leather. This is a small detail for most, but it does mean that the cabin is entirely vegan. For some very specific buyers, however, that one detail could make all the difference.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that on Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters.
  • Officials plan to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone.
  • It has been revealed that the aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters. This time, the alert is targeting a much different kind of public threat: sneaky standardized test cheaters.

Officials plan to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone. Proctors will also inspect all pairs of glasses for hidden cameras, and students wearing clothes with buttons will have to cover them with stickers.

It has been revealed that the aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score. That surprise revelation sent educators and officials scrambling to come up with solutions to instill confidence in the upcoming test.

Sources indicate that korea’s measures come as educators around the world are struggling to keep up with a growing arsenal of AI-enabled tools that make cheating easier than ever. But while AI is the focus today, students have been tinkering with latest tech and other creative ways to skirt the rules for as long as tests have carried weight.

Sources indicate that the sudden rule changes in South Korea come days after a 34-year-old man named Han Won-seok posted a video on his lawyer’s YouTube channel admitting he used AI to cheat on the country’s national tax exam. According to the Associated Press, Han scored 397.5 out of 400 points on the first stage of the multiple-choice test, a suspicious result that made him the subject of several media interviews. Other test-takers saw those results and accused him of trickery.

According to recent reports, days after denying those allegations, Han reversed course. In the video, he admitted to using a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions, which were then fed to an AI tool. He then viewed the AI-generated answers on his smartphone. Now, Han notes he is cooperating with investigators and is warning others against following his lead.

In a recent development, “I cheated on the tax accountant exam. I sincerely apologize for causing damage to a lot of people,” the student said in the video, according to CNN. “If there is someone thinking of cheating like I did, I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught.”.

In the days since the videos, officials have rushed to put in place latest anti-cheating safeguards. South Korean Prime Minister Han Sung-sook reportedly held a meeting on Monday with the country’s top education officials, where they agreed to officially add smart glasses to the list of prohibited items in testing rooms. Some lawmakers had reportedly even called on officials to postpone the Suneung exam until they could come up with more rigorous anti-cheating safeguards, though the country’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin promptly shot that idea down, arguing delays would cause “even a larger disruption.” And while Han never stated he specifically used smart glasses to cheat, worries about that tech in particular aren’t hypothetical. Earlier this year, two other South Korean students taking an exam to assess English skills were also caught using camera-equipped glasses.

Recent findings suggest that concerns about AI-enabled cheating aren’t limited to South Korea either. Last week, England’s Office for Students, an independent higher education regulator, released a statement warning that AI tools are making it “close to impossible” to assess university classwork. In China, major tech companies disabled features on their AI apps during last year’s national college entrance exam (the gaokao), to keep students from using them to cheat. Educators in the United States and elsewhere are also increasingly requiring students to take exams in person and defend papers orally due to the pervasiveness of AI-generated submissions. Sales of Blue Books have soared as a result.

Industry observers note that while fancy AI tools and camera-equipped smart glasses may be newly introduced concerns, creative cheating isn’t. In fact, evidence of sneaky test-takers dates back centuries. One example is this replica of a linen vest from China’s Qing dynasty (1644–1911). The impressive garment has 62 essays, more than 40,000 characters in all, hidden inside. Students wearing the vest would sneak peeks during the country’s grueling imperial exams, which played an important role in determining government employment and social status. An even older Ming Dynasty (1368 to 1644) jacket was covered with some 50,000 characters from classical texts likely served a similar purpose.

Sources indicate that creative cheating has of course persisted into the modern era. In 2015, police in India’s Bihar state detained more than 1,000 people after relatives of test-takers were photographed scaling the walls of an exam center to pass cheat sheets to students through a window opening. A college student in the U.S. made headlines in 2011, after he was arrested for allegedly using fake IDs to stand in for at least six high school students during SAT exams. In China, a team of exam proctors equipped with  surveillance drones regularly seizes a variety of wearables and other devices students use to try and cheat. Among the seized items were a hidden camera placed inside a pen and glasses with cameras connected to a tiny receiver embedded in a coin.

One has to wonder if all that time and effort spent devising intricate cheating methods could have been used to study instead.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The work to continue streamlining Challenges in Battlefield 6 is clearly not done.
  • This latest round includes far fewer tweaks, but quite surprisingly, it also removes a few of the more annoying ones from the game.
  • In a recent development, the updated list, which Battlefield shared on Twitter, includes changes to the dreaded Recon 2 headshots beyond 150m Challenge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The work to continue streamlining Challenges in Battlefield 6 is clearly not done. Having just released a latest patch - which already included several updates to Challenges and Assignments - Battlefield Studios has gone in and made even more changes.

This latest round includes far fewer tweaks, but quite surprisingly, it also removes a few of the more annoying ones from the game.

In a recent development, the updated list, which Battlefield shared on Twitter, includes changes to the dreaded Recon 2 headshots beyond 150m Challenge. Now, any headshot beyond 75m will count. Recon Expert 3 is another headshot-themed one that’s been updated, and now requires getting headshot kills beyond 125m, rather than the practically impossible beyond 200m that it required previously.

The Rapid Fire 2 Challenge, which required getting kills beyond 50m with Assault Rifles, has been changed so it now tracks anything beyond 40m. The painful ‘Inflict damage under 15m while hip-firing with Assault Rifles’ has been entirely replaced with one that requires - the far more sensible - inflicting damage while in ADS with Assault Rifles.

A couple of Challenges, such as the one that required suppressing enemies with LMGs, and another that wanted you to deal damage to laser-designated vehicles using lock-on weapons, have both been removed.

The journey to make Challenges and Assignments easier to complete has been a long one. Progression has been one of the key areas of criticism Battlefield 6 received at launch. The matter encompassed more than just slow player and weapon XP earn rates, it also prevented players from accessing latest Training Paths for the various classes, and several of the game's weapons.

Battlefield Studios attacked the problem from multiple angles, initially boosting the XP players and their weapons would earn, before later reducing the requirements of the Challenges themselves. The developer continued to streamline those requirements over multiple patches, including majorly overhauling the system earlier this month.

It seems the studio is more confident than ever in the game, as it recently announced that Battlefield 6 will be getting its first free trial next week, offering players who do not own the full game access to iconic modes like Conquest, and Breakthrough - though on an unusual selection of maps.

The 'Possibility Couple' Is a Gen Z Dating Trend

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • So, say you want to be one half of a power couple—you know, a romantic pairing where both of you are successful and influential like Beyoncé and Jay-Z or Mr.
  • Well, how about trying to be part of a "possibility couple" now?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

So, say you want to be one half of a power couple—you know, a romantic pairing where both of you are successful and influential like Beyoncé and Jay-Z or Mr. and Mrs. Incredible. But the problem is you are still early on in your own personal power trip—meaning that you yourself have not become successful yet. What then can you do?

Well, how about trying to be part of a "possibility couple" now? That's a pairing that's all about the P's—namely "potential," "possibilities", "prediction," "potent," and, yes, maybe "power" eventually. A "possibility couple" is one that doesn't have power per se at the present. But it's got the potential to become quite potent in the future. In other words, based on what you are seeing now, you predict that together you'll have lots of potent possibilities down the road.

Recent findings suggest that it shouldn't be super-surprising that the "possibility couple" is central to Hinge's third annual Gen Z D.A.T.E. (Data, Advice, Trends, and Expertise) Report titled: “Dating While Dreaming Big.” Since Gen Zers are those born between 1997 and 2012, they are now no older than 29 and thus are mostly still in the fruitcake batter stages of their lives—still forming their identities and possibilities.

The Hinge report hinged on surveys administered to the over 13,000 users of the dating app. The survey results did suggest that many Gen Z respondents are looking into the future when evaluating their present dating prospects. For example, 81 percent of Gen Z respondents felt that "ending up with their ideal partner would make achieving their ideal life more likely," and 67 percent "would prefer a partner who makes them feel hopeful and inspired over someone who simply fits the life they’re already building." This forward-oriented view seemed to be more present among the Gen Zers, with 76 percent of them vs. 65 percent of millennials saying that "when they imagine their ideal romantic partner, they’re also imagining the person they want to become.".

According to recent reports, none of these are terrible things. Thinking more about your future and playing more of a long game when dating can be good approaches. The opposite would be just considering the here and now and trying to satisfy your immediate urges, such as, "Sure, that person is a bit crazy but so, so hot, and I'm so, so horny." Focusing too much on the present when looking for a partner can be like buying a pair of low-riding skinny jeans and thinking, "I'm going to wear these for life.".

When you think only about who you are right now, rather than who you might become, you could be destined for some D's—meaning dispute, despair, and potentially divorce. You could end up outgrowing the other person. Or the person could end up holding you back. So, yes, it does make sense to find a person who is more open to possibilities for both of you.

A seemingly big challenge, though, of finding a possibility pairing is having to P a lot—meaning predicting, projecting, and prognosticating. It's not like a potential power pairing, where you can simply say, "I got the power. Do you?" and find the answer to be "yes" in both of your eyes. Whether the two of you might last without an eventual power outage is a different story.

It has been revealed that with a "possibility couple, any potential projections are further complicated by having to prognosticate for not just one but both of you when you don't know each other very well. In fact, neither of you may even be that self-aware yet. Plus, as stock market investors, weather forecasters, and the makers of Crystal Pepsi, Segways, and Joker: Folie à Deux will tell you, predicting what will happen in the future is not easy.

It has been revealed that sure, there are present-day signs. For example, someone right now in law school is very likely to become a lawyer in a few years. But that lawyer could easily one day say, "Forget the law. Bring on yarn bombing." And who knows what twists and turns life may bring, such as health challenges, unexpected people entering or exiting, workplace and industry overhauls, or encountering a life-changing piece of tiramisu. I have previously warned in "A Funny Bone to Pick" about the dangers of dating someone's potential future self rather than who the person currently is because that person may end up never changing.

Therefore, the best possibility might be to balance the present with the future. You can ask yourself the question that I've already posed for "A Funny Bone to Pick"—namely, are you stronger with or without the person? Look for qualities that potential partners already have that would project well into the future.

According to recent reports, one such quality is open-mindedness—being open to different possibilities and people. After all, you may become a very different person at least outwardly. So, beware of anyone who stereotypes, focuses too much on superficial things, and holds strong biases.

A second quality is adaptability—the ability to accommodate future changes, such as the two of you growing in different ways. Or is your potential partner more like a starched denim thong—rigid and inflexible in a way that's surely going to drive a wedge between you in the future?

Thirdly, do they even want you to succeed and have a true teammate mindset where they want their partner to be as potent as possible? Or must they outshine everyone, including you? Beware of the people who make themselves feel high by keeping those around them low.

Finally, are they a match for what's inside you—your core, your core personality and values, what won't change over time? If the two of you are attracted to each other's hot legs, abs, job, wallet, memberships, pick-up lines, car, or cast-iron cookware, remember those things definitely change over time—with the possible exception of the cast-iron cookware.

By contrast, what allows for growth is having strong roots beneath the surface. If the two of you can connect those roots—those things that go beyond the superficial—then the resulting possibilities could be endless.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that TESTOSTERONE GOES BEYOND building muscle.
  • Industry observers note that testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) can help raise T levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that TESTOSTERONE GOES BEYOND building muscle. T helps you maintain muscle mass, facial and body hair, sex drive, and red blood cell production. So when your T levels start to decline—which happens naturally in your thirties—there’s a whole range of symptoms like low libido or just feeling blue.

Industry observers note that testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) can help raise T levels. After a couple of weeks to a month, you’ll start to see some changes, some big and small. Some pleasant and not so pleasant. Below, urologists explain what happens to your body a month after taking testosterone.

Industry observers note that IF YOU HAVE low T, your doctor will conduct some tests to see if you’re a good candidate for the therapy. Ryan Smith, MD, urologist specializing in men’s health at the University of Virginia Health, claims a doctor will perform two blood tests in the morning (on different days) when testosterone is at its highest.

In a recent development, low is considered under 300 nanograms per deciliter (ng/dL) by some accounts and under 264 ng/dL by others. Doctors also factor in any symptoms you’re having, like trouble getting erections or orgasms, fatigue, or just feeling blah.

According to recent reports, nowadays, testosterone is more accessible without a prescription, with many people only having to complete an online assessment. Leaving out a doctor’s approval and supervision, however, can be harmful, indicates Justin Dubin, MD, urologist at Baptist Health.

Recent findings suggest that in a 2022 study that Dr. Dubin co-authored, researchers found that many online platforms are not providing testosterone therapy in accordance with the American Urological Association and the Endocrine Society guidelines. Using a secret shopper, the researchers found that the platforms offered therapy to men who didn’t meet the guidelines and didn’t mention the risks or benefits of testosterone therapy.

It has been revealed that working with a doctor ensures that you’re prescribed testosterone only when you need it and that you’re taking the right dose. Then, they can work with you to make sure your testosterone levels respond appropriately. Doctors like to recheck everything every six months to make sure you’re not having any negative side effects.

A number of testosterone options are available. You can choose between injectables, topical gels, creams, under-the-skin pellet therapy, pills, and nasal sprays. You can learn more about them here.

Each comes with its own set of side effects, so it all comes down to your personal preference, health situation, and what your insurance covers. You can read about the real-life experiences of guys of different ages and body types and their experiences with taking testosterone.

According to recent reports, IT CAN TAKE a few weeks to a month or two to see your symptoms improve after starting testosterone replacement therapy, states Dr. Smith. Here are some of the side effects—some obvious and some not—that come with testosterone therapy.

When you’re low on testosterone, you might notice your sex drive dip. But when you take TRT, the treatment reactivates the androgen receptors in the part of your brain that controls desire, indicates Abraham Morgentaler, MD, associate clinical professor of urology at Harvard Medical School and author of Testosterone for Life. Regaining a healthy sex drive is one of the biggest benefits of testosterone replacement therapy, he says.

Industry observers note that TRT may also make your erections more satisfying, though this isn’t the only piece of the puzzle. Erections also rely on healthy nerves and blood flow. That means that testosterone therapy by itself won't always help erectile dysfunction.

Sources indicate that muscles respond to testosterone and starting TRT can increase muscle mass, claims Dr. Morgentaler. That’s because testosterone activates the androgen receptors in muscle tissue to stimulate growth.

The effect of a testosterone replacement dose on your muscles, however, is fairly minimal. To make the most of this muscle-building benefit, you’ll need to be doing your part through strength training and possibly raising the amount of protein you consume (depending on your current intake). Don’t know where to start? Check out MH’s four-week muscle building guide.

According to recent reports, some men also report fat loss. While testosterone doesn’t directly incite fat loss itself, part of it may be thanks to the uptick in muscle mass. The more muscle you have, the higher your basal metabolic rate (BMR). That means your body will burn more calories at rest.

Another indirect way testosterone can help with fat loss is motivation to keep pushing once you see results. Jed Kaminetsky, MD, urologist at NYU Langone Medical Center, testosterone can increase your energy levels, making it easier to get up and sweat it out.

Fatigue is a common symptom of low T. “When we treat them, a lot of men will say that their energy has improved,” indicates Dr. Morgentaler.

Sources indicate that scientists studying testosterone aren't sure exactly how the hormone plays a role in energy—just that it does. One of the prevailing hypotheses Dr. Morgentaler can get behind is that testosterone somehow affects your mitochondria (that organelle you learned in high school is the powerhouse of your cells). The theory is that “testosterone turns them on, so they're more productive in terms of creating the energy that the cells need.”.

It has been revealed that ronald Tamler, MD, PhD, associate professor of medicine at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, notes changes in energy may also be tied back to androgen receptors. “If they don't get sufficient input, that can cause fatigue,” he says. Bringing testosterone levels back up can help reverse this.

Recent findings suggest that experts don't have a definitive answer to why testosterone impacts mood so deeply—after all, “the brain is a complicated thing,” says Dr. Tamler. But the positive effect of TRT on mood is a potential life-changing benefit.

In a recent development, an old but highly referenced clinical trial in 2003 looked at how testosterone gels affected middle-aged men with treatment-resistant depression and low T. After 8 weeks, the men highlighted greater improvements in the psychological aspects of depression (sadness, guilt, and anxiety) than those given a placebo. The men taking testosterone gels also showed nearly the same rate of improvement in somatic aspects of depression (improvements in sleep, appetite, and libido). A more recent review of 27 clinical trials involving 1,890 men with low T found that TRT provided a significant reduction in depressive symptoms, especially at higher doses.

One of the most key things to know before starting TRT is that the treatment decreases sperm production and may cause infertility.

Testosterone might affect the size of your testicles, too. "Most of the size of the testicle is dedicated to making sperm, so when you're making less sperm, the testicles get smaller," states Dr. Morgentaler.

Sperm production may or may not go back to normal even after stopping treatment, claims Dr. Kaminetsky. One study found increasing age and longer TRT linked to lower chances of normal sperm recovery.

It has been revealed that some people notice a little swelling in their feet and ankles because testosterone can encourage your body to hold onto excess fluid, states Dr. Morgentaler.

This isn't a big deal for most people, he indicates, and swelling is more common if you're taking a non-daily treatment like an injection, when you're getting a higher dose of T in one sitting.

Testosterone replacement therapy may change your skin type—for better or for worse, notes Dr. Morgentaler.

Testosterone can increase oil production, which isn't necessarily a bad thing. Oil production is important for healthy skin, so you may actually end up with a better complexion. However, too much oily buildup can lead to breakouts.

It has been revealed that while Dr. Morgentaler says testosterone-induced breakouts aren’t common, they are more likely to occur in men with a history of acne. Skin changes may also be more common if you’re taking testosterone injections versus other modes of administration since you're getting a higher dose all at once.

In all men—whether you’re taking T or not—some testosterone is converted into the hormone estradiol, a form of estrogen. In men who naturally have more breast tissue, testosterone can be converted into estradiol, which may stimulate breast tissue to grow.

It has been revealed that this is called gynecomastia, says Dr. Morgentaler, and it's not as common as other side effects. If gynecomastia does happen, your doctor will likely stop treatment for a month or two to allow your breast tissue to go back to normal. Then, you’ll resume T along with a drug that blocks the conversion of testosterone to estradiol.

If you’re going the topical testosterone therapy route, one matter to watch out for is transference with women and children.

Darshan Patel, MD, assistant professor of urology at the University of California San Diego’s Men’s Health Center, claims testosterone from gels or creams can be transferred through skin-to-skin contact or from clothing and absorbed by someone else.

“You really have to be careful to wash your hands well and not expose others,” adds Dr. Smith. Contact with excess testosterone can affect children’s genitalia and cause premature pubic hair development and aggressive behavior.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.
  • Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.
  • Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.

Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.

Typical treatment for early onset type 2 diabetes is often a combination of lifestyle changes, like diet and exercise, and medications.

However, this upcoming study suggests that a supervised low calorie diet and exercise program may help some people with early onset type 2 diabetes enter remission.

The RESET for Remission trial included 96 adults from England and Canada who were between the ages of 18 and 45, had early onset type 2 diabetes, obesity, and were not on insulin treatment.

Recent findings suggest that the participants had an average age of 38 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 35.2 kg/m2. They were randomized into a control group that received usual care alone and the intervention group, which ate a low calorie diet and participated in supervised exercise programs.

During the first 12 weeks, participants in the intervention group followed an 800–900-calorie-per-day diet and completed twice-weekly supervised aerobic and resistance exercise sessions, along with one independent exercise session per week.

For weeks 13–24, they transitioned to a weight-maintenance diet and independent exercise.

Both groups were supervised by physicians, and the intervention group was also closely supervised by licensed dietitians.

It has been revealed that the low calorie diet consisted of 30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, and 20% fat. Participants were also encouraged to drink at least 2 liters of calorie-free fluids per day and given access to a fiber-based laxative as needed.

Sources indicate that in the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). Then, in weeks 3–12, the participants maintained the same calorie intake but had more flexibility in their food choices.

It has been revealed that this second phase of the diet included one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables. Typically, this meant 60 to 90 grams of protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, and two portions of non-starchy vegetables.

According to recent reports, at the end of 24 weeks, 54% of the intervention group entered remission of type 2 diabetes, compared with only 4% in the control group. Researchers defined remission as an HbA1c level below 6.5% without glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks.

It has been revealed that “This study proves what most physicians have advocated for quite some time. Clearly, diet and exercise can work to improve or even resolve diabetes,” David Cutler, MD, board certified family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline.

According to recent reports, cutler also added that this study provides a clear example of how difficult it can be to enter diabetes remission with diet and exercise alone. He stated that the small number of participants in the study also makes him wonder if these findings can be applied to all populations.

Another limitation of this study, as Cutler pointed out, was that the strict dietary limits imposed on study participants would be very difficult for the average adult to adhere to.

The study also followed participants for only six months, so it’s unclear how many would remain in remission over the longer term.

“It is worth trying diet and exercise first because they can work to achieve meaningful weight loss and remission of diabetes,” he said.

It may be possible to prevent or delay the onset of type 2 diabetes by:.

The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) notes that losing 5%–7% of your body weight can help reduce your risk of type 2 diabetes.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is a growing issue worldwide, coinciding with the rise of obesity.

Industry observers note that research from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) projects that the number of people in the United States under age 20 with type 2 diabetes could reach 220,000 by 2060. This is an increase of 700%.

People diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at a younger age face more decades of living with the condition, along with a higher risk of developing complications earlier in life and reduced life expectancy. These complications can develop as early as midlife and include:.

Speak with a healthcare professional about your risk of type 2 diabetes and changes you might be able to make in order to prevent or delay diagnosis.

A later diagnosis can help reduce the risk of some complications of the condition.
