💡 Key Takeaways
  • Iceland’s first utility-scale wind farm comes with a useful perk: When the wind picks up, its hydropower reservoirs can save water for later.
  • Sources indicate that vaðölduver Wind Farm plugs straight into the existing Búrfell hydropower infrastructure, sharing 220 kV transmission lines, substations, and access roads.
  • Landsvirkjun, Iceland’s national power tech giant, officially commissioned Vaðölduver on September 15, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Iceland’s first utility-scale wind farm comes with a useful perk: When the wind picks up, its hydropower reservoirs can save water for later.

Sources indicate that vaðölduver Wind Farm plugs straight into the existing Búrfell hydropower infrastructure, sharing 220 kV transmission lines, substations, and access roads. And Iceland’s windiest months coincide with the time of year when less water flows into its reservoirs.

Landsvirkjun, Iceland’s national power tech giant, officially commissioned Vaðölduver on September 15, 2026. The first 14 turbines are online; another 14 will be installed in a second phase, and the entire wind farm is expected to be operating by the end of 2027.

In a recent development, once complete, Vaðölduver will have 120 megawatts (MW) of capacity. When I met with the folks at Landsvirkjun in Reykjavik last month, they told me that’s enough to power the equivalent of 90,000 Icelandic households. Vaðalda’s electricity feeds into the grid and is sold through power purchase agreements.

Recent findings suggest that vaðölduver sits on a lava-and-sand plain east of the Þjórsá River, south of Sultartangi Dam. Landsvirkjun already operates seven hydropower stations in the surrounding Þjórsá and Tungnaá region.

The wind farm was sited in this region of Iceland because the seasons line up nicely.

Recent findings suggest that the winds are strongest in winter, when inflows into hydropower reservoirs can be low. In summer, wind speeds tend to drop, but glacial melt increases water availability for the hydropower system.

When the wind turbines are generating plenty of electricity, Landsvirkjun can ease off hydropower and leave more water in its reservoirs. When the wind drops, hydropower can pick up more of the demand.

That gives the utility more control over when it uses its stored water and helps that water go further.

Sources indicate that german wind turbine maker Enercon manufactured Vaðölduver’s turbines. The project also includes a service and maintenance agreement with Enercon.

Landsvirkjun had a decade of experience operating pilot wind turbines before building Vaðölduver. One massive thing they learned: They didn’t need tall towers to find plenty of wind.

Industry observers note that there’s little vegetation or other surface obstructions across this unique, exposed landscape. That allows the turbines to capture productive winds closer to the ground than they could at a more wooded or sheltered location.

Sources indicate that “Lower” is relative, of course. The turbines still reach 150 meters (492 feet) at their highest blade tip.

The wind farm covers 17.1 square kilometers (6.6 square miles). Twenty-five turbines are rated at 4.26 MW each, and the remaining three at 4.5 MW. Landsvirkjun’s presentation puts annual generation at 440 GWh and lists a P50 net efficiency figure of 43%, which is considered strong for onshore wind.

Recent findings suggest that the ability to tap into existing infrastructure was a major factor in Landsvirkjun’s site selection. Where a wind farm goes affects its cost, its environmental footprint, and the people who live nearby.

Landsvirkjun also identifies active engagement with communities and other stakeholders as essential to building wind projects. At Vaðölduver, the immediate task is to finish the remaining 14 turbines while the first phase completes its trial runs.

It has been revealed that the tech giant sees wind as a potential third pillar of Iceland’s electricity supply alongside hydropower and geothermal. Vaðölduver shows how those resources can work together, with wind adding generation while helping conserve stored water.

In a recent development, iceland is a world leader in clean energy. It generates nearly 100% of its electricity from renewable sources, combining hydropower fueled by glacial runoff and rivers (around 70%) and geothermal energy (around 30%).

Over 90% of Icelandic households use direct geothermal hot water for space heating and hot water, while the remaining homes use renewable electricity.

Industry observers note that but it’s got the same grid capacity challenges as every other country. Adding wind – and anything else that uses power – means paying close attention to what the grid can handle. Iceland has an isolated transmission system, so maintaining stability and ensuring sufficient capacity are increasingly important as the country develops more projects.

While in Reykjavik, I met with the Minister of the Environment, Energy and Climate, Jóhann Páll Jóhannsson, who told me that the Icelandic grid’s capacity is expected to grow from 20 TWh to 24-25 TWh within a decade. Jóhannsson also noted that he is pro-data center and that investors are keen to establish more of them in the country.

Sources indicate that when I asked Jóhannsson and his team, as well as the teams at Landsvirkjun and publicly owned ON Power, Iceland’s second-largest electricity generator and largest EV charger network, about grid expansion aims to handle that pipeline, they all said that legislative reforms were being passed to speed up energy permitting processes. There is also financing in place to grow the grid. The physical transmission network is being expanded, but the process is slow because NIMBYism is creating bottlenecks.

In learning about new and completed Icelandic power projects during my visit, it was apparent that the companies in the power and geothermal heat sector regularly collaborate on projects – everyone brings their expertise to the table and works for the common good (yes, really).

It has been revealed that but what was striking in discussions about grid expansion was that there seemed to be no prepares to pitch in with the Icelandic transmission system operator (TSO), Landsnet hf. It seemed that the initiative was to let the TSO come up with the solutions on its own. At most, Jóhannsson’s team noted its legislative reform “opened the door” to possible grid innovations.

When I asked the Landsvirkjun team whether they were considering working with the TSO on distributed energy resource (DER) projects like virtual power plants and onsite battery storage for its heavy-industry clients, which make up 80% of its business, they said they hadn’t considered it.

I often wonder why Quebec hasn't followed this strategy. They have huge dams with world-leading power connections, and one of the issue they are facing is a lack of water to refill those dams, due to several years of relative drought. I know it costs a lot to build wind power up north, but siting a project there would re-use their massive investment in power lines. The dams would act as gigantic batteries, because they wouldn't need to drain their reservoirs when the wind is blowing.

It has been revealed that iceland has earned its reputation as a clean energy leader. Bringing that same collaborative and creative approach to expanding its grid would help it keep setting an example for the rest of the world.

Fiona the hippo remains under the watchful eyes of veterinarians and staff at the Cincinnati Zoo after swallowing a hat last week. As a full-grown hippo, surgery is not an option for Fiona, but her caretakers remain hopeful she will pass the foreign object naturally.

In a recent development, last week, a knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Given her size, zookeepers initially thought she’d simply pass the hat, but it remains stuck in her digestive track. She has undergone a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope and multiple ultrasounds that show intestinal bunching, indicating her body is continuing to try and expel the hat. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests.

Sources indicate that “Fiona ingested an object that a visitor accidentally tossed into her habitat,” the Cincinnati Zoo said in a statement. “Our veterinary team and hippo care staff are monitoring her around the clock and doing everything they can to help her pass the object safely. Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self. Fiona will remain off habitat until this is resolved. We will share updates as we have more information.”.

Recent findings suggest that the zoo also reminded patrons to be careful with their things when observing animals: “Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats. Ingesting foreign objects can cause serious health problems for animals. If something falls into a habitat, please notify a Zoo staff member immediately.”.

On Wednesday, November 18, the zoo shared a new approach in Fiona’s ongoing treatment: a vibration plate borrowed from a local Ohio horse farm. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers. “The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the team explained.

Recent findings suggest that fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. She was the smallest known hippo to survive such a low birth weight. As she grew, Fiona took social media and the real world by storm: she photobombed an engagement shoot, had a local ice cream named in her honor, and even starred in her own reality-TV series appropriately called “The Fiona Show.”  Her surprise baby brother Fritz was born in 2022, after their mother’s birth control went “on the fritz.”.

Industry observers note that this is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arc Raiders has received a newly introduced update today that’s almost entirely dedicated to balance and economy tweaks. Patch 1.3.0 arrived earlier across all platforms, coming in at just under 1GB. This is an especially interesting patch because many of the changes it makes can be seen as a response to player behaviour on Stella Montis, the game’s latest map, which just joined the roster last week.

Stella Montis is available for players who’ve put in a decent number of rounds, and its close-quarters, enclosed environments have essentially turned it into the new “PvP map”, where constant action can be found.

That, of course, also means that the map has exposed a few balance issues with some of the game’s weapons and tools. Case in point: the Venator, a pistol that saw a lot of use recently. The weapon is especially powerful when fully-upgraded, something Arc Raiders developer Embark said pushed it beyond what had been originally intended.

Sources indicate that in today’s revision, the Venator's fire rate is the thing getting hit the hardest, with each upgrade now offering slower gains to the weapon's rate-of-fire compared to the way things were. The weapon’s weight is also being increased to five from two.

Another powerful item players have been getting a lot of mileage out of recently has been the Deadline mine. Unlike the Venator, the Deadline is mainly a threat to Arc enemies, and it’s proven incredibly powerful against the largest and most fearsome, such as the Bastion, and Leaper. In fact, the mine was considered essential when taking down a Queen.

In a recent development, the patch vastly increases its purchase price, and makes it more difficult to craft by upping the amount each of its components requires. Perhaps the most effective nerf, however, is the reduction to the Deadline’s stock at traders from three to just one, which means you’re going to be seeing a lot less of it topside.

Beyond those specific changes, Embark has also tweaked explosive damage across the board. According to the developer, explosive damage was being applied to multiple parts at once, which trivialised some encounters.

This change mainly affects larger Arc units, such as the Bastion, allowing them to withstand more explosive damage before bits start coming off of them. The Hullcracker, one of the best explosive damage weapons, has also caught a nerf as part of that.

Recent findings suggest that check the official blog for the full change log for patch 1.3.0. If you’re just getting started with the hottest extraction shooter ever, our Arc Raiders tips offer plenty of help. You should also learn what all the different Map Conditions do in Arc Raiders, and how to best make use of each of them.

#87206. 6 Ways to Conquer Your Worst Fears

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1230 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

6 Ways to Conquer Your Worst Fears

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1230 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • According to recent reports, life presents many reasons to worry and fret, but there is one that universally affects everyone.
  • An area of research in psychology that goes back several decades tackles this fear head-on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

According to recent reports, life presents many reasons to worry and fret, but there is one that universally affects everyone. An inevitable aspect of life is that it will end, a reality that you face from the moment you’re old enough to realize death’s universality. The question is how much fear over this inevitability will interfere with your ability to appreciate what your life now has to offer.

An area of research in psychology that goes back several decades tackles this fear head-on. Death anxiety, as it is called, affects everyone, but to varying degrees. Why some people become obsessed with their mortality and others remain more placid over the whole matter is an concern at the heart of this field. Research and theories devoted to the understanding of death anxiety can provide insight into how to transform those who are obsessed with this fear into those who can approach their mortality with greater acceptance. A new paper by Holy Spirit of Kaslik (USEK)’s Ruth Younes and colleagues (2026) lays out the prominent theories of death anxiety, theories that can provide a guide to intervention.

Industry observers note that one theory receiving the greatest empirical support is terror management theory (TMT), whose name says it all. We fear death, the theory proposes, because we live in “terror” of our mortality. However, we can’t live our lives continually in terror, so instead we “manage” the fear by suppressing it. Once in a while, though, that suppression stops working, and we face mortality head-on.

It has been revealed that A second theory has its origins in Erikson’s psychosocial approach to lifespan development. Erikson proposed that at any time in life, but especially in later adulthood, we take what Younes et al. call a “retrospective look-back on life.” If people are able to look back not in anger, but with satisfaction, they can cope more successfully with mortality than if they believe they failed. “Ego integrity,” the positive resolution of this problem, means that you view life, and the inevitability of death, with acceptance. “Despair,” the opposite, means that you see yourself as a failure and wish you could have a do-over to fix the mistakes you made when you were younger.

Sources indicate that the third theory relevant to death anxiety is called gerotranscendence, and proposes that aging allows people to experience “transformative” shifts in their outlook on life. This occurs through the Cosmic dimension (deepening connection with the universe), the Self (unity and cohesion within the self), and Social/Personal relationship dimension (need for more selectiveness in social interactions). By developing these three qualities, individuals should experience less fear of death.

Through distilling the available literature, the USEK author team arrived at six common themes in interventions designed to mitigate death anxiety. They are as follows:.

According to recent reports, developed as an approach based on Erikson’s theory, reminiscence therapy uses the life review as its main tool. In life review, you return in time to the main events of your life and rework them from your present vantage point. Perhaps you jilted a lover who could have become your life partner by carelessly breaking things off over a silly argument. In retrospect, you ponder why you hurt this person so badly through this insensitivity. You can’t repair the damage, but you can gain perspective from your life as it unfolded since then. This breakup helped you learn to be kinder and to appreciate the importance of healing within close relationships.

According to recent reports, in this approach to therapy, people also relive their past, but they do so in an attempt to form an integrated “narrative” or story of their lives. Instead of reworking the past as in reminiscence therapy, you attempt to come back into awareness of it. As you do so, your life takes on shape and meaning. For example, you might try to prompt your recall of such events as the birth of your children and their early development up to the present. This allows you to piece back together events that you may have forgotten simply because your life was so busy at the time, balancing work and family demands.

Sources indicate that instead of rehashing the lows and highs of past events in your life, you might try instead to focus on the highs. This could be useful if reminiscence proves too painful. By starting with the positive, you can eventually confront the negative. Regarding yourself as someone who made good decisions in life, you may then approach the times you didn’t with greater self-compassion.

According to recent reports, this might not be something you should “try at home,” but insights from the way that psychodynamic theory works could be useful. Younes et al. mention, for example, the “grieving” process that people experience as they think about the end of their lives. Research on end-of-life complications suggests that people engage in anticipatory grief about their own lives as a way to come to greater acceptance. If you run from this form of grief, as TMT might suggest, it could come back to haunt you when you come much closer to your life’s end.

5. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy.

This is a form of therapy used for a number of psychological disorders in which an individual learns to accept distressing events and pain without avoidance. The “commitment” piece of this involves setting and acting toward your goals. Rather than run away from thoughts of death, you would therefore confront them and reflect on how you can live your life according to your values.

6. Dialectical Behavior Therapy.

An approach used in the treatment of people with borderline personality disorder (invented by the late Marsha Linehan), this therapy involves accepting your feelings and behaviors while also trying to change your behaviors. Again, you may not be able to do this on your own as a formal therapy, but the idea of rethinking your feelings and behaviors is very doable.

Recent findings suggest that each of the six ways of addressing death anxiety takes a slightly different slant on the processes of reflecting back on your life, reworking some old issues, and tackling fears of death through acceptance. The authors suggest that people vary in which approach works best for them.

Sources indicate that additional factors from the study that might influence the way you go about trying these yourself or with someone close to you include your age and health. A health scare, such as an acute cardiac event or bad news from a screening test, can set anyone off, regardless of age. On the other hand, social support can help you get through these and other tough times as you confront your feelings about mortality.

To sum up, death anxiety stems from the inevitability of our own mortality, but it need not be an inevitable feature of your mental health. Being able to recognize and work through these feelings can prepare you for whatever lies ahead.

Younes, R. S., Rahme, E., Rajha, F., & Abboud Mzawak, M. (2026). Exploring death anxiety among older adults: An integrative review of associated factors and interventions. Omega: Journal of Death and Dying, 93(3), 1799–1829. https://doi.org/10.1177/00302228241272578.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taking a vintage muscle car and swapping in modern components to make it run better or add power is a story as old as, well, the LS2 V-8. Vintage Modern’s new Fastback Mustang turns that formula upside down—by swapping old-school body parts onto a modern S650-generation Mustang GT. But the Vintage Modern Fastback, officially revealed on Wednesday at Retromobile New York, is more than just a body kit.

For starters, Ford’s standard 5.0-liter V-8 is mated here to a 3.0-liter Whipple supercharger for a total output of 840 horsepower and 615 lb-ft of torque. Prospective buyers can choose between a six-speed manual transmission with rev matching or a 10-speed automatic with steering-wheel-mounted paddle shifters. Other high-end Mustang features like active-valve performance exhaust with four sound modes, MagneRide adaptive suspension, six selectable drive modes, and Brembo performance brakes are also standard fare.

Industry observers note that “The Vintage Fastback is a car we’ve always wanted to build. We’ve blended classic-inspired design with modern safety, technology, and performance,” stated Chau Nguyen, founder and CEO of Vintage Modern. “This is what Vintage Modern was created to do.”.

Even though the bones of the Fastback are from a current-generation Mustang, the heavily modified vehicle still underwent crash testing to meet applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards. This retro-inspired Mustang features eight airbags, crumple zones, side-impact beams, electronic stability control, traction control, and anti-lock brakes. That’s more than most restomod Mustang owners can say.

It has been revealed that most of the custom body panels, including the functional hood scoop, are carbon fiber; the only obviously metal pieces are the billet-aluminum grille, door handles, mirrors, and twin auxiliary driving lights. Similarly, the interior of the retro Fastback build features Alcantara and billet-aluminum trim over three different seat upholsteries: pleated, diamond-quilted, or woven. Each buyer can choose from more than 40 standard paint colors, as well as paint-to-sample finishes and stripe options, along with their own interior configurations; Vintage Modern is also offering an optional JL Audio premium sound system and leather-trimmed floor mats.

Vintage Modern’s carbon-fiber body panels are hand-made in Detroit before being assembled and finished at its Atlanta facility; all told, each unit requires around 900 hours of hands-on labor. The builder has major aims, too; it says it has plans to move into a latest factory three times the size of its existing facility, hire more than 100 additional team members, and triple production capacity within two years.

No pricing details about the Vintage Modern Fastback were available at the time of publication, but we’ll update this story when we learn more.

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

According to recent reports, if you’re into personal audio, you might not want to spend all your money during Black Friday/Cyber Monday (but feel free to spend a little, and keep coming back here for some great suggestions as to how). Just within the last week, several innovative newly introduced headphones and earbuds have been confirmed, so read on for wired, wireless, and TWS options for every taste.

First up is Klipsch, the Hope, Arkansas-based heritage brand celebrating its 80th anniversary. But that doesn’t mean the acoustic design team is stuck in the past. Originally teased as Atlas at CES 2026 during a behind-closed-doors preview alongside powered standmount speakers and other surprises, the upcoming Stratos Series uses an atypical (for headphones) two-way coaxial array, which aligns a mid/bass driver with a dynamic tweeter on a single axis to deliver low-distortion, high-efficiency, full-range sound.

In a recent development, the 380g Klipsch HP-2 (above) is the closed-back option, with a 40mm bio-cellulose woofer and 10mm tweeter achieving a frequency response of 15 Hz-18 kHz (+/-5 dB), plus isolation for more critical monitoring. The 458g HP-3 (below, and the one we’re most excited to audition) is a semi-open-back design that expands the woofer to 50mm to make up for some of the low end typically traded for a more expansive soundstage, and it achieves 16 Hz-22 kHz (+/-5 dB). Both promise “warm, punchy bass and crisp, sparkly highs,” and the pre-production units I heard in January delivered a good bright/bouncy balance, with rich, fun-colored but still composed mids as I recall (though it’s been many months removed).

Both models have an appropriately mid-century modern aesthetic, with auburn-stained sapele wood earcups and copper accents, machined aluminum yokes and contact points, Klipsch Heritage Twitchell grille cloth, replaceable microseude earpads, and protein-leather-wrapped open-cell-foam-filled headbands. Both 4.4mm balanced and 3.5mm unbalanced cables (plus a 1/4-inch adapter) with dual-mono connectors are included.

While both the Stratos HP-2 and HP-3 can be paired with smartphones and dongles of all sorts, they’ll really open up with a more refined signal chain, like the simultaneously announced $649.99 Onkyo HA-70, featuring two premium ESS ES9039Q2M SABRE DACs feeding an amplifier with plentiful inputs and three gain settings versatile enough to drive sensitive IEMs to 600Ω flagship headphones.

Compared to Klipsch, Brooklyn’s Grado Labs is a relatively young’un at the spry age of 73. First (and still) known for decades of producing phono cartridges, the family-owned company expanded into distinctive, hand-built headphones in the late ’80s (and still produces some fabulous flagships). The GW200 carries that tradition into something you can carry. The 235g GW200 takes a 44m S paper-composite diaphragm derived from the drivers in the company’s multi-thousand-dollar Signature line and puts it in an open-back wireless headphone. This helps deliver expressive bass and treble articulation within a frequency response of 16Hz – 34kHz.

According to recent reports, being open-back means a more spacious presentation with more instrument separation than your typical Bluetooth headphone (at the expense of isolation, of course, so don’t expect these to stand in for ANC travel headphones). Helping ensure this is Bluetooth 5.4 with support for Qualcomm aptX Lossless, aptX Adaptive, aptX HD, aptX, AAC, and SBC, plus 60+ hours of battery life. And there’s a single-sided 3.5mm audio input for passive use in case the battery does run out (or you just prefer an external DAC/amp combo).

It has been revealed that as for comfort and tuning, the GW200 comes with the Grado Labs F Cushions but is compatible with Grado’s complete line, so you can change both the physical and sonic feel by swapping them. Another trickle-down from the Signature series is the padded leather headband, which goes nicely with the matte black finish. We’re looking forward to getting a pair to try out.

Over in eastern Texas, Noble Audio has been producing artisan IEMs since the early 2010s (and founder John Moulton was doing custom in-ear monitors for enthusiasts even before that). In recent years, the organization has been showing what’s possible when the multiple-driver mentality of IEMs (some costing many thousands of dollars) is turned to portable audio, and the Astrid is the latest example. A tribrid architecture featuring an 8.3mm dynamic driver with a PU diaphragm and an aluminum-magnesium alloy dome, a 6mm planar driver, and one balanced armature in each earpiece, the Astrid brings a wired configuration and sophistication to true wireless earbuds.

Industry observers note that the overall tonality of the Astrid is rich, full-bodied, but not boomy … punch but not paunch. While sitting beneath the company’s top TWS model, the 4-driver Prestige Encore, Astrid still delivers a detailed soundstage. What really brings the best out of it is the Audiodo Personal Sound feature, which uses a short tone recognition test to test each ear and saves per-channel adjustments on the earbuds to make up for any anatomically incurred frequency range deficiencies. Then Audiodo Equalizer lets you address sensitivities/preferences, overlaying further adjustments on your personalized curve (3-band on iOS, 5-band on Android). There’s also an assessment-independent 10-band EQ if that level of control is more your vibe.

To ensure the most cohesive playback possible, there’s multipoint Bluetooth 6.0 with high-resolution LDAC/aptX Adaptive support for compatible devices, as well as AAC and SBC. Plus active noise cancellation. Battery life is rated up to 11 hours on a single charge, with the wireless/USB-C case bringing the total carry capacity to 40 hours. All that is wrapped in IPX4 ABS enclosures featuring “divinely beautiful” glass fiber faceplates adorned with a dense lattice of silver filigree, like electro-acoustic etching … a metallic polyphony of colliding chords and intersecting transients.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, jupiter joins US solar panel recycler Solarcycle and PedalPoint Recycling, Korea Zinc’s US recycling and metals business, into a single, fully integrated organization.
  • For a solar farm or data center operator, that means a single firm can take equipment out of service, resell parts with remaining useful life, and recycle the rest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that old solar panels have silver and copper worth recovering. A new US recycling company called Jupiter intends to send metals recovered from retired solar panels and data center hardware to Korea Zinc’s refineries, including a $7.4 billion plant planned for Clarksville, Tennessee.

According to recent reports, jupiter joins US solar panel recycler Solarcycle and PedalPoint Recycling, Korea Zinc’s US recycling and metals business, into a single, fully integrated organization. Jupiter claims it’s launching with eight certified US facilities, nearly 1 million square feet of processing space, and about 250 employees. It’s also taking on customers from both businesses, including Microsoft, Prologis, and Brookfield.

For a solar farm or data center operator, that means a single firm can take equipment out of service, resell parts with remaining useful life, and recycle the rest. Customers can track where the materials go and bring them back into their own supply chains.

It has been revealed that korea Zinc will hold a majority stake. Solarcycle’s Suvi Sharma will lead Jupiter as CEO, and PedalPoint’s Kevin Hahm will be CFO. Microsoft and Prologis Ventures are among Solarcycle’s existing investors.

It has been revealed that as Electrek reported in January, Solarcycle’s Cedartown, Georgia, plant was processing thousands of old solar panels a week when it opened. Solarcycle remarked the plant could handle up to 5 gigawatts’ worth of panels annually at full capacity, recovering materials such as glass, aluminum, copper, and silver.

The Tennessee plant adds a US refining step. Korea Zinc is developing the facility, called Project Crucible, with US government backing. It expects to start production in phases in 2029. The plant is designed to process about 1.1 million tons of raw materials per year and produce roughly 540,000 tons of finished products.
